#3208. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

Max G. Levy is an independent science journalist based in Los Angeles. His work has appeared in Wired, Quanta Magazine, and MIT Technology Review.

This is a tantalizing, multidisciplinary technology, but the latency issue seems really important. It seems like once they're through the medical hoops national telecoms regulators will have to figure out whether the necessary connections as emergency or critical infrastructure that deserve special spectrum allocation or similar, especially since this seems to have the most promise in more rural or remote settings.

#3207. Leaker claims Apple developing four models of 20th anniversary iPhone

Leaker Ice Universe says Apple is currently developing four models of the 20th anniversary iPhone which we’ve been referring to as the iPhone 20. We’re expecting next year’s flagship models to be a radical new design with an all-glass appearance.

Why four models rather than two is unclear, but it seems possible Apple is testing two versions of both the Pro and the Pro Max to determine just how ambitious it can be with the final product …

Didn’t the iPhone 6 or the iPhone 11 already have a curved front glass?

Ice Universe says that two of the four models have quad-curved glass backs and two have flat glass. They indicate that Apple has already had to ramp back its ambitions with the curvature.

Apple is currently developing four models in total: two with flat glass backs and two with quad-curved glass backs. Apple has been prototyping this quad-curved design for three years, making several revisions along the way—particularly regarding the glass curvature, which is still being refined. The earliest version had a very pronounced curve; it was later reduced somewhat.

It’s standard practice for Apple to develop multiple competing prototypes of new devices, evaluating them for everything from usability and durability to ease of manufacturing.

We’re expecting Apple to use a combination of ultra-thin bezels and curved glass to create the illusion of no bezels at all – a more sophisticated version of the effect seen on the Apple Watch. Today’s report says the bezels are around 1mm thick.

The curved edges on the quad-curved version are approximately 1mm wide. However, because the glass curves around all sides, when viewed straight on from the front, the bezel becomes nearly invisible, creating a near‑borderless appearance. The actual visual effect could be quite stunning.

We yesterday saw an AI-generated render of what the design could look like. It’s expected to be the biggest redesign of the standard iPhone since the iPhone X.

#3206. Anthropic shares jump 34% at open in record Nasdaq debut

The Claude maker opened at $111.50, a bigger first-day pop than SpaceX got in June.

Anthropic’s shares opened at $111.50 on Nasdaq on Thursday, 34% above the $83 IPO price, valuing it at more than $2T, per Business Insider. The company raised $107.3B with its IPO and a private placement, the largest listing on record.

Anthropic’s shares opened at $111.50 on Nasdaq on Thursday, 34% above their $83 IPO price, Business Insider reported. The jump, bigger than the 27% grey markets had pointed to, valued the Claude maker at more than $2T. The stock trades under the ticker ANT.

Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the opening bell with staff earlier in the day. By midday in New York, the shares had eased to about $107, still up nearly 29%, according to Bloomberg data.

The open beat SpaceX’s debut in June. SpaceX, which priced its IPO at $135 a share, opened 11% higher and closed its first day up 19%.

Anthropic raised about $81B by selling shares at $83 on Wednesday, above its $70 to $78 range. It is also raising $26B from a private placement at the same price, with Alphabet, Microsoft and Nvidia among the buyers. Together, that makes $107.3B, the biggest IPO on record.

The debut lifted the wider market, with the Nasdaq Composite up more than 1% after the open. As the first big pure-play AI stock, Anthropic is likely to be watched as a test of investors’ appetite for AI.

Not everyone is convinced. In October, research firm New Constructs said Anthropic might be worth as little as $144B. On Wednesday, a group of scientists signed a statement calling it “not a safe AI company”.

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

#3201. iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2 get new release timing updates

Apple only launched high-end ‘Pro’ and ‘Duo’ iPhones this fall, marking a departure from previous years when more affordable models debuted too. But iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are still coming, and a new report offers an update on release timing.

A new report from Kim Yeong-ho at ETNews provides a fresh update on timing for the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2.

Rumors have indicated for well over a year that Apple planned to push these models out of the typical fall launch window and introduce them in early 2027 instead.

Per ETNews, Samsung and LG are providing the display panels for the new models, with Samsung the sole supplier for iPhone Air 2 and both companies splitting orders for iPhone 18. And their mass production plans signal a March release for the products.

Samsung Display plans to begin mass production in January, while LG Display will start late this year…The Korean panel makers appear to be aligning their production plans with an expected March launch.

A March launch window lines up well with when Apple tends to ramp up product introductions following a slower winter. Earlier this year, iPhone 17e debuted in March alongside new Macs and the iPad Air.

The year before, however, the iPhone 16e arrived in February instead.

With Apple shaking up its normal iPhone rollout schedule, it was anyone’s guess how soon the new models would debut. But a March launch makes sense and gives Apple a trio of new iPhones every six months—three unveiled in September, and another three in March.

Are you holding out for an iPhone 18 or iPhone Air 2? Let us know in the comments.

#3200. Model ML raises $250m at a $1.5bn valuation for bankers’ AI agents

Model ML’s annual recurring revenue grew 12 times in a year. Its CEO says the startup’s AI agents now help banks earn money, and are no longer just tools that save time.

Model ML co-founders Chaz and Arnie Englander in London.

Model ML, a London startup that builds AI agents for bankers, consultants and investors, has raised $250m at a $1.5bn valuation. General Atlantic and QED Investors co-led the Series B round, the company said on Tuesday.

Evolution Equity Partners, Airtree, Forestay Capital, Y Combinator, FT Partners, Latitude, Inception Fund and 13Books Capital also took part. The round takes Model ML’s total funding to $350m. FT Partners led its $75m Series A in November 2025, and HSBC Asset Management invested in August.

In the third quarter, Model ML’s annual recurring revenue grew 12 times year on year and its daily active users rose 26 times, the company said. It will use the money to grow its research and engineering teams in London and New York.

Brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander founded Model ML in 2023, Bloomberg reported. They previously co-founded Fat Llama, a rental marketplace that Sweden’s Hygglo bought for $41.5m in 2022, TechCrunch reported.

Each user gets an agent that runs on the firm’s own systems and data. When news breaks on a company a banker covers, the agent judges whether it matters and prepares the analysis in the firm’s formats. It works in tools such as Excel and PowerPoint to build pitch decks and due diligence reports.

“AI should do more than give you another answer or notification. It should understand your work and get things done,” said Chaz Englander, Model ML’s co-founder and CEO.

Model ML sends each task to the AI model that suits it best. A growing share runs on its own fine-tuned open-source models. On the work they handle, these cost 2% as much as frontier models and are in most cases five times faster, the company said. It added that customer data is never used to train AI models.

Banks have tied job cuts to AI. Barclays said in October it would cut 5,000 jobs, and Standard Chartered plans to cut 7,800 jobs in back-office roles by 2030. Englander played down the idea that Model ML is mainly a way to cut costs.

“The average age of a Model ML user is 33 years old, not 23 years old,” Englander told Bloomberg. “These tools are no longer productivity and efficiency tools. They’re revenue generative.”

Revenue is split fairly evenly across banks, consulting firms and asset managers, he said. Model ML’s rivals include New York’s Rogo, which raised $160m at a $2bn valuation in April. OpenAI and Anthropic also sell AI tools to financial professionals.

#3199. iPhone Duo is getting three new features in iOS 27.3

iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo users one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

If your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most users, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

On a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

You can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great new option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a new setting so users can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

By default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

It’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and new keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:

iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how

#3195. Google’s Gemini can now take over tasks on your Mac

Google's assistant works in a background window, but it can also delete or share files by mistake.

Google’s Gemini assistant can now take over tasks on a Mac, clicking through apps, typing and filling in forms for you. Google announced on Thursday that computer use is rolling out in the Gemini app for Mac.

You describe a task, and Gemini works through it across local files, desktop apps and websites. It runs in a separate background window with a live preview in the chat, so your screen and cursor stay free. You choose which apps it can use, can pause it, and must approve key actions.

Google’s examples include pulling weights and addresses from PDFs into a shipping quote form, and turning dashboard data into a Google Slides deck. It can also batch-edit photos or prepare resale listings from pictures in a folder.

Google warns that Gemini can make mistakes, including permanently deleting files or sharing them with others. It is designed to ask permission first, and it can only see folders you connect. Backups of changed files are deleted after 24 hours or when you start a new task.

Google is also building Gemini into the operating system of its Googlebook laptops, as rivals race to put agents on the desktop. OpenAI’s ChatGPT can log your keystrokes on a Mac to build its memory. Agents built on the OpenClaw framework have helped drive Mac mini demand.

#3194. Anthropic IPO Live — everything you need to know about the $1.5 trillion AI giant

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Anthropic, the AI giant behind Claude, is officially entering an IPO with aggressive stock prices set at $83 share, though it's expected to begin trading at $110 per shared based investor interest.

The company recently reported third quarter revenue of $17 billion, the IPO values the company at trillions more.

At the same time, Anthropic's public stock debut comes at a strange time in the AI industry. Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang just resigned after accusations of affairs and being in a spy web.

AI stocks in general have taken huge hits in the last few weeks. Plus, Anthropic faces major competition from its main rival OpenAI as well as from Google and Meta.

Now the market will determine if Anthropic is as viable as CEO Dario Amodei thinks it is.

Claude might be best known as a ChatGPT competitor, but Anthropic's biggest opportunity may be inside the workplace.

According to the company's IPO prospectus, more than half of Fortune 500 companies were Anthropic customers generating at least $100,000 in revenue over the preceding 12 months as of September 30, 2026.

Anthropic also reported more than 1,900 customers generating at least $1 million in revenue over the same period, along with approximately 250 generating $10 million or more.

Those numbers offer a glimpse into why investors are willing to value the company so highly.

Businesses are using Claude for everything from software development to document analysis, insurance underwriting and cybersecurity. Unlike a consumer paying $20 per month for Claude Pro, large organizations can spend millions annually as they expand their use of AI.

Anthropic's success with Claude Code has also helped it establish a strong foothold among developers.

For everyday users, this is important because the next generation of Claude features may focus more on work rather than casual conversations like a typical chatbot.

Anthropic's historic IPO is attracting enormous excitement from investors, but buried in the company's financial disclosures is a warning about the technology making it so valuable.

Advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic warned in its IPO filing.

It's a striking admission from a company seeking billions of dollars from investors to develop increasingly powerful AI systems.

Anthropic has long positioned itself as a company focused on AI safety. Its founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, previously worked at OpenAI before launching their own AI research company in 2021.

But even Anthropic acknowledges that testing advanced AI models has limitations. In its IPO prospectus, the company warned that AI systems could develop unexpected capabilities during training, and that some potential dangers might not become apparent until after deployment.

These aren't predictions that an AI disaster is inevitable, but they are risks the company believes investors need to understand. For users like you and me, the warning highlights the challenges facing AI developers as chatbots become more capable than ever of taking actions, writing software and handling sensitive information.

Anthropic's IPO is a financial milestone, but its safety disclosures are a reminder that the technology's long-term consequences remain uncertain.OpenAI said they waited to file IPO for safety reasons.

Anthropic just became a $2 trillion company, but does that mean Claude users should expect to pay more? Not necessarily.

For now, Anthropic's IPO doesn't automatically change the price of a Claude subscription.

Claude still offers a free version, while its Pro subscription costs $20 per month, or about $17 per month with annual billing. The company also offers higher-priced plans for people who need more extensive access to its AI models.

However, running powerful AI systems is expensive. Every conversation, coding session and complex research task requires computing resources.

As a public company, Anthropic will face greater scrutiny over its revenue, expenses and ability to become sustainably profitable.

That could influence future decisions about subscriptions, usage limits and premium features, although there's no evidence that the IPO itself will trigger an immediate price increase.

What might happen, is competitors might offer more, for less. ChatGPT already offers unlimited chatting, but we might see more Pro options among the free tier. This is something to watch for from Anthropic's biggest competitors.

Anthropic's blockbuster IPO is a major moment for the AI industry, but it also raises a question that has nothing to do with the stock market. If AI is becoming so powerful, what does this mean for the future of work?

The company behind Claude is developing technology that can already write code, analyze documents, conduct research and complete tasks that previously required human employees. And Anthropic's own research offers an interesting glimpse into how that could change the workplace.

In a recent study of its employees, the company found that coding-focused AI agent sessions among nontechnical workers increased dramatically, from two per month in August 2025 to 90 in May 2026.

The research also found signs of slowing junior employment in roles that use Claude for particularly complex tasks, although that doesn't establish that AI caused the slowdown.

Anthropic's IPO gives the company additional resources to expand its models and workplace tools. For employees, that could mean more opportunities to automate repetitive work, but it also raises concerns about which tasks companies will continue paying people to perform.

As we know, AI has already entered the workplace, so for now, it's about how quickly businesses adopt these tools and whether workers benefit from the productivity gains.

Anthropic just became one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies. But does its enormous valuation mean Claude is better than ChatGPT?

The answer depends on what you're asking AI to do. Claude has built a strong reputation among developers, particularly through Claude Code, which can help write, debug and work with code across software projects.

It's also a popular choice for writing, analyzing documents and working through complex problems.

ChatGPT, meanwhile, offers an extensive collection of consumer-facing features, including image generation, voice conversations, research tools and coding capabilities through Codex.

Both companies are continually releasing new models and features, making it difficult to declare one chatbot the overall winner.

And Anthropic's IPO valuation isn't a measurement of Claude's intelligence. But it does reflect what investors are willing to pay for a stake in the business and their expectations about its future growth.

Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT or Claude, many people use these tools interchangeably, so the question isn't which one is better, but how can I best use each one.

Not everyone is celebrating Anthropic's blockbuster IPO. One AI CEO believes the company is making a massive bet on infrastructure that could eventually become obsolete.

David Stout, co-founder and CEO of webAI, is questioning Anthropic's valuation after the company priced its IPO at $83 per share.

"Anthropic's IPO asks public investors to bet that the future of AI belongs to whoever spends the most to centralize it," Stout said in a statement shared with Amanda Caswell.

His biggest concern is Anthropic's nearly $900 billion in computing and infrastructure commitments, some extending through 2045.

Stout argues that cloud-based AI becomes more expensive as people use it more, while AI running directly on phones, laptops and other devices could eventually offer a cheaper alternative.

"Anthropic is asking investors to pour billions into an infrastructure model that AI itself is making obsolete," he said.

There's an important catch to his argument. Smaller AI models are becoming more capable, but running the most powerful models locally still presents significant technical challenges.

For investors, the debate raises a question about Anthropic's future. Can the company generate enough demand for Claude to justify decades of infrastructure spending, or will cheaper alternatives eventually change the economics of AI?

Anthropic may be worth more than $2 trillion, but the company behind Claude is offering some businesses discounts of more than 30% to keep them from switching to ChatGPT.

According to a new report from The Information, Anthropic is offering aggressive discounts and credits worth as much as $100,000 to encourage companies to adopt its growing lineup of AI products.

The catch? Some businesses must commit to spending a certain percentage of their overall AI budgets on Anthropic. The company has reportedly started requesting invoices and other documents to verify that customers are meeting those commitments.

It's an interesting strategy for a company celebrating a historic IPO. Claude Code helped Anthropic become a major force in AI, but the company now wants to bring Claude into more workplaces through tools for finance, marketing, human resources and cybersecurity.

That puts Anthropic in direct competition with OpenAI, Microsoft and Google, all fighting for a larger share of corporate AI spending.

For everyday Claude users, these discounts aren't necessarily coming to individual subscriptions. But the competition could eventually mean more capable AI tools and better pricing.

Anthropic now has a massive valuation to justify, and winning over businesses beyond software development could be critical to its next chapter.

#3192. Arista Networks vs. Palantir Technologies: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Arista's 40% net margin and zero debt stack up against Palantir's 87% revenue surge, but the valuation gap may decide which one fits your portfolio.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 19, 2026 at 1:13PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Arista Networks ›

As the race for artificial intelligence dominance accelerates, investors are comparing the infrastructure backbone and the software brains. Should you bet on Arista Networks (ANET -1.64%) or Palantir Technologies (PLTR -1.17%) for 2027?

Arista Networks specializes in high-speed networking equipment for data centers, while Palantir Technologies provides advanced data analytics and decision-making platforms. Both companies are primary beneficiaries of the current spending boom in the artificial intelligence industry. Comparing them requires looking at how they balance hyper-growth against high valuation multiples in a rapidly shifting competitive landscape.

Arista Networks designs and sells data-driven networking systems for large AI, cloud, and routing environments. The company serves internet giants and specialty cloud providers. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as two significant end customers represented nearly 16% and 26% of total revenue in 2025. This focus allows Arista Networks to remain a top choice for investors seeking high-growth tech stocks.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $11.9 billion, representing a growth of roughly 40.7% compared to the prior period. During this same time frame, the company recorded a net income of approximately $4.8 billion. This resulted in a net margin of roughly 40%, reflecting the company's ability to turn a significant portion of its sales into profit.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.0x. This measure compares total debt to shareholder equity, and a ratio of 0.0x indicates the company has no debt. The current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets, was approximately 3.0x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $4.3 billion, which is the cash remaining after paying for operations and capital expenditures.

Palantir Technologies builds software platforms like Gotham and Foundry that help organizations integrate and secure complex data. The company derives revenue from both commercial and government clients, often forming deep partnerships with global system integrators. Note that its top three customers accounted for nearly 16% of total revenue in 2025. It continues to expand its presence by helping enterprises deploy its AI-focused platforms for real-world decision-making.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $7.3 billion. This represents revenue growth of roughly 87.1% compared to the previous 12-month period. The company also reported a net income of about $3.7 billion during this time frame. This helped the business achieve a net margin of approximately 50.3%.

As of the December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.0x, indicating a lack of total debt. The current ratio was roughly 7.1x, providing a substantial cushion for meeting short-term obligations. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was around $2.1 billion. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 32% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Arista Networks faces risks from its significant revenue concentration among a small number of cloud and AI giants. These customers have immense bargaining power and can vary their capital spending cycles with little notice. Furthermore, the company relies heavily on Broadcom Inc. (AVGO -1.76%) for silicon components. Any supply chain disruptions or lead-time issues with this primary vendor could impact its ability to deliver hardware on time.

Palantir Technologies operates with long and unpredictable sales cycles, particularly when dealing with massive government contracts and large enterprise deals. The company also faces intense competition from established software firms like Microsoft Corp. (MSFT -1.15%) and Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN -3.54%), as well as in-house development teams. There is also a level of reputational risk given the sensitive nature of its government work and the public scrutiny surrounding its leadership.

Arista Networks appears to be the more conservative value choice, as its valuation multiples are significantly lower than the premiums currently demanded for Palantir Technologies.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Palantir started out as a tech contractor to the U. S. military, and the federal government still accounts for half of revenue. But the business has been successfully expanding beyond government work, with about a quarter of sales coming from international customers and a significant minority of revenue from the private sector. For the first time last quarter, private sector revenue exceeded U.S. government revenue.

Palantir says customers are drawn to its "sovereign AI," which is its term for systems that can help build themselves while protecting what makes each system the AI is refining, so it is not commoditized. Companies like Nvidia Corp. (NVDA -2.21%) and L3Harris Technologies (LHX +0.26%) are notable customers of Palantir's sovereign AI.

The boom in private-sector AI business should double Palantir's sales in 2026 to $8.6 billion, with a $2.7 billion jump in net income to $4.4 billion. 2027 should see continued fast growth, with consensus analysts' estimates projecting revenue of $13.1 billion and net income over $6 billion.

Arista Networks, meanwhile, is experiencing strong demand for its Ethernet solutions as AI drives growth in cloud networking. Cloud Titans, a term for the largest AI operations, increased their spending by 30% in 2025 after a 30% increase in 2024. Arista is a big beneficiary of their spending and should continue to be. In addition to double-digit revenue growth for Arista from Titans, the company is seeing strong momentum in the Arista campus and mainstream switching and routing markets as it introduces and updates a slew of product offerings targeting those operations.

For fiscal 2026, revenue is expected to jump nearly 40% to $12.6 billion, with net income rising by a similar margin to $4.9 billion.

The top-line growth of Palantir is difficult to ignore, but its shares trade at an exceptional premium that may not account for the long-term threat of AI displacing its business. Arista trades at a cheaper relative valuation and still offers strong AI growth exposure, driven by demand for its networking hardware. The better bet in 2027 is Arista stock.

#3190. The Apple executive behind the iPhone’s Camera app has left

He argued photos should show real moments, as rivals lean into AI image editing.

Jon McCormack, Apple’s head of camera and photo software, retired at the end of October after more than eight years, Bloomberg reported. Apple has not named a replacement, and his deputies are taking over his work under other executives.

Jon McCormack, the Apple executive in charge of the iPhone’s Camera and Photos software, has retired, Bloomberg reported on Thursday. He left at the end of October after more than eight years at the company, according to people familiar with the matter.

Apple has not named a new vice president for his role. His former deputies are taking on his work under other executives, Bloomberg said. An Apple spokesperson declined to comment.

McCormack oversaw the software behind how iPhone users take, view and edit photos and videos. His team worked on the redesigned selfie camera in the iPhone 17 and the new camera controls this year, when the iPhone 18 Pro got Apple’s first variable-aperture camera.

He was a strong opponent of using generative AI to create or alter photos, people inside Apple told Bloomberg. Google and Samsung have leaned into AI tools that can make big changes to images.

“A photograph is of something that actually happened,” McCormack told Wired earlier this year.

Unlike its rivals, Apple added a mode that lets the iPhone 18 Pro prove photos are real. Bloomberg’s sources said his retirement was not linked to any clash over Apple’s AI strategy.

McCormack reported to software chief Craig Federighi, whose team is under pressure to speed up AI work. He follows Apple Pay head Jennifer Bailey out the door this autumn, as new CEO John Ternus cuts management layers to move faster.

#3184. Microsoft says MAI Code 2 matches 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price

MAI Code 2’s price comparisons use a launch discount that ends in May 2027. Microsoft will also let trusted customers license its model weights and customise them with their own data.

Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI, speaks at Microsoft Ignite 2026 in San Francisco, 17 November 2026.

Microsoft has released MAI Code 2, an in-house coding model. It says the model delivers 98% of the performance of OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price.

The company presented it at its Ignite conference in San Francisco on Tuesday. New models for security and image editing launched alongside it.

Against Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, Microsoft says MAI Code 2 gives 96% of the performance at 5% of the cost. The figures are averages across four coding benchmarks that Microsoft chose.

Both comparisons use a launch price. A footnote to Microsoft AI’s announcement says the cost is shown at a 50% promotional rate. That rate runs until 17 May 2027, GitHub’s pricing page shows. After that, input tokens rise from $0.50 to $1 per million. Output tokens rise from $2.50 to $5 per million.

MAI Code 2 and a smaller model, MAI Code 2 Flash, are available in GitHub Copilot. Microsoft says Flash matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the price. It matches Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 at 20%.

Mustafa Suleyman, chief executive of Microsoft AI, led the launch on stage.

“Right now, token spend is going through the roof,” Suleyman said, describing what he hears from CIOs and CFOs.

Microsoft says both coding models are not yet tuned for harder problems. Those include fundamental science research and very long agentic work.

Microsoft is also building a general-purpose frontier model, Suleyman told Axios. He said the company has reached state-of-the-art pre-training results. It is also making strong progress in reinforcement learning. He gave no release date.

“My team is building true superintelligence,” Suleyman told Axios.

He gave no target for how much Copilot traffic will move to Microsoft’s own models. He predicted significant adoption.

MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model, beats OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Suleyman said. It does so at less than 2% of the cost per task. A larger MAI Cyber 2 is in preview inside MDASH, Microsoft’s agentic code scanner.

MAI Image 2.7 is now the top image editing model, Suleyman said. It costs a fifth of what its rivals charge.

Microsoft is also launching MAI Licensed Weights. Trusted customers can take a Microsoft AI model and customise it with their own data. They then run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Company team.

Suleyman told Axios the approach would “feel like open source” with more security and control.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into somebody else’s model,” Suleyman said on stage.

AT&T built a custom version of Code 2 Flash. It beats GPT-6.1 Sol at standard 5G network analysis and costs 50 times less, according to Suleyman.

Microsoft still sells OpenAI and Anthropic models. Satya Nadella announced OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 for Microsoft Foundry on the same stage. Earlier, Microsoft’s commercial chief pitched Copilot as cheaper than ChatGPT and Claude.

Microsoft cut back Claude Code licences for its own engineers in May over token costs. In September, Suleyman took on Anthropic over how it trains Claude.

#3183. Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple responds]

The Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable users to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow users to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed users to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”

A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of New Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta said they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

Update, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:

“We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for users. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

Just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

The company added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the company said does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

As for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The company said that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

Every once in a while, Instagram rolls out an update that addresses one of its users’ most longstanding requests. Today is one of those days.

This means users will be able to add stickers and drawings, fix typos or adjust text, and even change the music without having to delete the Story and publish it again, which would mean losing any views it had already received.

Today’s update is the latest in a series of changes Instagram has made this year to address longstanding user requests.

Back in March, the app introduced the ability to reorder photos and videos in a carousel after publishing. In April, it added an option to edit comments (also within 15 minutes of posting), and in June, it began letting users manually rearrange posts on their profile grid.

More recently, Instagram also brought its free Edits video editor to the Mac, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, and 4K exports.
