Thereafter, the rig may undertake drilling or accommodation activities subject to the customer operational requirements. Collectively, these awards demonstrate the strength of our commercial execution across diverse set of markets.

Despite subdued contracting activity in the Middle East, we continue to add work at a pace that exceeds the backlog consumed, maintaining a positive book-to-bill ratio in 2026, both in days and in value. Importantly, these commitments have increased forward visibility across our portfolio. Following the recent awards, our 2026 coverage currently stands at 79% with an average day rate of approximately $133,000 per day. Looking to 2027, we secured more than 50% of the contract coverage at an average day rate of approximately $137,000 a day. In the Middle East, the prolonged conflict and uncertainty surrounding has resulted in reduction in activity.

Since the onset of the conflict, the count has declined by four rigs, excluding the impact of all suspensions of Saudi Aramco. At the same time, important tender activities continue in the region. Several key tenders have recently progressed to award, while the Saudi Aramco tender remains ongoing. This demonstrates that customers remain shallow water portfolio, and substantial underlying drilling requirements remain in the region. However, while we expect recovery towards pre-conflict, the persistent conflict continues to lead the timing and pace of their recovery. In Southeast Asia, contract activity continues to develop positively. Since the end of Q2, the count has increased by absorbing much of the previously idle supply.

This is driven primarily by Vietnam, with contracting activities in Malaysia also beginning to strengthen. While competitive pressure on pricing remains, our team has done well filling near-term availability for continued deployment. Looking ahead, we anticipate some near-term availability on the Mist and the Skald as their current contracts conclude during our regional monsoon season. However, we see a healthy pipeline of opportunities for both units as we move towards the middle part of the year. As broader market utilization continues to tighten, we believe the region has potential to support an improving rate environment through 2027.

In Mexico, the contracted rig count has increased by six rigs since the end of Q2, with previously available rigs from local contractors now being largely absorbed. Mexican oil production remains below the government's stated ambitions, reinforcing our views that additional drilling activity will ultimately be required. Our relationship with international operators, together with our strong local partnership, provide us with a solid position in a market that has further capacity to grow. Importantly, we have also made progress deploying our expanded fleet. Earlier this year, through BC Ventures, our joint venture with our local partners, we acquired five rigs from Fontis. At the time of the acquisition, only one was employed.

By the completion of the transaction in July, the joint venture had secured additional commitments, and today, three rigs are contracted for drilling, while a fourth is employed for accommodation, with line of sight to return to drilling work in the coming months. We expect these four rigs to remain contracted for most of 2027, while the fifth remains stacked, with active customer discussions around potential reactivation. Elsewhere in Americas, the Skald is now expected to finish its campaign with Petronas in early 2027. While we are exploring multiple opportunities in the region, we expect idle periods for the rig following the Petronas campaign. In the North Sea, we now have all of our three rigs on contract.

Operators in the region continue to navigate permitting and regulatory challenges, which limits visibility around meaningful new commitments. Based on the current opportunity pipeline, we expect regional utilization to remain relatively stable through 2027. In West Africa, contract activity remains robust, with Nigeria continuing to drive demand for both international and indigenous operators. Our recent award for the Hild, which was previously idle, reflects the strength in demand environment. More specifically, we are tracking a substantial pipeline of opportunities in Nigeria that could represent incremental demand of more than five rigs.

While we do not expect every opportunity to materialize on schedule, the breadth of the pipeline gives us increased confidence that Nigeria market will require additional rigs by the end of 2027. We are also seeing [inaudible] investment activities elsewhere in North Africa, reinforcing our constructive view for the broader region. Turning to China, one of the largest consumers of modern jack-ups globally, with nearly 60 units contracted today. Industry sources indicate a requirement for up to six incremental jack-ups for local deployment.

With limited readily available domestic capacity and low new build order book, we anticipate most of this demand may need to be met acquiring modern jack-ups from the international fleet, which will be another positive catalyst for a ready tight in global market. Taken together, these developments reinforce our constructive view on the jack-up market. Outside the Middle East, demand continues to improve and is steadily absorbing available capacity across several key regions. In the Middle East, underlying requirements remain, but the ongoing conflict continues to obscure the timing of that demand. Should it materialize, it will be further supportive to the pace of the global recovery.

From a macro perspective, based on industry research, the combination of depleted inventory, lower spare capacity, as well as persistent logistical and refining constraints has raised the structural floor for oil price, supporting future investments across the upstream sector. We believe shallow water resources are well-placed in this environment, given their economically attractive and short cycle barrels. With that, let me close with three key takeaways. First, regarding the Prospector 5, our immediate priority remains supporting those affected by the incident. The independent investigation is ongoing, and we remain committed to understanding exactly what occurred, applying the findings appropriately across our organization, and sharing the learnings with the industry. Second, we remain positive on the outlook for jack-ups.

Demand visibility is improving across several regions outside of the Middle East. Contract durations are lengthening, and available supply is gradually being absorbed. Market utilization is already 93%, a healthy level that provides a strong starting point for pricing appreciation as further demand volume materializes. We remain cautious on the timing of this recovery given market volatility. Our higher fleet availability in the first half of 2027 means near-term performance will lag, but it also gives us meaningful upside as the market tightens through the year. Third, the company's strong liquidity position provides the financial flexibility to capitalize on opportunities as the market recovers. With that, I will now turn the call over to Q&A.

Operator: Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star one again. Once again, please press star one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star one again. We are now going to proceed with our first question. The question comes from the line of Doug Becker from Capital One. Please ask your question.

Doug Becker: Thank you. Bruno, I would also like to extend my deepest sympathies to those affected by the Prospector 5 incident. With that in mind, insurance is set to pay out $200 million by late November this year. Could you just expand on the requirements to repay debt with some of those proceeds, and then the preliminary thoughts on applying payouts toward CapEx and investments going forward?

Bruno Morand: Very good, Doug. Thanks for joining the call, and thanks for the kind words. Definitely been a very difficult time for everyone involved. In relation to the insurance, I will let Magnus comment here a little bit more on the deployment of the proceeds. This is obviously something that we are still evaluating as we go along, and it is obviously a very recent aspect. But the proceeds in general would follow the same application of proceeds as you would normally have under the bond, similar to if the rig had been at sale. But let us allow Magnus maybe provide you a bit more color.

Magnus Vaaler: Yeah, that's correct. As Bruno states, it's following the requirement as with the sale. In summary, it gives us 365 days to apply the proceeds to either debt repayments, including the regular scheduled amortizations that we are due to pay in July. It would be CapEx, including investments or maintenance CapEx, which we typically have in a regular year as well, plus around 25% of the proceeds are free to use for other general corporate purposes. So, I would say, in sum, it's relatively flexible as long as we keep within those buckets. It's a cost that we would have in a regular year as well.

So, it is not a lot of restrictions compared to what we would normally pay.

Doug Becker: Got it. Then just quickly on the 2027 outlook, I thought it was interesting you said based on the current forward coverage. Does that mean that outlook is just based on the 52% contract coverage that's in-house today, or are there some assumptions about increasing demand later in the year? Just given your positive outlook, are there any day rate assumptions kind of baked into that outlook as well?

Bruno Morand: Yeah, no, thanks for the question. Again, when we look at our forecast for 2027, our outlook for 2027, at this stage, we anticipate that the level of activity that we'll see in 2027 is going to be comparable to what we have seen in 2026. So, let's say a number near 80% kind of coverage for the fleet. Obviously, this is based on what we see. As I mentioned in earlier remarks, there are a couple of moving pieces that are very interesting here in terms of the recovery.

Should those things start to materialize earlier than planned, including some of the demand in China, including some of the demand in Nigeria, I would expect that things could start to accelerate as we get to the second half of the year. I think the way to think about it, Doug, I think we discussed this with the industry repetitively here during the year. I think that the sector utilization has been moving in the right direction, and I would say 93% has been an improvement. It's a pretty healthy level. I think what the space here needed more to see a stronger outlook, it's not so much a utilization play, it's more a forward coverage play.

I think because of the slowdown towards the Middle East, the general forward coverage has been coming down. The Middle East is one region that provides kind of very lengthy contracts, and that's been, I think, what has been affecting the dynamics in general. In the last couple of months, I think we continue to see an acceleration of not only the tenders, but even the length of the tenders that are in the pipeline, and I think this is constructive. For now, I think we keep maybe a more sober view of the future.

We recognize the uncertainties with the Middle East, and we would project utilization or coverage to be similar in 2027 and 2026, and hence our thought on the guidance. I think as the year progresses, hopefully some more good news come, and that could give us some upside potential.

Doug Becker: I think that makes a lot of sense. Thank you.

Operator: We are now going to proceed with our next question. The questions come from the line of Fredrik Stene from Clarksons Securities. Please ask your question.

Fredrik Stene: Hey, Bruno and Magnus. I would also like to express my sympathies after the incident and for all those involved. My question today, first one, appreciate you giving a soft guidance for 2027. Obviously, it is a bit lower than sell-side consensus had in their models, and you have given some color also through the prepared remarks on certain rigs that will idle periods, et cetera. But if there's anymore color to give in the likes of average rigs in the quarters it will be very helpful. Also the recent contract awards since the second quarter results, I think average around $138 thousand per day, so rates definitely at solid levels already.

This to me seems to be more like a utilization thing rather than a rate thing when we try to reconcile why this was a bit lower than what we had expected initially. Any additional color you can provide to help us kind of understand and think about this as we go forward would be very helpful. Thanks.

Bruno Morand: Very good. Thanks, and thanks for joining, Fredrik. We tried to include some comment in the prepared remarks to help the analysts and the community to understand what kind of utilization and coverage in the first half of the year looks like. I think the way to think about it at the moment, if you look across our rigs, we have two rigs available in the Middle East, or a second one to become soon available in the Middle East, and we have two rigs in the shipyard in Southeast Asia.

Obviously, the redeployment of those units are heavily dependent on first the situation in the Middle East and how quickly things resume in the Middle East, because that is, for now, a market that we see largely as being landlocked. The ones in Asia certainly would need an acceleration or maybe the realization of some of these larger demand pockets that we are talking about. You know that those four rigs are largely a risk for us, and that is a bit of the starting point. Beyond that, we provide a bit of commentary.

We have two rigs rolling off contract in Asia, the Mist and the Skald, that we see an interesting outlook for them as we kind of get through the middle part of the year, maybe into Q2. But inevitably, being monsoon season in that region, demand tends to kind of track a bit lower in the first part, in the first quarter of the year. I think that is something that you should think about as having a potential exposure for the company. In addition to that, I provided some comments on the Sif. I think we had a very interesting campaign with the Sif in Suriname.

The rig has stayed there with the customer longer than we had initially anticipated. I like to think that going forward, there will be an interesting play for a rig of that kind of capability in that side of the world between Suriname and Venezuela and those markets. But inevitably, I think by the timing of things kicking up, you will see, you will experience some idle time on those rigs. I think the broad commentary is, and maybe picking up from your statement, that you are just right. If you look at the recent fixtures that we have had, the day rate has been moving in the right direction, which is positive.

I think we are focused on that, but more importantly, we are focused on keeping coverage on the rigs, and that is kind of how we see. I think at the moment for us, as we look into 2027, as I mentioned in the prepared remarks, I think it is more a matter of timing and the lag that we will see as this demand materializes. I think we saw into 2026, or we expect into 2026, that disruption in the Middle East to drive further demand across other regions. We see that happening. Allegedly, I would say, or admittedly, I would say that it has been slower than we expected.

So that is a bit what is creating, I would say, this kind of pocket in Q1, Q2, that hopefully we will see improving as we get to Q3 and Q4. I like the fact that when we started the year, and we were looking at the sector recovery, there was a lot of talk and a lot of questions about the Middle East and Aramco in particular, and clearly at that point, they were the keys to the recovery of the sector.

I think we get now to the end of the year, and what is interesting is, I think the recovery is playing out, and despite all the Middle East, and I think despite the Middle East, which is interesting. I think if the Middle East comes through in the next couple of months, if things stabilize, that could be a further catalyst to accelerate the recovery. But as I said in the remarks, we are sober here. I think we need to understand that these exposures exist in the near term. Hopefully, we will see some of this coming through in a brighter kind of second half of the year.

Fredrik Stene: All right, appreciate those details. Maybe trying to connect this, I would guess that you are going to prioritize in keeping utilization high on the rigs that are warm and working. Then you have the Groa, the Freyja, and the Var, which are idle at the moment with no future commitments. You also said that you had one contract, sorry, one rig in the BC Ventures that were kind of stacked at the moment. Just as a side question in a way, you also mentioned, and we heard the same news, that China maybe through COSL is on the lookout to buy rigs, and some of those rigs definitely have to come from the international markets.

Would you ever be willing to consider selling any of these stacked rigs?

Bruno Morand: Yeah, it's a good question, Fredrik. Indeed, I mean, I think we need to look at what is available to us and how that makes sense to the company. I think we've been fortunate to have been able to grow the fleet in the last year or so with good assets and attractive valuation. I think at one point in time, if we have the right offers and we feel that it's accretive to the shareholders, I think we will look at that. I think what is very interesting about the Chinese demand, as we understand, it seems to be a demand that is focused exclusively in serving their local market.

I think not only that could be an interesting look at how that transaction could be accretive, but there is a recognition as well that some of that capacity moving into China helps the international market. I think that holds true whether we do something in that regard or whether it just it's rigs from the general fleet. I think what is important and interesting here is that if you see a demand of that size materializing, it's quite interesting for the sector. If you look at the modern jack-up space, we anticipate right now about 20 or low 20 rigs available across the globe, right? Truly available across the globe.

If you take six rigs off that pool, it helps quite a bit in tightening the market. So, we'll look at that in due course. I think that the dynamics of buying rigs at attractive price, and if you have the right price and to actually sell it onwards to a captive market, is not something that we rule out.

Fredrik Stene: All right, appreciate that. Thank you for good and detailed answers as always. I'll get back. Have a good day. Thanks.

Operator: We are now going to proceed with our next question. The question comes from the line of Greg Lewis from BTIG. Please ask your question.

Greg Lewis: Hey, thank you and good afternoon, or good evening, and thanks for taking my questions. I did want to go back to the guidance. I guess, we gave it, so we got to ask a lot of questions about it. Those three, I guess, hot, warm, stacked rigs, it does not look like, based on your comments around utilization, that those are any work in 2027 is contemplated in the existing guidance. Is that a fair statement?

Bruno Morand: Yeah, I would say in general, Greg, the anticipation in our statement that there's no meaningful amount of work that we put in our guidance for those rigs through the year. If I look at the Groa, it's a rig stranded in the Middle East at the moment. Obviously, the outlook for the rig to return to work is largely depending on the situation in the Middle East. I think for the rigs in Asia, maybe slightly different, but as we said before, I think the focus is primarily at the moment in optimizing utilization for the rest of the fleet. So, you're right.

I think when you look at our guidance, there's not a very large amount of assumption that goes as contributions for those rigs into the year.

Greg Lewis: Okay. I did want to follow up with that on those two rigs potentially. You did make some positive comments around West Africa. It seems like that market is an opportunity for growth. I think you mentioned there's a handful of potential rig jobs. Is the right way to think about that just pretty much means that the utilization on our existing fleet in West Africa is going to tighten up here over the next couple quarters, and utilization's going to be pretty high in that market, or was the read-through we could also actually see some incremental rigs, whether they're Borr's or others, going into that market?

Bruno Morand: Yeah, I think it's a good description, Greg. I mean, the West Africa market has been running pretty much at capacity, so there's not a whole lot of availability in that region other than rigs that just roll off contract in due course. If I speak for ourselves, our own fleet, I do think that the outlook for those rigs to remain contracted, despite or beyond the additional demand in Nigeria, is very true. The way we look at that is indeed, I think if there is a demand of reasonable size in Nigeria, which we have a strong confidence on, that is likely to demand more rigs coming into the region.

Exactly as you described, I think that is the sort of pocket that could create an opportunity to pull rigs that are currently in the sideline and readily available to come back into the active fleet. That all said, I remain cautious and optimistic, but cautious that we know that concluding arrangements for these awards in places like West Africa generally takes a little bit of time, and that means that I would not expect these rigs to be going to that market in Q1. I think this is probably more second half of the year. That's the way I would describe it.

Greg Lewis: Okay, great. Then just my last question around utilization. We just touched on West Africa, where it seems like rigs are going to move rolling from one contract to the other. Just backing into that, the 80% utilization guidance, what regions do you think we could see some off, or maybe on a relative basis, what regions do you think we could see more off-hire in between contracts on a relative basis, as we kind of look at the first half or the next three quarters in 2027?

Bruno Morand: I would say a lot of that exposure, Greg, sits in Southeast Asia, not because the overall demand is expected to come down. It's just because it is a market that, generally speaking, the contracts are a bit shorter in nature, and then obviously, not always you have this perfect continuation between the contracts. It is a market that has normally some seasonality relating to monsoon seasons. Customers obviously prefer not to have rig moving risks or delay risks during the monsoon season, so that kind of creates a little bit of that. But as I said, I think that's a risk that is largely a timing issue. I don't see, I think, as much the opposite.

I think when we look at the actual demand in that space, we are quite encouraged to see Vietnam doing quite well, Indonesia kind of following the same footsteps, and even more recently, the demand in Malaysia. I think the demand there is good. I think there may be some timing constraints here that could cause some idle time.

Greg Lewis: Okay, super helpful. Thank you very much.

Bruno Morand: Very good. Thanks for joining, Greg.

Operator: We are now going to proceed with our next question, and the question comes from the line of Dan Kutz from Morgan Stanley. Please ask your question.

Dan Kutz: Hey, thanks. Good morning, and thoughts and prayers out to everyone impacted by the Prospector 5 incident. I just want to ask a couple of questions on the cash flow statement. I guess just first of all, maybe anything that you could share on the CapEx outlook for the balance this year for the fourth quarter, and any early thoughts on 2027? I think, Magnus, last quarter you'd said that kind of $60 million-$70 million is sort of the normal CapEx range for the size of Borr's fleet. But you're trending, and absent, I guess, a year where there's higher SPSs, but 2026, and it looks like 2027, that's not the case.

In fact, we look to be a little bit below normal from an SPS perspective. But yeah, just given that year-to-date CapEx is trending pretty far below that $60 million-$70 million range, and just any thoughts on 2027 CapEx. Thanks.

Magnus Vaaler: Hi, Dan. Thanks for the question. Indeed, we have been guiding to a normalized year of $60 million-$70 million. It's normalized CapEx levels and normal SPS year. As you stated, this year we're trending lower. So year-to-date, we have $27.5 million of jack-up additions or CapEx so far. So, I expect us to come in below $50 million for the full year, or around $50 million. It is mainly attributable to, as you say, less SPSs than in your average year. I do expect that to normalize and actually be increasing next year. So, if you think about two years in a row, $70 million each year is $140 million total.

So, if you get to around $50 million this year, I would actually expect it to be more on the $90 million level next year. So, overall, two years, $70 million each on average, but lower this year and higher into next year because of the timings of when SPSs occur. Next year, we do have more SPSs, special periodic service, than in your regular year. So, that's the expectations.

Dan Kutz: Great. That is really helpful and very clear. Then maybe just on free cash flow, you kind of given us an outlook on relatively flat EBITDA sequentially in Q4 and year-over-year. Now, we have the CapEx component of the answer. Are there any other factors influencing free cash flow this year and next year that you would point to, or any kind of framework for free cash conversion, or just anything you could help with on what could improve the free cash generation potential for next year or so?

Magnus Vaaler: Yeah. I think from our fixed costs after EBITDA, they are relatively transparent and easy to follow. We do obviously have the CapEx that we just touched on. We have tax payments annually. I think for the past couple of years, we have been trending around $50 million-$60 million of tax annually, and that is obviously linked to earnings as well. Then we have our debt payments or interest payments, which is trending, or is expected to be $200 million into next year. Additionally, we have amortization on the bonds. However, it does not start up until July, so there is a regular amortization payment of $50 million in July.

That being said, I think we are, like I said in my remarks as well, we are in a very solid position when it comes to the liquidity. We have $200 million on the balance sheet on Q3. We have a $250 million RCF facility, which is available to us. I think from the company's perspective, we are stronger than we have been in the past when it comes to a base liquidity balance to go through what we do see, as Bruno talked about, the softer first half of next year. We can get through that with the liquidity balance that we have comfortably.

Dan Kutz: Great. That is all really helpful. Thanks a lot. I will turn it back.

Operator: We are now going to proceed with our next question. The question comes from the line of Aaron Rosenthal from JPMorgan. Please ask your question.

Aaron Rosenthal: Hi, and thank you for the time. I echo the sentiments expressed earlier with respect to the loss of lives and the incident. I guess maybe trying to touch on the Prospector 5 dynamics one more time. Can you confirm if the $200 million is what you expect to receive next week? If you are able to elaborate on what material liabilities or other cash costs could remain afterward, whether it is around the wreck removal and/or the third-party claims?

Magnus Vaaler: Sure. Hi, Aaron. I think it is, like we said in our remarks, still too early to talk about the full impact of this incident. The starting point is the insurance payment that is coming in next week is for the insurance on the asset itself. We also have a comprehensive third-party liability insurance, P&I insurance, that we expect to cover anything around wreck removals, pollutions, and other third-party liabilities that will arise. So, we have very good coverage when it comes to that insurance as well. I think on other potential losses or impacts or financial impacts from it is still too early to say.

I think looking at historical similar incidents, our coverage should be very much sufficient to cover these type of situations. Every situation is obviously different from previous ones. So, a bit early to say, but we have good coverage.

Aaron Rosenthal: Okay, that's fair. I guess going back to the 2027 outlook, I think the implied $138,000 per day from the recent awards, that includes, I think, mob fees and other items. So, maybe if we can take a look at the Hild for some leading-edge dynamics. I guess, can you detail the economics on that award? What the mob fee is like? Is there any CapEx to get the rig ready from, I believe, what was a stacked position in Mexico? Then, overall, what are you baking in for your per-day or per-rig OpEx assumptions? I understand that there's been some inflation this year, and with the insurance settlements, your per-day rig insurance might be going up as well.

Bruno Morand: Very good, Aaron. Let me maybe take a stab into addressing your question specifically on the Hild. We have not disclosed specific economics for that contract, but we've been mentioning before that running rates in West Africa were, generally speaking, in 140, 160 range. That contract for the Hild is no different from that perspective. So, I think we're still tracking within what we think is being a good and maybe leading-edge rates in that area. Inevitably, when you move a rig from across the world, you would have some CapEx associated with that. You have, let me rephrase, you have some expenses associated with that go beyond just the scope of a heavy-lift vessel.

There's always some country-specific compliance things that you have to do or some customer-specific aspect that you have to address. That contract does include a pretty healthy mobilization that should cover, I would say, the general mobilization expenses to get the rig from Mexico to West Africa, but we will have some additional expenses on top, which is regular expenses where you prepare to start a new contract with a customer. I think that's the simple way to think about it. So, I would say mobilization fee, I will guide you to think about a number that looks in the $7 million-$10 million as revenue coming out of that.

Our expenses will be higher than that just because we, as I said, we have crew costs and other things that we have to go through before a rig is ready to go into operation.

Aaron Rosenthal: Okay. I guess, with respect to the range of day rates at 140, 160, I guess let's just pick the midpoint, 150, and then let's say $10 million of move fees. Is the clean rate 150, and then you net out the amortized 10, so it's like a 123, or is that kind of incremental?

Bruno Morand: No, no. As I mentioned, the rate ranges that we've seen in West Africa, that's really the run rate in country. That's not really with add-ons or mobilization. So that's the way I would describe it, Aaron.

Aaron Rosenthal: Okay. That's fair. Maybe just one more on the CapEx component. The roughly $90 million next year, I guess that incorporates some of the additional CapEx for in-country certifications on this rig. If you can confirm that's correct, does that also cover the capital needs for the JV rigs? I guess just overall at the SPS cadence, do you have more or less SPSs currently on the books for 2028 versus 2027?

Magnus Vaaler: I can answer that. The CapEx number we've mentioned now is more on a regular fleet CapEx, excluding any additional moving of rigs or preparation of rigs, activation of stacked rigs. That would, in that case, come as additional cost. So this is just regular maintenance and maintenance CapEx, as it is for the 28 rigs of our fleet. The JV rigs would be outside of that, but we also expect the JV to be self-funded because of its contract structure soon, or all four rigs in four out of the five rigs in the JV is already contracted. So the working assumption there is that the JV is self-funded when it comes to OpEx and CapEx as well.

Operator: We will now be taking one last question. The last question comes from the line of Gregg Brody from Bank of America. Please ask your question.

Gregg Brody: Good morning, guys, and thank you for your time, and my condolences on the loss of life recently. Just a few here. Aaron covered a lot of mine, but on the operating cost side, last quarter, there were some higher costs that were, some were rolling off, and how should we think about how much showed up in this quarter and if that should persist after going forward? I have one more after that.

Magnus Vaaler: Yeah, sure. We have had two quarters now with inflated, I would say, operating expenses due to the startup of the Odin, as we covered in our commentary in the previous quarter. That will normalize now. The Odin is up and running in the U.S. However, at a higher OpEx per day than in most other countries. Additionally, we have moved some rigs into West Africa, as we talked about, and the Hild is going over there, and West Africa is typically a higher operating cost area, especially with Nigeria.

If we previously the costs across regions are a bit different, but let's say that across the fleet as an average, I would probably say we're going to trend around $55,000-$60,000 per day for every operating rig going forward, with the way that the rigs are deployed at the moment, so on an average basis. But the additional cost that occurred in this quarter and previous quarter for the Odin startup is not going to reoccur.

Bruno Morand: Greg, just to supplement what Magnus mentioned, one of the cost components that we've seen climbing over the last couple of quarters as well, worth mentioning, has been the insurance cost for our rigs in the Middle East. Obviously, until the conflict is resolved, this is a cost that will likely stay. Somewhat associated with the Middle East conflict, we have been experiencing a slightly higher cost in terms of freight for parts as we kind of move parts around the rigs to service our rigs. Those components will stay. The Odin is one that should normalize as we go along.

But as Magnus said, keep in mind that the U.S. is an operating region that has a generally higher operating cost. I think that when you think across the fleet from these developments, but as well as from the way the rigs have been reshaping around the world, or reshifting around the world, we have a bit more exposure to higher-cost geographies, which will mean that our operating expenses will track a bit higher now for the foreseeable future.

Gregg Brody: Then just in terms of your stacked rig costs, your warm stacked rig costs, how should we think about that?

Magnus Vaaler: It is also in the different categories. So we have the ones that are stacked for longer terms, such as the two in Singapore, the Var and the Freyja. They are typically lower costs, so around $15,000 per day, give or take $10,000-$20,000 per day. Then you have these rigs which are between contracts that you keep relatively warm and active to keep it available for upcoming contracts. That would be more in the region of $30,000, $25,000, $35,000. But very much dependent on the outlook for work and how warm you want to keep it. But on the flip side, then you do not need to pay a lot on reactivation costs.

So for a shorter term stacking, I would say between $25,000-$35,000 per day. Longer term stacking is more in the region of $15,000 per day.

Gregg Brody: Got it. Now, this is my last question. I know estimating what total cost will take some time to figure out from the incident in Gabon. How should we think about the timing of the investigation? Do you have a sense of how long that is expected to take in terms of having a final conclusion?

Bruno Morand: Yeah. It is difficult to precise, Greg. What I can confirm is that the investigation is in its full course. So we think, as I mentioned earlier, DNV has been engaged. They are very experienced and specialized in that field. They are going through the material available. The fact that obviously the rig sunk and a lot of the evidence that has to be assessed to come to a conclusion sits at the seabed does not necessarily facilitate things for us. So it is early for us to say. I think we are still waiting for DNV to run their initial assessment.

I think in the next couple of weeks, we will likely start having some more firm hypothesis of what could have happened. The timeline of actually getting to conclusion remains a bit uncertain. I think at this stage, it is obviously very important that we have some visibility of that. We want to make sure that whatever investigation is completed is not rushed, is thorough, and really gets us to the bottom of what happened. It is the sort of event that is extremely tragic, and we have a duty to make sure it does not happen to our company again. Hopefully, we can assist the industry to make sure that it does not happen across the global fleet.

Gregg Brody: Thank you for the time, guys, and good luck with the investigation.

Operator: This concludes the question and answer session and today's conference call. Thank you all for participating. You may now disconnect your lines. Thank you.

#3139. Giving the iPhone Duo a Spin at the Apple Store? Be Sure to Test These Things Out

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Want to test out the iPhone Duo? Here are six things you need to try with it.

Now that the iPhone Duo is in stores, there are plenty of people who are curious about Apple’s first folding device. Foldables are hardly a new sector in the smartphone world, with Samsung leading the charge, but Apple’s entry into the market is a big deal, and the iPhone Duo is a stunner.

If you’re planning on checking out the iPhone Duo at the Apple store, it might be easy to just marvel at how cool it looks, but if you’re considering making this your new phone that’ll be in your pocket all of the time, you’ll probably want to get an idea of how it will be living with this new design. After all, you should be in love with all aspects of the device if you’re going to drop $2,000-plus on it.

Below, we’ve listed a handful of features and things to try out when you’re test-driving the Apple iPhone Duo in the store.

When the Duo was first revealed, Apple showed off a very intriguing animation when you unfold it. Leave it to Apple to make a function so simple look so aesthetically pleasing.

It’ll likely be the first thing you notice when you first open the Duo up to see its inner display, and there’s a good chance you’ll continue to open and close the device to see the effect. At the end of the day, it’s a parlor trick — but a very good one, adding delight to ordinary use.

Read more: The iPhone Duo Crossed 517,000 Folds and Counting in Our Custom Machine

Foldables, well, fold, and they typically come with creases. The Duo has a minimal crease and a matte display, both of which are wins. That said, even the most noticeable creases tend to “disappear” when you’re viewing content — you just get used to them while watching TV shows or YouTube videos. The Duo’s minimal crease should be even easier to ignore.

And let’s not forget about the matte screen. Several foldables ship with glossy displays, but the iPhone Duo will have a less shiny screen, making it easier to view in bright environments without annoying reflections.

The outer passport-size display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for watching videos because of how it crops content to fit the new aspect ratio. Still, it’s handy to prop the phone up in tent mode and watch shows that way. You also have a large inner display to work with, but because of its passport-style design, even that screen has a different aspect ratio than the widescreen format people are used to on regular phones, so there will likely be some letterboxing in videos.

Try watching something with the phone set up in both ways to see if it bothers you enough to dissuade you from buying the phone.

Again, it’s not an iPhone Duo issue but a foldable phone issue — the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the same size and format. The aspect ratio of the display might crop the top or sides of videos, so it’s worth trying out if you expect to watch a lot of full-screen videos.

Like videos, apps on foldables can sometimes appear a little weird, and that could be the case with the iPhone Duo‘s aspect ratio. When you’re at the Apple Store, check out how your most-used apps look and feel on both the inner and outer displays, and make sure you rotate the inner screen to see how apps behave in this orientation, too — that wide screen could be great for watching vertical videos or scrolling through social media.

If some apps, such as Instagram, look a little different or are wonky, it’ll hopefully be just a matter of time until the developers make an update that optimizes the experience for this new design. Keep in mind that you can also have two apps open onscreen at once, making it easier to multitask.

If you want the best camera experience on an iPhone right now, you should be looking at the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, but that doesn’t make the Duo a slouch for shooting photos, either.

Yes, the Duo is missing a third camera (telephoto), and if that’s important to you, then you probably shouldn’t even be considering Apple’s foldable. But still, if you’re going to shell out this much money for a new phone, test out those cameras — even if it’s in a controlled environment like an Apple Store.

Another thing to check out before you pull the trigger is your selfie shots with this new phone. There are two main ways to do this: with the phone closed, holding it up in the regular way you’d take a selfie using the outer screen’s 12-megapixel front-facing camera, or with the inner display open and shooting with the twin 48-megapixel rear cameras (the outer screen will show a preview of the shot).

There’s also a front-facing camera underneath the inner display, which is mostly for video calls — and which we suspect would produce the least-impressive shots from the device. Try them all and see what you think of the pics. And since you’re at an Apple Store, make sure you delete them afterward.

The odd but interesting aspect ratio of the front display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for typing, so it’s best to do a typing test when you have one in front of you. While the inner display will provide a roomier and more comfortable typing experience, you probably won’t want to have to open up the Duo every time you want to shoot off a quick text to someone. If you have bigger hands, typing on the front screen could be a bit of a nightmare.

Typing one-handed on the small cover screen should be manageable, but try it out to see if it works for you. Some may find it convenient; others may find it cumbersome.

And when you’re typing on the inner display, try the Duo in both portrait and landscape orientations to see which feels better. You can also choose between a split keyboard and larger keys. It’s thoughtful of Apple to offer options that let you tailor the typing experience to your preferences, but you may find that none of them suit your style.

#3138. iOS 27.3 beta can cause HomeView issues, Apple confirms

Apple’s new HomeView just launched last Friday, but some early adopters reported issues with Siri AI in their first days of use. Apple shipped fixes in HomeView 27.2.1 yesterday, but it also confirmed the iOS 27.3 beta is responsible for some of the problems.

Yesterday Apple released its first post-launch software update for HomeView, less than a week after the product debuted.

Per the company’s official release notes, HomeView 27.2.1 focuses on bug fixes, including a fix for the following issue:

Pairing with an iPhone or iPad running the iOS or iPadOS 27.3 beta may cause Siri requests to fail

It’s unknown how many reports of Siri issues on HomeView can be attributed to the iOS 27.3 beta. However, it wouldn’t surprise me if many of the reports were from beta users. That’s in part because early HomeView reviewers didn’t seem to have the same problems.

With HomeView 27.2.1 now available, those problems should hopefully be taken care of. However, if you’re on the iOS 27.3 beta, there’s a new issue you’ll need to deal with temporarily.

As discovered by pdfu, if you try to make a Personal Content request on an iPhone running iOS 27.3, Siri in HomeView 27.2.1 now says: “I can’t help with that because your personal device is on newer software.”

If you’re on iOS 27.3, Siri on HomeView can’t use your iPhone for personal context, likely until December.HomeView won’t send Siri requests to an iPhone on newer software. Without a HomeView update, your only option is iOS 27.2.x.On-device requests like timers still work. https://t.co/8UbRs7z496

It’s understandable that issues might arise from having iOS and HomeView software that’s out of sync. Unfortunately though, there’s no beta software available for HomeView at the moment.

That means unless Apple releases a beta soon, users might have to wait until the public launch of HomeView 27.3 in December to get Personal Content features back.

How has Siri AI been working for you on HomeView? Let us know in the comments.

#3137. I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes – it was satisfying

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

A new Gemini Notebook feature lets you create interactive sites from intricate data.

Google’s Gemini can now turn your notes and other sources in your Gemini Notebook (previously called NotebookLM) into interactive pages or sites to help you better process complicated information.

Complete with flashcards, dashboards, and colorful panels, the sites make it easier to study and understand intricate concepts. I tested the feature, announced Tuesday, to see how efficient it is at creating a navigable site that is actually helpful and stays loyal to sources.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s new Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector in my tests

Because Notebooks are built with the sources you provide, like textbooks, files, or notes, the sites are created with the data that is in your Gemini Notebook. Notebook has three tabs: Sources, Chat, and Studio. The site option is in the Studio tab, listed under what you can create.

If you’re taking a college class, you could put all the information you need to prepare for a test and use the interactive site as a study guide that you can share with others.

To test this, I gave Notebook the following prompt:

“Make me a site that visually explains how cellular respiration works, breaking down each stage with interactive diagrams and self-check flashcards.”

Since I’m not in a class that would give me those study materials, I gave Gemini online sources to use for this. Gemini cited the sources in my notebook, then spent a few minutes creating the interactive site. Gemini will give you a quick update when it’s done, including a summary of the source information as it pertains to your request and instructions on where to find the site.

Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours

As promised, my cellular respiration notes were complete and organized on an interactive, visually appealing site that was easy to navigate. The coolest feature on the site was the flashcards, which you can hover over to see which ones you’ve studied.

The interactive site feature is now available to Gemini Notebook users and will soon come to the mobile app. As someone who knows very little about coding, I was pretty satisfied to see the information Gemini put together presented in explorable, easy-to-understand tabs on a site.

#3136. The Novilla Bliss is an Amazon best-seller, but is this memory foam mattress worth it? I slept on the budget bed for a month to find out

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Novilla Bliss Memory Foam is an all-foam mattress that’s particularly suited to side sleepers and lightweight back sleepers. I slept on a Full size 10" mattress for a month, along with my husband, and I found it especially comfortable for side sleeping. I was also really impressed with the support it provided, considering its low price. But support at the edges left a lot to be desired and it won't be supportive enough for heavier sleepers, and my hot-sleeping husband found it slept way too warm, too.

Far more supportive than its price would suggest

Not robust enough for stomach sleepers or those over 230lbs

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Insanely popular on Amazon, the Novilla Bliss Memory Foam Mattress is a cheap and cheerful all-foam offering that I freely admit I wasn’t expecting much from. However, there were lots of things about the Novilla Bliss that surprised me in a good way and overall, I was quite impressed by the support considering the mattress’ very reasonable pricing.

Name: Jo PlumridgeAge bracket: 45-55Weight bracket: 100-130lbsPredominant sleep position: Combination sleeper who spends slightly more time on her sideSleep issues: Suffers with back pain which can easily be exacerbated by an unsupportive mattress

It’s not going to rival the very best mattresses on the market but if you’re on a budget, this should definitely be on your radar. With a queen mattress currently priced at $269.99 in the Black Friday mattress deals, I think this is one of the best budget beds currently on the market.

In terms of firmness, I’d suggest that most sleepers will find it at the firmer end of the medium scale. There is sinkage and this is an all-foam mattress, but there’s still some support underneath. I can’t think of any other all-foam mattresses I’ve slept on that are as firm, except for the Nectar Classic Memory Foam. However, I must stress that I’m a lightweight sleeper and my husband, who is lightweight to average weight for a man, found it softer than I did.

Still, we both enjoyed it for side sleeping particularly and, as someone who is ultra fussy about lumbar support, I found it more comfortable for back sleeping than I expected. Motion isolation on the Novilla Bliss is exceptional, and I couldn’t feel my husband moving around at all, but edge support is lacking both when you lie or sit on the edge. I didn’t feel as if I’d actually fall off the bed, but there was some definite tilting.

Type: Memory FoamFirmness: Medium (lighter sleepers will find it medium firm)Height: 10"Trial period: 100 nightsWarranty: 10 yearsPrice: From $179.99 at Novilla

The mattress' one big failing, though, is temperature regulation. I sleep cold so this wasn't an issue, but my husband found it stuffy and, while he didn't wake up sweaty, he didn’t find it massively comfortable either. Hot sleepers on a budget might be happier on the Siena 10" Signature mattress, which kept our testers comfortably cool. But value for money is the Novilla Bliss' big selling point and considering its price, I was really impressed overall with the mattress.

Read on for my full assessment of the Novilla Bliss Memory Foam mattress so you can decide if it’s worth investing in.

A queen size Novilla Bliss is listed at $269.99 with a 20% discount from $337.99 on the brand’s own website, while Amazon currently has the price at $269.99. This sale price seems to be fairly set, so here are the MSRPs for each size, plus the usual sale price you can expect to pay:

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Of course, November is one of the best times of the year for mattress sales and we’re seeing some Black Friday deals — a twin size Novilla 8" hybrid mattress is down to $90, for example, and on Amazon the queen size 10" Novilla Bliss has dropped below $210 a couple of times in 2026. So, it’s definitely worth keeping an eye on prices but do remember that, at $269.99 for a queen, the Novilla Bliss is already incredibly well priced.

Benefits differ very slightly depending on where you buy the mattress. On the brand’s own site, you’ll bet a 100-night trial, 10-year warranty and free shipping and returns. Amazon, on the other hand, offers a 90-night easy returns system, manufacturer’s warranty and free shipping and returns.

An extremely affordable all-foam mattress that offers far more support than you’d expect for its price tag, a queen size Novilla Bliss is currently priced at $269.99 on both the brand’s own website and on Amazon. Keep an eye on prices as Black Friday approaches.

I tested the 10" version, but as detailed above, you can buy the Novilla Bliss in a variety of heights. But for this review, I’m concentrating on the middle ground of the 10” version. Starting at the top, there’s a breathable cover with OEKO-TEX certified fabric. This is helpfully removeable and washable — mattress covers that can’t be removed for freshening up are a real bugbear of mine, although I’d obviously recommend that you use a mattress protector anyway.

Underneath this is a layer of cooling memory foam that’s CertiPUR-US certified and contains the brand’s NanoGEL cooling particles, which Novilla says are designed to ‘capture and redirect excess body heat away from the surface’.

Next up is a layer of adaptive cushioning foam that provides comfort and a transition layer to the high-density support foam layer underneath it. This layer provides most of the support and prevents the mattress from sagging.

Underneath this you’ll find the zip to remove the top cover, plus a non-slip fabric to stop the mattress from sliding about on your bed base. Somewhat annoyingly, the mattress doesn’t have handles to help move it about but as it’s all-foam, it’s not impossible to rotate it without them.

As a lightweight sleeper, I rated the Novilla Bliss as a medium-firm mattress but my husband (and additional testers of a heavier build that I asked to try out the mattress) felt it was a medium, albeit a firmer medium. Averaging out scores, I’d probably place the mattress at a 6 out of 10 on the firmness scale.

There’s definitely some ‘squidge’ when you first lie on the mattress, but this is backed up by a decent amount of support from the lower levels. This combination makes it particularly suited for side sleepers. My husband in particular found the mattress instantly comfortable in this sleeping position, but it did take a couple of days for the foams to soften up a little at the shoulders for me — after this, it was extremely comfortable.

Pressure relief around the pressure points was also really good and I didn’t wake up with any symptoms of a dead hip (something that I can be prone to if the mattress is too unyielding).

I wasn’t expecting great things from this mattress when it came to sleeping on my back, as I’ve historically found all-foam mattresses can lack the firmer lumbar support that I find essential. And, when I first lay down on the bed, I did notice a tiny amount of pulling through my lower back. However, this eased quickly and as a lightweight sleeper, I actually found the mattress supportive enough to keep my spine aligned.

My husband, who boarders the lightweight and average weight category also found it pretty supportive. It’s not going to rival the very best mattresses for back pain but, overall, I thought it did an excellent job on pressure relief for both side and back sleeping.

If you’re of a heavier weight though, I don’t think you’ll find the Novilla Bliss supportive enough and even average weight sleepers towards the higher end of that weight bracket may find it lacks support for back sleeping. I asked a couple of friends who are larger than my husband and I to try the mattress out and while they both thought they could just about get away with it for side sleeping, they felt that support was lacking for both back and stomach sleeping.

In fact, strict stomach sleepers of any weight probably won’t get on with the Novilla Bliss as it’s just lacking in enough support to keep the hips lifted, leading to the spine sinking out of alignment. If you’re a stomach sleeper, have a look at our recommended mattresses for stomach sleepers instead.

I’m in the UK so the mattress was shipped over the Atlantic and, despite its long journey, it arrived none the worse for its voyage. Order on the Novilla website and you’ll receive a tracking number within two business days, with delivery within three to seven business days. Novilla uses FedEx, UPS and GOFO Express for delivery. If you order through Amazon, you can expect delivery in around five days and there’s also the option to pay for the delivery drivers to unpack the mattress and take away packaging.

I recruited my long-suffering husband to help get the mattress upstairs although, being all-foam, it was considerably lighter than the hybrid and pocket sprung mattresses I’ve tested in the past.

Once released from its vacuum seal, the Novilla Bliss did take longer than a hybrid mattress to inflate and I left it for a good 10 hours before sleeping on it. It did definitely continue to expand minutely over the next few days, so I’d say it was around 48 hours before it was fully expanded. The brand suggests that it will take 24-72 hours to fully expand, so this was bang on the money. Some Amazon customers have reported issues with the mattress not expanding fully but in fairness, I didn’t have any issues on this front.

Like most foam mattresses, there was some off-gassing from the Novilla Bliss. It wasn’t the worst I’ve come across but it did last for a couple of days.

My husband and I slept on the mattress for four weeks to get a clear overview of how it performed in key areas. In addition, I carried out some objective tests in an approximation of our comprehensive sleep lab testing methodology.

Through both objective and subjective testing, I’ve assessed the mattress in three key areas. I’ve looked at motion isolation (will a partner moving about at night disturb you?), temperature regulation (does the mattress keep a hot sleeper comfortable through the night?) and edge support (how solid does the edge of the bed feel when you lie right on it or sit on the mattress?). These are the results.

If you share your bed with a restless partner or are a light sleeper, a mattress with good motion isolation is a must. Good motion isolation stops movement from one side of the bed travelling over and waking up another sleeper. I can report back that the Novilla Bliss is particularly strong in this department.

My husband does tend to flail about in bed when he’s rolling over, channeling a walrus trying to leave the ocean and I’m a pretty light sleeper, so even a little motion transfer can be enough to wake me up. I’m pleased to report that I wasn’t disturbed by him at all during our testing period, which was an unusual and pleasing thing.

This was backed up by my objective tests. Firstly, I performed a series of drop tests. I placed a wine glass on the left-hand side of the mattress and dropped a weight from 24" above the bed surface on the right-hand side. This is a similar sensation to a person getting into bed.

I dropped the weight five times consecutively 30" away from the wine glass. Each time, the wine glass gave a very slight wobble but otherwise stayed upright, which was impressive. Next up, I got my husband to perform some subjective tests, starting with low force movements and then increasing to moderate and high force movements. I rated the mattress 10 out of 10 at low force and nine out of 10 at both moderate and high force. Overall, the Novilla Bliss really excelled when it came to motion isolation.

When I talk about temperature regulation, I’m looking at how well the mattress manages heat build-up throughout the night and whether it leaves a sleeper feeling stuffy. I’m afraid this was one area where the Novilla Bliss didn’t perform brilliantly, despite claims of a breathable cover and gel-infused memory foam.

My husband sleeps hot and he found the mattress stuffy after only 15 minutes of lying on it. And while he didn’t wake up seriously overheating, he did feel slightly clammy and uncomfortable. It was not a particularly breathable mattress and, on some hotter nights during testing, he did actually decamp to our spare room.

I’m something of a reptile at the best of times but even I noticed some heat building up around my lower back while lying on it. However, thanks to my cold nature, I wasn’t ever uncomfortable on it.

We tested through the tail end of an unusually warm period in the UK and through to some slightly cooler nights, so it gave me a good overall view of the mattress. For context, temperatures in the room ranged from around 75F down to 60F. However, I should point out that I wouldn’t expect an all-foam mattress to perform as well as a hybrid for temperature regulation and, if you are a hot sleeper, you’d be better off investing in one of our best cooling mattress picks.

A mattress with good edge support allows sleepers to use the whole width of the bed, as well as providing a stable surface to sit on while getting in and out of bed. My husband and I foster cats for a local charity and, as any cat servant will tell you, these little furry creatures have the ability to take up 90% of the bed overnight, leaving human subjects very much clinging to the edges.

Unfortunately, the Novilla Bliss wasn’t the strongest candidate when it came to edge support. There was some definite tilting when we lay on the edges, although I didn’t feel as if I’d actually fall off. It was a similar story when sitting on the edge of the bed — there was some definite tilting, but I didn’t feel as if I’d actually slip off.

To back up my experiences, I placed a 53lb weight midway across and 3" in from the foot and sides of the mattress. The weight sunk in by 5" immediately and dropped further to 6.5" after five minutes. And I had to get my husband to hold the weight the whole time (he only took his hands off very briefly for a photograph).

I repeated this test midway down and 3" in from the side of the mattress and got exactly the same results, with the weight needing to be held the whole time. Just for context, the same weight placed in the center of the mattress compressed by 5" immediately but then didn’t drop any further.

The Novilla Bliss receives overwhelmingly positive reviews from sleepers on both Amazon and the brand’s website. There’s lots of praise for the “exceptional” price and many sleepers praise it for its good quality. Sleepers also praise the mattress for pressure relief, with one customer describing it as the “perfect balance of softness and support…I woke up feeling much more rested without the usual aches and stiffness.” Overall, this is a recurrent theme, along with frequent praise for the motion isolation.

There are nearly 45,000 reviews for the mattress on Amazon so, as you might expect, you will find some complaints in there. The most common one seems to be poor expansion of the mattress, so it would seem that this might be something you’ll need to look out for. And, while many people praise the mattress for soothing aches and pains, stomach sleepers and those of a heavier build complain that the mattress is nowhere near supportive enough for their sleeping style or body weight.

✅ You’re a side sleeper of light or average weight: The Novilla Bliss excelled in pressure relief and comfort for side sleepers, easing tension and providing enough support for a really comfortable night’s sleep.

✅ You share your bed with a restless partner: There really wasn’t any motion transfer to speak of with the Novilla Bliss and I never felt disturbed by my husband moving about.✅ You’re on a budget: At $269.99 for a queen size, the Novilla Bliss is exceptionally good value for money and holds its own against some more expensive options.

❌You sleep on your stomach or are of a heavier build: The all-foam construction of the Novilla Bliss simply isn’t supportive enough for stomach sleepers or those who weigh over 230lbs. Try the Siena Signature mattress instead if you’re on a budget and fall into these categories.❌You’re a hot sleeper: The Novilla Bliss left my hot-sleeping husband feeling pretty stuffy and uncomfortable and its all-foam construction does trap heat a little too easily. The SweetNight CoolNest Memory Foam mattress offers excellent temperature regulation and is another budget option. ❌You need excellent edge support: The Novilla Bliss suffered with some sinkage at its edges and didn’t feel like the most secure surface to lie on the edge of or sit on. If you need an affordable mattress with decent edge support, check out the EGOHOME Black 12” Memory Foam mattress instead.

There are plenty of positives about the Novilla Bliss, but the price is the overwhelming winner. At under $300 for a queen, it’s a bit of a bargain and I was impressed by how well it performed considering that price tag. It certainly beats out quite a few more expensive mattresses when it comes to side sleeping in particular. The soft foams at the top and some decent support underneath mean that this is a great option for side sleepers, except for those of a heavier weight.

It also boasts some of the best motion isolation I’ve come across, and it will be a winner for co-sleepers thanks to this. But, as mentioned, I don’t think it’s a great fit for hot sleepers and I would like to see better edge support.

But overall, I was hugely impressed with this mattress, and I think that most lightweight and average side and back sleepers will be comfortable on this mattress.

This plush pillow is available in two sizes and two different firmness options. In our SquishPillow review, our tester found it best suited to side sleepers, which will match well with the Novilla Bliss. It's also only $29.99, so a bit of a bargain.

Rated the best bed sheets for hot sleepers by our bedding testers, these sheets are silky-soft and cool-to-touch — so they could help to make the Novilla Bliss a bit cooler to sleep on. And there are over a dozen colors/patterns to choose from.

Another way to help make a mattress cooler is to add a cooling mattress topper. The Lucid Gel Memory Foam mattress topper did a great job of keeping our tester cool and it's reasonably priced for such a nice thick topper. A thinner and cheaper 2" version could also save you some money.

#3135. Nvidia’s Earnings Calmed Markets, but AI’s Harsh Reckoning Marches On

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Jensen Huang's departure was only a symptom of a bigger problem in the AI economy.

Though Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday offered some reassurance to investors after Jensen Huang’s departure as CEO, it did little to resolve the political, regulatory and leadership questions hanging over the entire AI economy.

The semiconductor giant at the heart of the AI infrastructure boom saw its shares plunge by 35% from last month’s high following the scandal around Huang — wiping out nearly $2 trillion in market cap and triggering Wall Street panic around a broader AI reckoning.

Nvidia’s finance chief and interim CEO, Colette Kress, sought to project stability, telling investors it was “business as usual” and raising Nvidia’s fiscal 2028 outlook. Though the chipmaker’s stock price rebounded after reporting better-than-expected results, it’s likely to face a rocky future, as concerns linger around national security violations amid illegal export deals. Market confidence is also shaky amid supply chain backlogs for advanced chips and servers that remain critical to AI compute and the training of large language models.

In the lead-up to the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Huang issued a statement that he would return as CEO if the board of directors decides it’s in the “best interest” of shareholders and the country. Despite calls from President Donald Trump and other tech executives to reinstate the former GPU boss, Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia’s appointed first-ever chair of the board, said there is no intention to reinstate Huang, and no successor was named.

Prior to the call, The Wall Street Journal reported that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Huang over concerns that the company misled investors.

Huang maneuvered Nvidia into a linchpin role for frontier AI labs and data center firms, not just by supplying hardware but also by providing equity, credit and financial backing and by mobilizing third-party capital to secure investment for the AI buildout of data centers. Nvidia’s circular financing schemes — in which the chipmaker helps fund a hyperscaler like Meta or Microsoft, which then uses the funds to buy its products — were allegedly a source of contention for Kress and other executives.

Critics have warned that this kind of vendor financing inflated the AI bubble by inflating growth projections and buoying the market valuations of chipmakers and hyperscalers.

According to Reuters, Kress was expected to pull back from some of the riskiest AI financial deals, including investments in OpenAI and AI infrastructure companies such as Lambda. Already, Nvidia has significantly scaled back financing for a $250 billion OpenAI data center deal. During Tuesday’s call, Kress failed to announce a sweeping unwind of Huang-era financing arrangements, focusing more on continuity than retreat.

Kress mentioned that chip producer TSMC, a key Nvidia partner, will continue working with Nvidia despite Huang’s departure. The company also said it was assuming no China data-center compute revenue in its next fourth-quarter outlook.

Nvidia supplies the lion’s share of the hardware necessary for data center construction and model training, and the company has long said that the demand for chips exceeds supply. Shortages of RAM and high-bandwidth memory slow down the production of AI servers and raise prices for cloud companies and other buyers. In an attempt to buy its way out of the bottleneck, Nvidia has committed large sums of money to secure future memory supply.

If Nvidia distances itself too much from its GPU commitments, that could be a problem for the entire tech industry. Semiconductor production is an incredibly specialized field dominated by very few companies, and any changes to the supply chain could have ripple effects on global markets and vendors, including in consumer electronics and cloud services.

Huang’s affair with a Chinese executive connected to the Singapore-based Megaspeed — whom US intelligence claimed was a Chinese intelligence asset — complicated an already tight supply chain. Megaspeed was under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese firms obtain high-value Nvidia chips through channels that violated US export controls.

According to the investment research firm Culper, up to one-fifth of Nvidia’s fiscal-year 2026 compute revenues were driven by movement of some of the company’s most advanced chips into China through nonrestricted intermediary countries in a process called diversion. When advanced Nvidia chips or servers are illegally routed to Chinese buyers, those units are no longer available to legal customers in the US and allied markets.

Huang was influential in shaping the Trump administration’s chip export policies, pushing back against export controls that limited Nvidia’s sales to China. But the recent scandal prompted new Commerce Department restrictions on chip shipments through third countries.

While Kress cited improving supply and sustained demand in raising Nvidia’s outlook, stricter export rules and tighter controls could further constrain capacity by creating more obstacles to compliance and delivery.

Nvidia’s better-than-expected earnings may steady investors in the short term, but any company that supplies essential hardware for the AI buildout is at risk if investor confidence in the industry falters. When Nvidia reports strong growth, AI-focused stocks and funds with large technology holdings are likely to go up. When Nvidia’s outlook weakens, investors worry that AI spending is slowing or that companies have overcommitted.

A handful of big tech companies — colloquially known as the Magnificent Seven — make up a big share of major funds and indices. Five of them account for roughly 30% of the S&P 500 index, and AI overexposure in those businesses translates into overexposure in many individual retirement accounts and 401(k)s. Because index funds hold substantial positions in Nvidia and other large tech companies, an AI selloff could affect retirement balances even for people who don’t own Nvidia shares directly.

The Magnificent Seven are heavily affected by AI stock swings. Alphabet’s stock price sank as Nvidia news aftershocks reverberated through the markets, proving that top firms are not unassailable. Other tech companies heavily focused on AI infrastructure, such as Intel and CoreWeave, likewise saw their share prices decline.

Despite growing concerns about AI dangers, Huang was one of AI’s most aggressive promoters, framing the technology as an economic and national security imperative. In early September, the now-disgraced CEO said that artificial general intelligence, or AGI, had arrived, congratulating OpenAI on its GPT-6 Astra model, which was trained on Nvidia’s Grace Blackwell GPUs.

Huang pushed against recent warnings from AI researchers, calling for unrestrained progress on frontier models and repeatedly arguing against new laws and safety regulations.

Even before Huang’s business and personal scandals came to light, AI companies were gearing up for a post-midterm-election PR campaign, as the technology has become increasingly unpopular and the backlash against data centers has grown. Democratic Party politicians pushed a platform to shift the federal government’s lax approach toward the AI industry. Some Democrats are also poised to craft legislation to prevent an AI industry bailout in the event of a bubble pop.

Amid bipartisan calls for Huang to testify before Congress, many politicians are also seeking to investigate high-ranking members of US intelligence and the Commerce Department for allowing export loopholes or for failing to act on knowledge of Nvidia’s China-related deals.

Kress might be able to lead Nvidia with tact and diligence, separating the company from some of its riskiest deals. But the national security implications of her predecessor’s relationships have opened up a can of worms that no CEO can close on their own.

The federal government is ruled by inertia, but right now there’s some investigative momentum aimed directly at the major AI players. That will almost certainly ice out some investor hype. It’s clear the AI industry is facing a reckoning that was not in the cards just months ago.

#3134. Microsoft To Do is retiring, including Mac and iOS apps

Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what users need to know.

The last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

“Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”

On the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly says it has no plans for a native Mac app.

You can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft plans to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the company.

The June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the company behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

Does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.
