#3133. Walmart: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Store-based fulfillment now covers most domestic digital orders, and fee-based memberships add a margin layer that sales growth alone does not capture.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 19, 2026 at 1:28PM EST

On its third-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call, held on Nov. 19, 2026, Walmart (WMT -1.03%) announced higher full-year sales and profit guidance as global e-commerce grew 17%. Strong operational execution across stores and digital networks is transforming retail fulfillment into a high-margin digital business. Three takeaways from management's comments show how the enterprise is positioning itself for durable long-term growth.

Management introduced a combined subscription pairing Walmart+ with Sam's Club Plus to capture broader household spending. Members spend roughly four times as much as non-members, making subscription expansion a direct catalyst for top-line growth.

Physical locations now fulfill more than 80% of domestic digital orders, turning retail space into last-mile shipping hubs. Rapid fulfillment increases order frequency and deepens customer engagement across all income brackets.

Growing delivery density and supply chain automation are expanding profitability across online channels. High-margin revenue streams like advertising and seller marketplace fees accelerate operational income growth beyond overall sales growth.

Store footprints and digital fulfillment networks are merging into a unified delivery infrastructure, and leadership is aggressively scaling this advantage.

Dense physical proximity to 96% of domestic households supports rapid order dispatch while shielding overall profitability from rising shipping costs. As high-margin advertising and membership services scale alongside digital sales, structural profit expansion will continue to outpace top-line revenue gains over the long term.

#3132. Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training – here’s how

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

You’ll soon be able to turn off Gemini model training but still retain access to your previous chats with Google’s AI.

Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me

In a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road.

Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two.

To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. With the second setting, you’ll be able to decide whether your chats, including all text and attachments, will be used for model training.

Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes

“With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google said in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email.

Here’s how this will play out. If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, both new settings will be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on, both new settings will be on. That means you’ll need to head to Gemini’s Settings if you wish to opt out of model training but still be able to view and access your previous chats.

ChatGPT offers a setting called “Improve the model for everyone,” which is double-speak for model training. But this is easy enough to turn off. Microsoft Copilot provides settings for “Training on conversation activity” and “Training on voice conversations,” both of which you can disable to opt out of model training. Claude’s AI training option is turned off by default. But you can always control this by checking the setting for “Help improve our AI models.”

The Chrome update includes more useful vertical tabs, easier screen sharing, and some handy keyboard shortcuts.

On Monday, Google rolled out an M157 update for the Chrome web browser on Googlebook OS, with a handful of new features and performance boosts to streamline your workflow and browsing experience.

While the first Googlebooks on the market have received mixed reviews, these features could help the laptops gain more useful features in Chrome that other browsers already offer.

Also: Googlebooks? The best laptop for Android users is something else

Here are the five new Chrome features on Googlebook OS to know about.

If you’ve ever had to share your screen on a video call, you know how irritating it can be to switch tabs without having to repeatedly start and stop sharing. When you hover over a collapsed vertical tab rail with your mouse or trackpad, it will expand, so you can read full tab titles, switch tabs, or manage groups. The rail will collapse again when you move the cursor away.

If you have Chrome set up to automatically download and install updates, you won’t have to lift a finger to take advantage of the new features and performance boosts.

#3128. Fathom Forthcoming: First Battery Cells Roll Out of Ford’s Michigan Plant for Electric Pickup

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Ford's BlueOval Battery Park Michigan is shipping its first lithium iron phosphate cells to Louisville for Fathom prototypes, a key milestone for the automaker's next-generation EV.

This week, Ford began shipments of the first lithium iron phosphate electric vehicle battery cells from its new BlueOval Battery Park in Marshall, Michigan, to its Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky. There, the prismatic cells will power early Ford Fathom electric pickup truck prototypes and validation vehicles. The automaker invited me into the plant to meet the people who build the batteries and to see how the so-called “jelly roll” is made.

In 2025, consumers lost access to the clean vehicle tax rebates of the Inflation Reduction Act, but the program and its incentives remain in the law for automakers and suppliers. So bringing this US-based, domestically owned battery plant online is kind of a big deal for Ford. It’s an important milestone for the automaker’s plan to make its new Universal Electric Vehicle, or UEV, platform a reality and to bring the Fathom — its upcoming electric pickup truck — to market in 2027 at a price that EV-eager customers can stomach.

Ford expects to sell the upcoming Fathom at an estimated price of $28,350 (well, $29,945, including the $1,595 destination and delivery fee), with the first preorder expected to open early next year.

BlueOval Battery Park Michigan is a $3 billion, 2 million-square-foot facility with a targeted annual production capacity of 20 gigawatt-hours. That’s a whole lot of batteries. Ford is expected to employ 1,700 people at the site across two 12-hour shifts, running around the clock to reach that capacity.

The plant is a clean facility, so getting in meant donning a clean suit, mask, hairnet, gloves and two layers of shoe booties. I then crossed special magnetic and sticky floor panels designed to pull any metal particles off the bottoms of those booties, before passing through multiple air-blower airlocks that blasted my body clean of loose dust.

From the outside, the building is huge and difficult to take in completely. On the inside, the scale truly comes into focus as I stare down a massive hallway just under a mile long end to end. Raw materials — rolls of copper and aluminum sheet, plus the chemical powders that coat them — enter the plant at the eastern end, move in a straight line through the facility, and completed battery packs exit at the western end. The first 0.7 mile of the fab belongs to cell production, split between isolated cathode and anode lines that join halfway through for final cell assembly.

Ford engineers, battery experts and executives tell me that the automaker chose lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, chemistry in a prismatic (rectangular) format for its affordability and structural benefits. LFP uses no nickel or cobalt, which keeps costs down, and Ford found the chemistry well suited to bidirectional charging.

To keep costs low enough to deliver a reasonably priced car, Ford couldn’t use a Chinese supplier and still qualify for IRA manufacturing credits. So it licensed the technology from one, working with a company called CATL, which one Ford exec described as “the world’s leading battery manufacturer,” whose batteries power 30 million vehicles worldwide.

Despite working with a Chinese company, Ford says the plant is completely US-owned, staffed and operated and is totally IRA-compliant, with no foreign entity of concern, or FEOC, involvement beyond the licensing agreement.

Charles Poon, who leads vehicle hardware engineering, said Ford didn’t simply copy a catalog part.

“We designed a unique cell that does not exist in the CATL catalog, specifically for the UEV,” Poon said, adding that the taller and simpler cell delivers “the energy density, the affordability, the durability that [Ford is] looking for” and allows the automaker to more completely integrate the cells and battery pack into the vehicle’s design.

Ford also had to build the supply chain, Poon said, sourcing an IRA-compliant stream for a battery chemistry that is only just entering the mainstream in North America, and working with approved global partners and North American suppliers.

On the cathode and anode assembly lines, meter-wide rolls of copper and aluminum are first coated with a chemical slurry that is baked on. The large rolls are then split into 10 smaller rolls, with tabs notched into their exposed edges at set intervals. As the continuous rolls pass through multiple machines like gigantic cassette players, AI-powered vision systems watch the foil for coating defects, scratches and wrinkles, marking problem sections so they can be automatically removed.

Next, the cathode and anode foils are layered and rolled into a cylinder, then pressed flat into what Ford calls a jelly roll. Imagine a roll of toilet paper mashed in a hydraulic press, and you’ll have a good idea of what it looks like: a flat rectangle with rounded ends.

The jelly rolls are then gathered in pairs, and the previously exposed tabs are folded together and ultrasonically welded to more solid terminals, which are in turn laser-welded to a cap. The jelly roll couple is then laser-sealed into an aluminum box, about the size and weight of a masonry brick, to form a nearly complete prismatic cell. Engineers vacuum out the air, check for leaks by pressurizing the cell with helium, and fill it with liquid electrolyte. Bob’s your uncle: you have a finished LFP prismatic cell.

Ford says the assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, which plant manager Tracy Church says makes BlueOval Battery Park “among the fastest LFP prismatic lines outside China.”

From the cell line, completed prismatic cells would normally pass through a door and straight into pack manufacturing, where full battery packs with integrated “e-box” electronics, integrated cooling and wiring are built. That part of the plant is still undergoing validation, so for now Ford is shipping just the cells to Louisville, not complete battery packs. The company plans to have pack manufacturing up and running in Marshall ahead of Fathom’s launch, with full pack deliveries to Louisville planned in 2027. Church told me that the plant aims to produce 50 battery packs per hour.

Ford hasn’t officially specified the energy capacity of the cells or the completed battery packs and wouldn’t comment when asked about expected range for the Fathom. The automaker wouldn’t even confirm how many cells go into the EV’s pack, but I estimate between 90 and 108 cells based on a cutaway of the finalized unit I examined (but wasn’t permitted to photograph) during my tour. I expect Ford is holding off on finalizing details until closer to the EV’s 2027 launch window.

Battery Park Michigan isn’t just sending cells to Kentucky; it’s also sending expertise. Ford’s Glendale Kentucky plant — which used to build batteries for the F-150 Lightning full-size electric pickup — is currently being retooled to build LFP cells for Ford Energy for large-scale energy storage applications, and the lessons Ford learns in Michigan are already being shared with the manufacturing teams there.

Ford has been in the EV business for over 15 years. In 2011, it revealed the Focus Electric at CES. 2019 brought the debut of the Mustang Mach-E — which Ford recently found is holding up well after years on the road with minimal battery degradation — followed by the arrival of the F-150 Lightning in 2021. This isn’t the brand’s first electric rodeo, but executives tell me that the automaker has never had this much control and ownership over its battery production, and it’s hoping that will make the difference as it prepares the next-gen UEV vehicles.

#3126. Goodbye, Gemini Gems: How to use Google’s new Skills – and share them

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Google is retiring Gemini Gems. Here's what to do to access the same tools as Skills.

Google is replacing Gemini Gems with Skills starting Nov. 17, 2026, and it’s carrying over features that let you share Skills and add files from Google products.

Google has announced that it’s turning Gems, a Gemini feature that lets you create customizable AI chatbots, into Skills, which let you create custom instructions for Gemini. Any Gems you have created will automatically convert, but you can transfer them manually if you want to start using them now.

To help with the transition, Google revealed that two Gems features are moving, too: the ability to share creations and to include Drive, Notebook, and Photos files as part of your Skill’s instructions.

While the Gemini Gems feature is technically going away, any Gems you’ve created aren’t.

If you access the Gems portion of Gemini (since the feature is on the way out, you now have to access this through Settings), you’ll see a message that says “Starting November 17, 2026, we’ll automatically begin migrating all of your Gems to Skills.” (The cutoff date for accessing your Gems will be Dec. 16, 2026. Workspace business, enterprise, and non-profit accounts will get cut off in March 2027, and Workspace education accounts will be cut off in June 2027.)

A Gemini Skill functions much the same as a Gem. You describe specific situations when Gemini should use the Skill automatically and tell Gemini what you want the Skill to do (it’s best to give specific examples of output). Google gives the example of a marketing team sharing a brand-voice skill that references their brand guidelines doc in Drive, or a team lead sharing an onboarding skill based on the team handbook.

The biggest difference is that Gems were standalone chats, while Skills are custom instructions that work in any conversation.

You can create as many Skills as you want, but only 100 can be active at a time.

To get users familiar with Skills, Google is bringing over two features from Gems.

First, you can now share any Skill with other users. When you share a Skill, you can choose whether the other person has permission to edit or view only. To share a Skill, go to the three-bar menu in the top left > Customize > Skills. You can view or change permissions from that screen.

Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours

When a Skill is added, Gemini can use it automatically, or you can @mention it in chat to trigger it. One small caveat, though: you can only share Skills through the Gemini web app at the moment, not the mobile app.

Additionally, when you’re creating a Gemini Skill, you can choose to include files of up to 100MB from other Google products like Drive, Photos, and Notebook, along with files from your local device. Gemini will reference these files every time the Skill runs and update in real time, Google says. These features existed with Gems; Google is just moving them to Skills to make the new feature more comparable.

#3125. Not Safe, Not Creative: 123456 Is Still the World’s Most Common Password

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Cybersecurity

Data breaches, hacks and cyberattacks. Guess what? Our passwords are still risky.

Our data keeps getting hacked, breached, stolen and exposed, and yet we’re still using the most predictable passwords.

For the seventh time in the past eight years, 123456 is the world’s most common password, and it’s got other uncreative companions on the list, according to the latest analysis by password and passkey manager NordPass, a division of Nord Security. The top three most used passwords in the US were: 123456, password and admin. Yikes.

In the 44 countries analyzed, the password 123456 was used more than 7.2 million times. The rest of the top 10 passwords: admin, 12345678, 123456789, 1234, 12345, password, Aa123456, Pass@123 and 1234567890.

NordPass said that even though many people prefer simple, easy-to-remember passwords, much more awareness of password safety is needed. The company recommends creating a unique password for each account that’s at least 15 characters long, including uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and special characters. Though it’s tempting to reuse the same passwords, hackers rely on that complacency.

NordPass suggests upgrading weak, old passwords to stronger ones. You can also add multifactor authentication, which requires an additional layer of security beyond a login password. That could mean entering a one-time passcode sent by text or email, answering security questions, or using facial recognition or fingerprint ID.

CNET managing editor Adam Benjamin said that the risk isn’t primarily from someone randomly guessing your password. The danger is from algorithms that collect data or bots that use credential stuffing (in other words, stolen username and password pairs obtained from a data breach).

According to Benjamin, using an obscure reference or a different language doesn’t make a password stronger. “A password is good when it’s too much trouble for an algorithm to crack,” he said.

You might remember the scene from the 1987 movie Spaceballs, where the combination to Planet Druidia’s air shield is 12345. Dark Helmet calls it “the stupidest combination I’ve ever heard in my life!” and says it’s “the kind of thing an idiot would have on his luggage.” The joke remains a staple reference for weak passwords and PINs, and yet, here we are.

Last year, two researchers hacked into McDonald’s hiring chatbot by guessing the password 123456 to access 64 million data records, including applicant names, email addresses and phone numbers.

In 2023, the Akira ransomware group hacked into KNP Logistics Group, a 158‑year‑old UK transportation firm, by guessing an employee’s weak password. The hackers locked the company’s data and demanded a $6.6 million ransom, forcing KNP to shut down and lay off 700 workers.

This year, suspected Iranian hackers gained access to US water supply systems due to internet-connected devices that used default passwords — or none at all.

The rise of the AI era has also made password hacking easier. One study even found that some AI systems could determine people’s passwords by listening to their keystrokes.

NordPass has conducted its Top 200 Most Common Passwords analysis since 2019. To compile its lists, NordPass and independent researchers examined passwords exposed in public data breaches and dark web repositories, then organized and categorized the data by country of origin.

NordPass has found that password habits are heavily influenced by current trends and culture. Over the last several years, some of the top three passwords have been Lebron0319 (in reference to NBA star LeBron James), Savage20 (musical group) and roblox.com1 (video game). In the 2010s, the top three were Lachimolala (meme), telegram (social media) and minecraft (video game).

But while these passwords might make us feel nostalgic for these time capsules of experiences, interests and entertainment, they don’t translate to strong internet security. “Unfortunately, fandoms make for terrible passwords,” the NordPass report notes.

Passwords based on pop culture, current events and sports can be easily predicted or cracked in seconds using automated tools, especially if your interests are visible on public social media profiles. Adding a number to the end of a password doesn’t help — attackers program their tools to test common number combinations and symbol swaps.

Given all the accounts we deal with — financial institutions, social media, stores, government agencies — creating dozens of unique passwords and remembering them can be exhausting and annoying.

“Inventing passwords that meet that criterion across hundreds of logins is virtually impossible, which is why we recommend password managers to create long, complex passwords and then store them all for you,” said Benjamin.

A password manager creates and updates passwords for apps, Wi-Fi networks and websites, ensuring that all your passwords are unique and resistant to bot attacks. Another plus is that you don’t have to remember them or write them down: They’re stored in an encrypted vault you can access by verifying your identity. Password managers can also auto-fill login credentials.

CNET senior writer Joe Supan said the best password managers also offer passkeys, which are ways of logging into apps and websites using biometric ID, such as facial or fingerprint scans, or PIN codes. “These are really the sign-in methods of the future, and I probably wouldn’t recommend a password manager that doesn’t include them at this point,” Supan said.

CNET’s top two recommendations for password managers are NordPass and Bitwarden.

#3122. Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Microsoft announced two new AI models at Ignite 2026 that promise impressive performance for much lower cost. They could reshape its relationship with OpenAI and Anthropic for good.

At today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the company introduced two new frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks. But there’s a bigger story: what these models might mean for Microsoft’s AI costs and its dependence on OpenAI.

Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model shows 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Microsoft says MAI Code 2 offers comparable performance to GPT-6.1 Sol or Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft’s Code 2 Flash model is comparable to the lower-end GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, also at considerably lower cost.

This doesn’t mean that those of us who pay for $100/month subscriptions will suddenly get the equivalent for five bucks. Instead, these are usage-based metrics based on API usage.

It’s also important to understand that the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests.

Throughout Satya Nadella’s keynote, Microsoft showed slides referencing a wide range of foundation models that are intended to work with Copilot and other Microsoft offerings. Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023, and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property.

But now, Redmond is benchmarking its internally built models against Anthropic and OpenAI offerings, and also touting that it’s integrating these new models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365, and Fabric.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex

One thing that Nadella made clear in today’s keynote is how central AI is becoming in everything Microsoft does. Nearly all of those AI operations previously involved the company paying some token fees back to the frontier model providers or customers doing the same thing.

But with high-performing models of its own, Microsoft may become substantially less dependent on outside model providers, especially for the incredible volume of fairly basic and routine AI requests that occur across the company’s vast product line.

If you think back over the history of agentic work models like ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork, you may recall that they originated as agentic coding tools. As users adopted the coding harnesses in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to off-label productivity applications, the AI companies noticed and packaged work-centric agentic tools that were more non-programmer-friendly.

Also: I let ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork loose on my files – only one made me nervous

There’s a lot of similarity between a coding agent and a work agent, including understanding a complex environment, using tools to change things, and producing reliable results. Coding turns out to be a very good environment for developing and testing these capabilities, particularly because code output is highly measurable. Coding agents are effective training grounds for non-coding work agents.

This becomes really interesting in today’s announcement. Along with Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, Microsoft announced MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash. Work Flash can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, track decisions and extract useful information from Teams, and more.

Think about the level of intelligence these tasks are demanding from the AI models. Not that much. As long as the models are good enough, they’ll be good enough.

If Microsoft can reduce its expenses and use reliable models at a much lower price, the company itself will be able to save quite a bit of money across its entire software economy, while at the same time maintaining a deeper level of vertical integration and, therefore, control.

Let’s run some hypothetical numbers. Let’s say a company is spending $0.01 per AI request, which, with these new models, can drop down to $0.001 per request.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first

A company with a daily inference cost of a million dollars (a company like Microsoft, for example) could drop that daily cost to about $100,000. Add that up across a year, and the change in models could save $325 million annually.

A million here, a million there. Pretty soon, you’re talking real money.

There’s no direct evidence that Microsoft is trying to produce replacement models for the frontier providers’ offerings. But it is an interesting and compelling story if we look at Microsoft developing its own engines for the software it sells.

Microsoft says the numbers it’s reporting at are using a 50% introductory discount. That’s why I measured against $0.001 per request instead of $0.0005 per request above.

Benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The numbers are impressive. But as we all know, there are lies, damned lies, and benchmark results. I’m fairly sure Microsoft isn’t padding these numbers too much, because it benefits from the new models more than even its own customers, but still. It’s an open issue.

The company also described clearly that these new models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads. You’re probably not going to use them to solve a decades-old mathematics challenge. But you’re very likely to use them to reformat your PowerPoint.

Speaking of reformatting your PowerPoint, Microsoft also emphasized that these new models did unusually well on visualization assignments. That’s a very good fit for not only UI design challenges but also graphics and slide production.

#3119. Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft could reshape enterprise spending, but there's a critical difference between estimated value and money saved.

We all know AI can get expensive. But does that expense result in real business value? That’s the trillion-dollar question Microsoft aims to answer with today’s introduction of Agent 365 Business Analytics.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

Earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees. With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft is attempting to build an accounting system for AI labor. The system attempts to calculate the economic value of the work performed by agents compared with what the agents cost, and then provide a return on investment estimate.

If it works, this is some very cool stuff. Microsoft is trying to map labor-market economics onto AI usage data to create value estimates.

Also: Work IQ is Microsoft’s big bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions

To do so, it uses real labor-costing information, including data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and its own LinkedIn Occupational Graph.

This data, along with data gathered from Agent 365, is aggregated into analysis intended to answer:

The goal is to provide a comprehensive picture of AI spend against value produced.

Software accounting is long established and straightforward. We measure subscription fees, cost per seat, compute costs, burden costs (like floor space and other infrastructure), and more. But AI work doesn’t fit that model, making it very hard to quantify value.

Instead, Agent 365 Business Analytics measures cost both relative to human labor and in terms of technological expense. For example, it might look at a task and determine how much human effort that task would normally take, and then price that effort based on prevailing common labor rates.

Then, it might factor in how much of the task was actually done by a human vs. how much was contributed by an AI, along with the estimated value of the AI’s contribution. Then it mixes in the actual AI processing cost (whether in subscriptions, tokens, on-premises infrastructure, and cloud support).

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s new

What comes out is a hybrid labor estimate that combines human contribution, human-replacement savings, AI costs, and then potentially AI savings over human costs. It sounds positively Orwellian. But the bottom line is that companies really haven’t been able to understand the AI bottom line.

There’s a catch. All these numbers are estimates. In its blog post, Redmond specifically says, “Assisted hours are a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return.”

In other words, what Agent 365 Business Analytics estimates might not actually line up with real-world experience or expenses. It’s also possible that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not that the AI was saving company labor costs with every token processed.

In other words, Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work, but it can’t demonstrate definitively that the company saved any real money.

Also: 5 reasons your company needs a chief AI officer in 2026

I find it particularly telling that this is from the company that makes PowerPoint. Because now, with Agent 365 Business Analytics, it’s entirely possible that you could produce economic dashboards that look really, really impressive, but are entirely irrelevant to real life.

That’s not to say the product is useless. But it does go to the idea that you will have to be quite disciplined in how you interpret the results and how much stock you put in them for decision-making. It is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth.

Microsoft has been investing for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. AI isn’t any different when it comes to the company’s overall mission.

With Agent 365 and the company’s related offerings, Microsoft wants to help you:

This means the company doesn’t necessarily have to provide you with the AI model to help you run your enterprise. With integration with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others, the company doesn’t even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities.

But if it can get in there and manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, Microsoft could own a central piece of your business’s operations.

The Java4Shell vulnerability could allow hackers to take over systems without a password.

A newly identified vulnerability in Oracle Java could give hackers unauthorized access to major applications and allow them to run code without logging in. The flaw could affect a sweeping array of big businesses, including tech companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Apple and Netflix, which rely heavily on Java’s server-side software and core products.

“Roughly 90% of Fortune 500 companies run on Java,” Thai Duong, CEO of cybersecurity firm Calif, said.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (and dubbed Java4Shell), corrupts memory when Java decodes Base64, a standard format used to transmit login credentials and file uploads.

Duong told CNET that his company identified the critical software vulnerability in October and notified Oracle, which has since patched the vulnerability. This week, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued guidance urging organizations to do the same immediately. CISA recommends identifying affected Java installations, reviewing software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, and applying vendor patches as soon as they’re available.

Oracle rated the flaw a serious 8.1 out of 10 on the standard vulnerability scale. It can lead to an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in Java, allowing hackers to run their own malicious commands or code over the internet without requiring a username, password or prior access.

Federico Kirschbaum, head of Security Lab, the research arm at cybersecurity company XBOW, told CNET that Java is primarily used at the enterprise level. As a result, the vulnerability could trickle across different sectors, including finance, government, transportation and large corporations.

“Java is a great language for creating solutions, but this vulnerability — it’s a reminder that maybe the languages that we’re using have flaws, and everything built on those might inherit that problem,” Kirschbaum said.

Amid recent technological disruptions, he suggested leaning on AI solutions to address vulnerabilities in AI.

“That new normal is that most of the technology we rely on has flaws, and now that we have resources using LLMs, we can find those problems,” Kirschbaum said.

He pointed out that bad actors and hackers can also find these vulnerabilities.

“We are in a race to find the problems first and help the industry by guiding them on what’s urgent so they patch it,” Kirschbaum said.

#3114. Voyager 1 Becomes the First Spacecraft to Travel a Full Light-Day From Earth

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Voyager 1 has been flying at about 38,000 mph since 1980. That steady pace carried it a full light-day from home.

NASA’s Voyager 1 left Earth on Sept. 5, 1977, carrying a camera, a set of science instruments and a gold-plated record of sounds and images from home. Forty-nine years later, it’s reached a distance no spacecraft has attained before: one light-day, or roughly 16.1 billion miles, from Earth. At that range, light needs a full 24 hours to make the trip between Earth and the probe.

At 5:16:07 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to reach that light-day milestone. From that point on, a radio signal between the spacecraft and NASA’s Deep Space Network takes more than a day to travel in either direction.

NASA puts the journey at 49 years, two months and 11 days, counting from Voyager 1’s launch in September 1977. The probe still sends data home, though at a rate slower than dial-up, and NASA plans a live discussion with the Voyager team on Thursday to mark the occasion.

It’s quite an accomplishment for a spacecraft built in the mid-1970s. One light-day is the distance that light travels in a single day at the speed of light, which is approximately 186,282 miles per second. That translates to 25.9 billion kilometers or about 16.1 billion miles in a single day. At an average human walking speed of 3 mph, it would take a human 612,015 years to travel that distance on foot.

Fortunately, Voyager 1 has been traveling a bit faster. It currently zips through the cosmos at a steady 37,763 mph, a speed it achieved in 1980 after a gravity-assisted Saturn flyby. It has been flying at that speed ever since.

The milestone comes 14 years after Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the point where the sun’s heliosphere ends, and entered interstellar space. It’s also 28 years after the spacecraft passed Pioneer 10 to become the human-made object that has traveled the farthest into space.

NASA marked the milestone with a global Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day event on Tuesday evening. Just after sunset, the agency wanted people to head outside and point their smartphone or tablet lights skyward to spark a planet-wide wave of light as Earth rotates, much like fans doing the wave at a stadium.

The space agency also made a website for the occasion. The website is simple. It flashes Voyager’s VGR call sign in Morse code. If you want to try it, click the link, hit begin, and then point your phone or tablet screen at the sky. The website does all the work for you.

NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory will follow up on Thursday at noon ET with a moderated discussion on the milestone, featuring status updates on both Voyager probes and a live Q&A with reporters and audience members.

The historic milestone isn’t without its drama. Voyager 1 has been in space for nearly half a century, and in that time, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory has done everything it can to extend the spacecraft’s life. That includes troubleshooting issues, performing maintenance, and shutting down various systems to save power and extend the spacecraft’s lifespan.

Several of those efforts took place in 2026. The team running Voyager 1 spent weeks shutting down three devices and powering on three low-power alternatives to reduce overall power usage. This initiative, which was internally called the Big Bang, was also performed on Voyager 2. The transition was completed in early September, giving Voyager 1 more time with its dwindling power supply while also keeping it warm enough to continue operating in the frigid conditions of interstellar space.

It was a tricky maneuver that required the team to simultaneously turn multiple instruments on and off. The difficulty of the maneuver was amplified by the fact that it took almost a full day for a signal to reach Voyager and another full day for Voyager to send a signal back, with hours of downtime while the spacecraft performed the operations.

All of this took place several months after Voyager 1 experienced a sudden drop in power, which necessitated shutting off one of its three instruments still in operation. Voyager 1 now has only two operational instruments.

Making it a whole light-day away from Earth is likely going to be Voyager 1’s final milestone while it still has enough power to communicate with Earth. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators. They are essentially nuclear-powered batteries that generate energy by converting the steady heat from decaying plutonium-238.

When Voyager 1 first launched, its radioisotope thermoelectric generators produced about 470 watts of power. But plutonium-238 doesn’t last forever, and after 50 years in space, those generators now produce about 215 watts of power, with an average loss of about 4 watts per year. Most of that power is used to keep Voyager 1 up and running, which is why NASA has shut down eight of the 10 instruments that Voyager had when it launched.

At its current rate of usage and decay, Voyager 1 is expected to shut down its final science instrument in the 2030s and will eventually lose communication with Earth in 2036 due to insufficient power to send back a radio signal.

The same fate is expected for Voyager 2, Voyager 1’s twin, which has also spent half a century in space. While it is labeled the sequel, Voyager 2 actually launched 16 days before Voyager 1, and the two have spent nearly identical amounts of time traversing the cosmos. Thanks to its slower speed and trajectory, it likely won’t reach the one light-day distance until after its instruments shut down.

Voyager 1 will lose all of its power before it hits its next milestone, which is the beginning of the Oort Cloud, a vast, icy shell of comets at the edge of our solar system. It’ll take about 300 years for Voyager 1 to make it there.

Thanks to the near-perfect vacuum of outer space, Voyager 1 will continue to fly at its current speed even after it shuts down entirely. So it’ll still hit that milestone; it just won’t be able to phone home to tell us about it.

#3112. Warren Buffett Says Berkshire Will Never Prefer Cash Over Good Businesses. History Says Your Portfolio Shouldn't Either.

Stocks can be wealth creators, but there's a case for having some cash on the sidelines.

By Jack Delaney – Nov 19, 2026 at 1:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›

Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.85%)(BRKB -0.68%) has often been criticized for keeping too much cash on hand. As of Sept. 30, its cash pile, which includes rail and utility cash and Treasury bills, sat at $377.4 billion. For an idea of just how large that is, it's about the market cap of Palantir Technologies (PLTR -1.17%).

That seems to conflict with the preferences of former CEO Warren Buffett, even when he was running the company. In a 2024 shareholder letter, he said, "Berkshire will never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets over the ownership of good businesses, whether controlled or only partially owned."

There's nuance in that statement, however, that offers insight into what investors should consider for their own portfolios.

Warren Buffett. Image source: Getty Images.

The stock market is known for being one of the best sources of wealth creation. As a hypothetical example, a $100 investment at the start of 1928 in the S&P 500 would have been worth $1.1 million by the end of 2025 (dividends included). In comparison, a $100 investment in a three-month Treasury bill in 1928 that kept rolling into those bills was worth $2,578 at the end of 2025.

Based on those numbers alone, it seems less than ideal to keep such a large cash position on hand.

That said, going back to Buffett's quote, there was an important word: "prefer." Buffett is famous for seeking value, whether through acquisitions, stock purchases, or Berkshire's own share buybacks. He may have preferred investing in good businesses over cash and cash equivalents, but if he didn't find any, he was OK with keeping his money on the sidelines until he did.

How much money to keep outside the stock market is a question only an individual investor can answer best, as they know their investing goals and risk tolerance better than anyone. But having some cash to work with allows for more flexibility and will mean an investor isn't selling a position to free up money to pay for another, which can trigger tax implications.

For instance, in 2026, Berkshire's flexibility allowed it to acquire the homebuilder Taylor Morrison in a deal that represented a total enterprise value of $8.5 billion, purchase $10 billion worth of Alphabet (GOOG -1.65%) (GOOGL -1.73%) stock in a private placement, and start a position in the Italian technology conglomerate Bending Spoons (BSP -0.23%), which just went public in July.

Long-term investors can follow a similar playbook. One strategy is to keep cash on the sidelines to deploy whenever an opportunity springs up. Another is considering holding some money back when starting an initial position. That way, either by automating the process or by actively investing during a pullback, an investor can lower their total cost over time.

The long-run returns show that stocks are the vehicles for driving true wealth creation, and owning shares of good businesses is preferable to having too much money on the sidelines. But just having some cash available offers flexibility.

The approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft said it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman said during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

The dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the company has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman said of the new coding model the company announced at Ignite.

The company also released its new image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.

#3110. iFixit Says Apple’s HomeView Breaks Easily. Here’s Why I’m Not Worried

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

iFixit found the HomeView nearly impossible to repair yourself, but smart displays don't face the same daily risks as iPhones.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

For the past few years, Apple was looking almost DIY-friendly. The company had been moving toward smart speakers that you could take apart without damaging and iPads with accessible batteries. But the new HomeView smart display broke apart when iFixit tried to access components in Tuesday’s full analysis.

The good news? I don’t think it really matters, at least not for this particular Apple device. Here’s why.

DIY repairs are a big deal for Apple products, not just because they’re difficult, but because many people believe they have a right to repair their own phones or computers.

Making repairs more accessible also sustains a secondary market of iPhone and Mac repair services that Apple would rather tightly control — or squash entirely. That’s one reason the EU has required Apple to make iPhone batteries replaceable in 2027.

The HomeView moves sharply in the opposite direction, held together by the toughest adhesive iFixit has ever encountered in an Apple product. The glue is so stubborn that the team accidentally snapped a speaker in half during disassembly, and the logic board was bound too dangerously tight to the aluminum chassis to remove.

“Obviously, when you buy a product you don’t anticipate the accidents, and there’s no way of knowing when wear and tear will become a problem,” iFixit said in its report. “But you can be sure of one thing: The HomeView will not be an easy or pleasant repair when that time comes.”

A representative from Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

iFixit also pointed out that if a HomeView device falls out of warranty, the repair typically costs as much as the $299 smart display itself.

I’m just not sure any potential HomeView users need to worry about the device’s repairability the way they would about an iPhone or Mac.

Smart displays don’t have the same DIY repair needs as the phone in your pocket. There’s no battery to replace, which is one of the most common reasons to open up an iPhone or MacBook. And while a shattered iPhone screen can easily be swapped out for a third-party replacement, no aftermarket alternatives exist for the HomeView’s custom 7-inch display. Since you can only get a replacement screen through Apple anyway, making the device easier to open wouldn’t actually help you fix it yourself.

Plus, smart displays don’t face the same environmental risks as phones and laptops, which are constantly on the move, encounter dust in pockets, accidentally dropped and exposed to potential heat and rain. The HomeView is designed to remain stationary in your home. The need for DIY repairs is simply far less of a concern.

I don’t mean to say iFixit’s teardown was unnecessary. We learned valuable information, including how the speakers and their connectors broke in several ways when iFixit tried to remove them. (The speaker assembly is actually one HomeView component I worry people may need to replace.)

“Embedded speakers are a relatively common source of failure. The under-screen speakers inside the HomeView in particular, more closely resemble laptop speakers than HomePod tweeters,” the iFixit report notes. “As far as laptop and MacBook speakers go, we’ve seen plenty of examples of damage caused by accidents and wear and tear.”

I’ve been testing smart displays and smart speakers since they first hit the market, and none of the devices I’ve tested have developed a blown or faulty speaker. In the HomePod subreddit, I couldn’t find any reports of speaker failures except from people already Frankensteining their Apple speakers with third-party components.

I wouldn’t let the fear of repair difficulties get in the way of buying a HomeView. A bigger concern is the HomeView’s compact 7-inch screen, which feels cramped for watching video, especially compared with the larger displays Amazon has rolled out across its Echo Show lineup.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

I've been using Ubuntu 27.04, and the speed boost is noticeable. Here's what else is coming.

Ubuntu 27.04, Tenacious T-Rex, is set for an April 22, 2027 release. Although that seems a long way off, it’s sooner than you think. As is implied by the release number, 27.04 is not an LTS release, so it only receives support for nine months (until January 2028). The good news is that you can migrate from 27.04 to 27.10, and then to the LTS release, 28.04. The entire upgrade path ensures that you don’t have to miss a single release.

But what’s coming in Ubuntu 27.04? Given that it’s an interim release, you’re probably assuming that there’ll be nothing exciting to be found. Although there won’t be any game-changing additions, there will be plenty of refinements and bug fixes.

Also: I’ve used Ubuntu for 22 years – and 26.10 might be its best release yet

I’ve been using the daily release of Ubuntu 27.04 for a bit. Let’s take a look at what is currently expected in Tenacious T-Rex.

This is probably the biggest addition to the next release of Ubuntu. And although you won’t find any major changes in GNOME, there are some important ones. First off, there will be editable quick settings, which allow for customizing, adding, removing, and rearranging toggles and widgets. GNOME 52 will also enjoy a revamped calendar popover, which streamlines the feature to focus primarily on events, time, and weather.

Also: Over Ubuntu? Fedora is the Linux distro I’d hop to next – here’s why

There will also be several improvements to window management, such as a spatial overview and a mosaic/tiling system for auto-resizing and organizing windows, a refined full-screen Alt+Tab app switcher, which will be capable of grouping older windows by application while showing newer ones individually, and finally, the ability to remember window sizing, placement, and workspace.

Desktop search is also getting a bit of polish by way of a redesigned popover and an improved results overlay that includes file previews, multiple actions, and search filters. And, as usual, there will be plenty of bug fixes and performance enhancements. The bump in speed is noticeable, too, in my testing.

Ubuntu 27.04 will ship with the Linux 7.6 kernel, which includes better VRAM management for gaming and expanded support for modern hardware, such as early enablement for AMD Zen 6, stable support for Intel Xe3P, mainline boot capabilities for Apple M3 Pro/Max/Ultra, and initial support for the 2026 Steam Controller.

There will also be performance gains for both the Btrfs and Ext4 file systems, which (along with the improvements in GNOME 52) will make Ubuntu 27.04 one of the best-performing releases in some time.

Also: This lightweight Linux distro revives old PCs destined for the junk pile – and it’s beautiful

With the repository added, you can install it with:

Once installed, you can use it as expected.

As of right now, that’s all we know about Tenacious T-Rex.

It’s so early in the release cycle that it still uses the default 26.10 wallpaper, but there will be more information soon. I will say this: I’ve come to count on Ubuntu’s latest releases to be an improvement over the previous iterations, and from what I’ve seen so far in my testing, 27.04 will not disappoint. #3106. Scout Motors Is Using AI Earpieces to Train Factory Workers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The automaker is replacing the instructional binder with an AI voice that walks new hires through hands-on tasks, and it sees the same approach reaching service centers and, eventually, owners' garages.

“AI training” usually refers to instilling artificial intelligence with human knowledge. Scout Motors says it’s been doing the opposite: using AI tools to help hire, onboard and train factory workers, including an AI assistant in an earpiece that guides trainees through tasks as they perform them.

CEO Scott Keogh spoke with CNET during a reporters roundtable at Scout’s still-under-construction factory in Blythewood, South Carolina. Keogh said that rather than “sitting new hires down with an instructional binder and a test,” workers are getting AI-driven, hands-on experience early in a push to make the training more efficient and effective. Meanwhile, the automaker can collect and feed training data back into the system to fine-tune its hiring, training and placement processes.

Keogh described the approach as starting from the work itself. Manufacturing, he said, can be broken down into a handful of fundamental tasks, and the AI system is built to teach each one. He offered parts picking as the simplest example: A worker walks to 12 boxes, pulls 12 parts, confirms they’re in the right sequence and checks them for defects. The AI in the earpiece can guide the worker through that sequence, providing real-time, adaptable instructions.

“We can train that within minutes,” Keogh said. “A worker repeats the cycle about 15 times, getting faster and better each pass, and then moves down the task line to the next skill.”

To my ears, that doesn’t sound like the sort of task you’d need an AI system to help with and, to some extent, Scout’s executives agreed.

However, the automaker’s representatives argued that the new method is far more productive than traditional classroom training — with increasing benefits as the trained tasks and concepts become more complex. Keogh also linked the speed at which the company has seen its newest factory hires become productive with how quickly Scout can ramp up the factory itself.

Scout execs say AI also plays a role in the hiring and onboarding before training begins. Todd Johnson, vice president of manufacturing, said the team feeds new hires’ backgrounds into an AI system, which suggests where each person might fit best: A former forklift driver might be steered toward logistics, someone with no final assembly experience might do better in the body shop and a person with paint shop experience could be placed as a painter.

Again, that sounded a lot like common sense to me. Isn’t that how people were hired before AI? According to Scout Motors’ leadership, the algorithm can potentially identify less obvious connections between skills and tasks that a human might miss, expanding access to jobs for applicants who may not have received traditional manufacturing training, which is important because Scout’s new plant is located in an area that doesn’t have a large pool of local dyed-in-the-wool traditional automotive workers.

To fill the over 4,000 roles that factory will need to reach full speed ahead by 2028, the automaker says it’s hiring from a national pool of applicants. However, executives told me that using AI to consider nontraditional factory workers — citing one hire who worked at the DMV — will allow Scout to identify and place more local applicants and bring fresh ideas to the factory floor.

Ryan Decker, vice president of strategy and brand, called Scout’s AI-forward approach to placement and training “a passion project for the company.” Decker told CNET that Scout’s training AI can tailor instruction to each person rather than delivering the same material to a room of 10 people over 10 days. People learn differently, he said, with different language skills and levels of technical depth.

Decker also said the system is bidirectional. The AI can learn from how each group responds to the training and use that information to modify instruction for the next cohort. Decker thinks that each subsequent batch of workers will be “1% better,” and that after 1,000 repetitions, he expects the AI to be “dialed in and know how to provide information to the people in the most productive way possible.”

Scout says it’s also exploring vision-based AI training, in which the trainee is guided via augmented reality glasses, as the next evolution of the technology. The automaker is also looking to eventually expand the tech for do-it-yourself use by owners at home. I imagine a future where owners can use an Apple Vision Pro or similar device — which would be a pricey investment — to guide themselves through installing a roof rack or performing routine maintenance.

In practice, the next step, according to Scout’s execs, is to scale its AI learning tools beyond the training room and into the actual factory and service centers, where the automaker believes the tech can continue to improve on-the-floor productivity and guide its workers as they advance through their careers.

Decker says the AI can ingest and organize decades of institutional knowledge, making it accessible to workers during and beyond the training process. Scout has been feeding the AI equipment manuals and manufacturing documentation spanning multiple decades, disciplines and countries — what Decker called “hundreds of years of accumulated enterprise know-how” — which the AI earpiece can surface in real time, something he said was near impossible to do before in a world of binders and PDFs.

Scout’s AI-fueled “passion project” arrives amid broader tensions across industries affected by artificial intelligence. Companies are eager for the efficiencies AI promises, while workers worry the same technology could eventually cost them their jobs. Scout’s executives didn’t address that concern directly in this exchange. Keogh framed the payoff in terms of speed — how quickly a new hire can be made productive — leaving the wider workforce conversation for another time.

Editors’ note: Antuan Goodwin’s travel costs were covered by Scout Motors. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

#3105. Gemini app for Mac adds computer use to control desktop apps

Google is upgrading the Gemini app on Mac with computer use capabilities that can work across local desktop applications and the web.

The existing Task (previously Gemini Spark) functionality in the Mac app could just access local files in conjunction with Connected Apps, like @Gmail or @Google Calendar.

Computer use lets Gemini for Mac click and type on your behalf to accomplish multi-step tasks in local desktop apps and the web, like navigating menus and filling out forms.

Gemini works in an “isolated background window with a live preview right in your chat,” while your main screen and cursor remain free to use. Many everyday tasks span desktop apps and websites that don’t connect to each other. Computer use handles the tedious steps in the background so you can save time without giving up your screen or cursor.
