To meet the increasingly sophisticated trading and asset allocation needs of high net worth clients, we launched over-the-counter derivatives trading in Hong Kong and introduced the wholesale fund to professional investors in Malaysia.

Our AI assistant has also expanded into wealth management, supporting clients throughout the investment process from portfolio analysis and fund selection to ongoing portfolio monitoring. As a result, wealth management penetration climbed to 28.2%, representing 1.13 million customers.

Leon Qi: [Interpreted] Turning to trading volume. Total trading volume was HKD 5.01 trillion, up 28.4% year-over-year and down 22% quarter-over-quarter, as softer equity market conditions, particularly the sharp pullback in semiconductor and AI-related names, dampened client trading activity. U.S. stock trading volume declined 24% sequentially to HKD 3.81 trillion. Hong Kong stock trading volume declined 19.2% quarter-over-quarter to HKD 942.5 billion.

Leon Qi: [Interpreted] On IPO services, amid continued strength in Hong Kong's IPO market, we provided IPO-related services to more than 70% of new listings and served as joint bookrunners for several prominent IPOs, including those of Momenta, Longsys and Mech-Mind Robotics.

Leon Qi: [Interpreted] Despite near-term volatility in global equity markets, we remain confident in our long-term outlook. Rising investable wealth across Asia, growing demand for multi-asset allocation and continued rising use of digital financial services remain our long-term growth drivers. Our priorities remain clear: deepening client relationships, expanding our wealth management capabilities and strengthening our international franchise, laying the foundation for sustainable growth.

Leon Qi: [Interpreted] Now I'd like to invite our CFO, Arthur, to discuss our financial performance.

Arthur Chen: Thank you, Leaf and Leon. Please allow me to walk you through our financial performance in the third quarter. All the numbers are in Hong Kong dollars, unless otherwise noted. Total revenue was HKD 6.7 billion, up 4.5% from HKD 6.4 billion in the third quarter of 2025. Brokerage commission and handling charge income was HKD 2.8 billion, down 4% year-over-year and 17% Q-o-Q. The year-over-year decrease was mainly due to the decrease in blended commission rate from 7.5 basis points to 5.6 basis points, partially offset by the 28% year-over-year increase in the total trading volume, while the sequential decline was due to lower trading volume as market sentiment softened from the previous quarter.

Interest income was HKD 3.2 billion, up 4% year-over-year and 1% Q-o-Q. The year-over-year growth was mainly driven by higher interest income from margin financing and bank deposits, while the sequential growth benefited from higher interest income from bank deposits and securities lending business. Other income was HKD 735 million, up 65% year-over-year and 3% Q-o-Q. The year-over-year increase was primarily attributable to higher currency exchange income and fund distribution service income. The Q-o-Q increase benefited from higher fund distribution service income. Our total cost was HKD 1.1 billion, up 34% compared to the third quarter of 2025. Brokerage commission and handling charge expenses were HKD 239 million, up 49% year-over-year and down 4% Q-o-Q.

These movements were broadly in line with the year-over-year increase and the Q-o-Q decrease in trading volume, respectively. Interest expenses were HKD 586 million, up 24% year-over-year and 14% Q-o-Q. The year-over-year increase was mainly due to higher expenses associated with margin financing. The Q-o-Q increase was mainly driven by higher interest expenses associated with our securities lending business. Processing and servicing costs were HKD 236 million, up 48% year-over-year and 5% Q-o-Q. Both the year-over-year and the Q-o-Q increase were primarily driven by higher product service fees. As a result, total gross profit was HKD 5.6 billion, broadly stable year-over-year. Gross margin was 84.2% as compared to 87.6% in the third quarter of 2025.

Operating expenses were HKD 1.6 billion, down 7% year-over-year and 9% Q-o-Q. R&D expenses were HKD 484 million, down 16% year-over-year and 3% Q-o-Q. The year-over-year and Q-o-Q decrease was mainly attributable to effective cost control measures. Selling and marketing expenses were HKD 545 million, down 7% year-over-year and 17% Q-o-Q. The year-over-year and Q-o-Q decrease was mainly driven by fewer funded accounts. G&A expenses were HKD 561 million, up 3% year-over-year and down 5% Q-o-Q. The year-over-year increase was primarily due to higher office rental expenses, while the sequential decrease was due to lower professional expenses. As a result, income from operations was HKD 4 billion, up 3% (sic) [ 3.5% ] year-over-year.

Operating margin was 60.4%, largely stable compared to the third quarter of 2025. Our net income was largely stable year-over-year at HKD 3.2 billion. Net income margin was 47.6% in the third quarter compared to 50.2% in the same quarter last year. Our effective tax rate for the quarter was 15.8%. That concludes our prepared remarks. We'd now like to open the call to questions. Operator, please go ahead.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question is going to come from the line of You Fan with CICC.

You Fan: [Foreign Language] This is You Fan from CICC. Congratulations on delivering another resilient performance through market volatility. I have 2 questions here. First, we note NASDAQ is planning to launch 23/5 Global Trading Hours in the next month. So how do you see this impacting Futu, both from a business and an operational perspective? And my second question is about regulation. Could you provide an update on the Mainland China client metrics, say, how Chinese Mainland clients' share of funded accounts, AUM and revenue have changed this quarter? And how does management see the future trend of potential outflows? These are my 2 questions.

Leon Qi: [Interpreted] Let me translate Leaf's first part of the answer briefly. We think about this development at 3 levels. First, from a global industry perspective, we think NASDAQ's move toward 23/5 trading reflects a broader structural shift in global capital markets. As more investors are getting used to allocating assets across time zones, global capital markets may gradually evolve from competing across geographies to competing around time zones. That's why we don't view 23/5 as simply extending trading hours. We see it as an important step in the evolution of the U.S. capital market into a truly global marketplace. It reflects the long-term trend of digitization, globalization and cross-time-zone investing. NASDAQ's own data also supports this view.

Extended trading hours, including pre-market, after-hours and overnight sessions, already account for about 11% of total U.S. equity trading volume, with overnight trading making up about 4%. That's a clear indication that the demand is real.

Leon Qi: [Interpreted] And the second layer is what does it mean for Futu? We see it as a structural positive. Our client base is global and across time zones, with a significant portion in Asia Pacific. U.S. equities have also long been one of the most important asset classes on our platform. Over the past few quarters, we've already seen clients gradually building trading habits outside regular market hours. Overnight U.S. equity trading has consistently accounted for a high single-digit to low teens percentage of our total U.S. equity volume. If you include pre-market and after-hours sessions, extended hours trading now represents more than 20%.

That said, the bigger opportunity is not just about near-term trading, but what's more important is client engagement and asset accumulation over the long run. 23/5 further lowers the barrier to global investing by allowing Asian investors to access U.S. markets during their local daytime hours. We believe the long-term implications of that are potentially more significant. From a product perspective, Futu and Moomoo have already supported overnight U.S. equity trading through ATS for some time. We have built experience in execution, clearing and risk management, and we will prepare our infrastructure ready to ensure clients have a seamless experience as market hours expand.

Leon Qi: [Interpreted] The U.S. market is expanding its global investor reach by extending trading hours. Asian markets may eventually face a similar challenge. For international financial centers like Hong Kong, Japan and Singapore, the question becomes how to improve the accessibility for investors across time zones, how to deepen international investor participation, how to balance liquidity and quality and how to use digital infrastructure to better serve global investors. These topics all deserve our ongoing observation. Thank you.

Arthur Chen: [Foreign Language] As we disclosed in our last earnings calls, as of the first quarter end, the Mainland clients' contribution in terms of the funded accounts, client assets and the total revenues accounts for the whole group, the ratio is around 13%, 17% and 20%. We do see a very meaningful steadily Q-over-Q decrease regardless of the absolute amount and also percentage contributions. For instance, the revenue contribution has already come down from 20% in the first quarter to low teens in the third quarter. And I do expect such kind of ratio will continue to go down in the consecutive quarters.

Hopefully, in the next 2 to 3 quarters, all these ratios will go down to just below high single digit. Then in terms of the client asset outflows, we do see in the third quarter, asset outflow from Chinese Mainland clients accounts for low single-digit percentage of our total client assets. Withdrawals from Chinese Mainland and Hong Kong clients were very concentrated in June and July, but Mainland client assets continue to flow out in Q3, though at a relatively slower pace, while Hong Kong and other overseas markets were no longer affected by regulatory-related outflow in 3 quarters.

And excluding Mainland China clients, the group's average client retention rate, as mentioned by Leaf during the opening remarks, in the third quarter still stood above 98%, with the retention rate across overseas markets remaining stable quarter-over-quarter. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Charles Zhou with UBS.

Cheng Zhou: [Foreign Language] This is Charles Zhou from UBS. So as management mentioned that over the past few months, the equity market has been pretty volatile, but I think your business also showed resilience, and we can see both the revenue and profit in line with the market expectations. So now I have 2 questions. The first one is on wealth management. What were the main drivers behind the Q-on-Q growth in wealth management AUM in the third quarter? And how is management thinking about this business going forward?

The second question is that I also noticed that you disclosed net asset inflows for the first time this quarter, which is the third quarter, and also delivering that level of net inflows against a third quarter market backdrop. Overall, this is pretty impressive. So could you please maybe share the rationale behind disclosing this metric and also the business driver behind it?

Arthur Chen: [Foreign Language] In the third quarter, actually, we see the market was pretty volatile, both in Hong Kong and the U.S. stock market. And we can see clients' risk appetite turned more cautious temporarily with capital rotating toward low-risk categories such as money market funds and fixed income products. As a result, our wealth management assets rose 9% Q-over-Q. But more importantly, in terms of the number of our clients holding wealth asset management products increased 5% Q-o-Q, which further increased the penetration rate in this segment. Then on the business front, as Leaf mentioned in the opening remarks, on the product side, we have some new initiatives.

For instance, in Hong Kong, we launched the first weekly dealing mutual funds and the tokenized gold ETF in Hong Kong. And also, we rolled out wholesale fund trading in Malaysia, continuing to broaden our product lineup for high net worth clients. And then in Hong Kong, the number of high net worth clients has already exceeded 10,000, with both client count and revenue in 3 quarters recording double-digit year-over-year growth. And OTC derivative trading capability was also launched in the third quarter to meet the increasingly sophisticated allocation needs for these clients as well.

Then on the AI side, we further extend our capabilities of FutuBull and Moomoo AI into the wealth management front, covering the full investment cycles from portfolio selections and fund screening to position monitoring to enhance both service efficiency and our user experience.

Leon Qi: [Interpreted] The reason we start disclosing net asset flow is to help investors better understand the quality of our client assets. As you may know, client asset balance is driven primarily by 2 factors. One is mark-to-market changes in asset valuation. The other is actual client cash flows. Simply looking at period end client asset balance alone doesn't always tell you how much the growth came from, whether it's coming from market movements versus client behavior. Therefore, we think net asset flows gives investors a clearer view of our ability to attract and retain client assets. In other words, it helps investors to better distinguish between the market beta and the company alpha behind our client asset movement.

Back to the third quarter, we've generated HKD 34.5 billion of net asset inflow. This was mainly driven by 3 factors. First, as both Leaf and Arthur just mentioned, we continue to expand our product offering, covering client demands in different market environments. Second, we see more and more clients are using Futu as a long-term wealth allocation platform rather than only a trading platform. Third, our international expansion has resulted in a more diversified client base. One additional point worth highlighting is the composition of these net flows. Over 60% of net inflow in the third quarter came from existing clients, which are defined as clients acquired prior to the current month.

In fact, this ratio has remained above 55% in every quarter over the past 2 years. To sum up, we view net asset inflow as one of the most important indicators of our long-term competitiveness. It reflects our strategic evolution from focusing primarily on the number of client growth to high-quality client growth, and it gives more visibility of our capability to attract and accumulate client assets. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Chiyao Huang with Morgan Stanley.

Chiyao Huang: [Foreign Language] Basically 2 questions about overseas markets. One is on the U.S. market. I wonder what's the latest update on product suite, customer base and profitability here, and also any outlook to share? And the second one is on Japan. We saw the regulatory penalty on Japan. What's the implication for Japan and the group for some time to come? And also, we are seeing probably resuming customer acquisition in Japan recently. And so what's the pace and any change in strategy there?

Arthur Chen: [Foreign Language] In the third quarter, the net new funded accounts in the U.S. grew against a softer market backdrop, and the revenue contribution from this new client cohort also increased Q-o-Q, reflecting the appeal of our products and the brand to high-quality clients. In terms of trading volume, it is largely flat Q-o-Q, while slightly declined on the U.S. cash equity side, but partially offset by a marginal uptick in option contracts. On the product front, the most prominent product is we launched the prediction markets trading in June, giving investors a new trading tool beyond the traditional equity and options.

In Q3 alone, event contract trading volume reached about 500 million contracts, making it the top revenue contributor among new client cohorts for the quarter. And the prediction market serves not only as a customer acquisition channel, but also helps reactivate existing users. The growth driver in Q3 shifted from World Cup to crypto-related contracts, signaling a gradual transition from event-driven catalysts to more recurring trading categories. And with that backdrop, the profitability of our U.S. retail business continues to enhance. And I do expect at some point next year, we will pass the breakeven point.

Leon Qi: [Interpreted] First of all, we take the issue raised by the Japanese regulator very seriously. We've maintained active communication with the regulator and continue to implement the required rectification measures. These efforts cover areas including internal controls, compliance procedures, client protection and organizational management, and the work is progressing as planned. Moomoo Japan has resumed normal account opening on September 24, following the expiration of the restrictions on new client acquisition. We are taking a prudent approach to client acquisition in Japan and have not resumed large-scale marketing campaigns, but we are accepting and processing new account applications in the normal course of business.

We remain in regular dialogue with the regulator and submit required rectification reports on an ongoing basis. Looking beyond the rectification itself, this process is also an opportunity to further strengthen our governance and institutional capabilities. As our business expands into more markets, we believe strong compliance, risk management and organizational management capabilities are all important components of the long-term success for a financial institution. Accordingly, the focus is not limited to addressing the specific issues identified. It also includes further strengthening of the group's governance framework, resource allocation process and risk management capabilities. Going forward, we will continue to deepen engagement with regulators across our markets and further strengthen our compliance and control framework.

From a group geographic footprint perspective, Japan remains an attractive market. It has a large household financial asset base, and the ongoing shift from savings to investment continues to support greater retail investor participation. Our long-term confidence in the Japan market remains unchanged. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Shuo Yang with Goldman Sachs.

Shuo Yang: [Foreign Language] This is Shuo Yang from Goldman Sachs. We have seen that accelerating adoption of AI across the sector. Could you share management's view on how AI is impacting your products and also the operational efficiency? And the second question is on interest income. We noticed that interest income delivered a strong print this quarter, which helped to underpin revenue growth in a challenging macro backdrop. So the question is, could management break down the key drivers of net interest income and also provide a forward-looking outlook for the net interest income and also the underlying drivers?

Leon Qi: [Interpreted] We tend to view AI as a tool that enhances capabilities rather than simply a tool for cost optimization. First, AI lowers the barrier to investing. In the past, many retail investors had limited access to professional knowledge, which made it difficult for them to fully understand derivatives, quantitative strategies and sophisticated trading tools. AI significantly lowers the barriers to strategy creation. Investors can use natural language to obtain market insights, generate trading ideas and even build and optimize strategies. We believe this can structurally increase market participation and trading activity. AI is also making investing and wealth management services more accessible. Historically, many tools and research resources were primarily available to institutional investors.

AI creates an opportunity for more retail investors to access information, understand markets and make investment decisions more efficiently. As these barriers come down, more people are likely to take a more active role in making their own investment decisions rather than relying on mutual funds or traditional advisory models. This could further expand the self-directed investing population. Given that Futu is a one-stop platform built around self-directed investors, we are naturally well positioned to benefit from that trend. Second, Futu has an ecosystem advantage. Over the years, we have built a relatively comprehensive ecosystem that spans market data, content, community, trading tools, open API, derivatives and wealth management.

With the emergence of AI, these capabilities can work together in combinations. AI connects previously separate functions, further improving user experience and stickiness. Looking ahead, we see agent-based trading as an incremental opportunity. For Futu, a more important opportunity is to use AI to upgrade the user experience of information, tools and trading, helping self-directed investors make better investment decisions more efficiently. Over the long run, we believe AI will not change the fundamental elements of our success in financial services. Technology innovation, product capabilities, compliance standards and brand influence will continue to be the keys of long-term competitiveness. That's why our strategy is always embracing technological innovation while continuing to invest in compliance, risk management and user experience.

Leon Qi: [Interpreted] In the third quarter, around 40% each of our interest income came from client cash and margin financing, with the remainder mainly from our securities lending business. For cash interest income, the increase was mainly driven by a higher interest rate environment in both Hong Kong and the U.S. during the quarter. Client net asset inflows remained resilient, although some client funds continued to migrate into money market funds and other wealth management products, which had some impact on cash balances, but we were still able to manage to realize positive cash interest income quarter-on-quarter growth. For margin financing interest income, the decline was mainly attributable to market volatility and pullbacks in both Hong Kong and U.S. equity markets.

For securities lending interest income, growth was primarily driven by market demand, while the higher interest rate environment also supported lending yields during the quarter. Looking at the longer term, as clients continue to increase their U.S. equity holdings, the pool of securities available for lending should expand accordingly. At the same time, we continue to optimize our lending inventory and broaden our counterparty network, which should provide structural support for the long-term growth of this business. Longer term, we would encourage investors to think about our interest income through 3 factors: client asset balances, client risk appetite and the interest rate. Among them, client asset scale is the most important and sustainable long-term driver.

Ultimately, what matters most is the continued growth of client assets and the increasingly diversified ecosystem across trading, financing and wealth management provided by our platform. More broadly, we have observed that over 20% of our total revenue today comes from businesses that are less correlated with equity markets. We see these as recurring revenue streams or low beta revenue, which primarily include client cash interest income, fund distribution income, market information and data services, trust services and structured products. In the third quarter, such low beta revenue continued to deliver sequential positive growth and achieved double-digit year-on-year growth. We believe this demonstrates the noncyclical side of our revenue model. Thank you for your question.

Operator: I would now like to hand the conference back to Leon Qi for closing remarks.

Leon Qi: That concludes our call today. On behalf of the Futu management team, I would like to thank you for joining us today. If you have any further questions, please do not hesitate to contact me or any of our Investor Relations representatives. Thank you, and goodbye.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect. Everyone, have a great day.

#3103. Your Wear OS smartwatch just got a new way to save battery life

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

It could make your Pixel Watch or Samsung Galaxy Watch more power efficient.

Some of the most popular Android smartwatches just got a battery-saving update. Google released an updated version of Google Play Services on Tuesday that can help extend the battery life of a Wear OS smartwatch.

The v26.45 update concerns location tracking during outdoor workouts. Wear OS smartwatch users can now use their phone’s Global Navigation Satellite System to track their location during an outdoor workout, which can conserve battery life by outsourcing the smartwatch’s energy to the smartphone when it isn’t in Battery Saver mode.

Also: Pixel Watch 4 vs. Watch 5: Is Google’s new model worth it?

Constantly communicating with satellites during an outdoor workout can be a battery drain, and every minute of battery life counts when you use your smartwatch for communication, workout tracking, and health monitoring. GPS services, a bright, always-on display, and continuous health sensors like SpO2 can squeeze the most juice out of your smartwatch.

Wear OS software is used by many of the most popular smartwatch brands, including Google, Samsung, and OnePlus. Both the Google Pixel Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch’s largest batteries last approximately 40 hours. That’s nearly two days of use from two top Android smartwatches, but you’d be surprised how quickly it can drain.

Also: Galaxy Watch 9 review: Health data overload, but built for the future

The update improves battery life without users having to take any action or change any settings — the Google Play Services version 26.45 works quietly under the hood.

That’s not the only Google Play Services update that Wear OS smartwatch users can take advantage of. Another recent update lets users view on their phone a larger preview of any watch face they want to install on their smartwatch.

#3101. At Scout Motors’ New Plant, Validation of Terra and Traveler EVs Has Begun

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Early preproduction Terra trucks and Traveler SUVs are coming together at the Blythewood Production Center. I got an inside look.

At Scout Motors’ South Carolina Production Center, the automaker’s very first electrified trucks and SUVs are being welded, painted and assembled. The revived American automaker has begun the first validation builds of its upcoming Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV at the Blythewood plant, but hold your electric horses — final production and customer deliveries are still a little over a year away.

After a period of slow sales, American interest in electric vehicles and hybrids is on the rise, driven by high fuel costs and the steady growth of EV charging infrastructure in 2026. Scout, with its battery-electric and gasoline range-extended powertrains, could have both of those bases covered when it arrives to compete in America’s most popular vehicle classes (trucks and SUVs) in 2028. It’s worth keeping an eye on Scout as it inches toward production.

I donned my hardhat, steel-toe caps and high-vis vest to get an early look inside the plant.

The Volkswagen Group revived the Scout Motors brand (formerly International Scout) in 2022, and in 2024, the public got its first look at the Terra and Traveler concepts. The two were initially revealed as full-electric models with the option to add Scout’s Harvester onboard gasoline generator to boost the range.

However, demand for the extended-range EV configuration was overwhelming — roughly 87% of the 160,000-plus reservation holders selected the Harvester spec over the all-electric version — and Scout pivoted to delivering the EREV first, then following up with the pure battery-electric model later in production.

Both models are expected to start under $60,000, though Scout has not yet confirmed the exact price difference between the Harvester and pure BEV trims.

In early 2024, the automaker broke ground on the Blythewood Production Center, pledging to invest more than $2 billion in the plant and create more than 4,000 local jobs. A year later, Scout announced plans to add a $300 million supplier park to the complex, supporting around 1,000 on-site jobs at parts suppliers.

Today, construction is mostly complete. (Executives told me it’s about 80% to 95% done, depending on how you measure it.) The walls are up, much of the equipment is in place, and the first movement toward full production of the brand’s extended-range EV and, eventually, battery electric trucks and SUVs has begun.

Scout’s manufacturing and production teams have begun building the first validation builds — early-stage preproduction vehicles that allow factory planners to dial in vehicle quality, confirm the accuracy of the engineering and hone the efficiency of the manufacturing and assembly lines.

These aren’t complete vehicles by any stretch, being pulled from the line at various points to check and double-check that the new factory equipment functions properly and that the right parts arrive when and where they’re needed. Executives warned me that, at this point, there would still be inconsistencies as they dial in panel gaps, welds and the application of various coatings, but that Scout expects the process to be dialed in by the time full production starts in late 2027.

I was able to get up close to these validation vehicles, checking out a body-in-white bare chassis in the body shop, seeing various stages of coatings applied to bare metal, and watching workers complete calibration and alignment of lights and sensors in the final assembly area.

Along the way, Scout told me that more than 160 individual parts must come together to form the vehicle’s chassis, a process supported by more than 750 robots and 5,000 weld points. Once up to speed, the factory body shop is designed to produce around 40 vehicles per hour, with pickups and SUVs sharing the same line.

However, while I saw the robotic welding arms and paint sprayers performing their motions to apply color, no vehicles were actually moving through the assembly line. This early in the process, the automaker doesn’t need a continuous flow of validation vehicles, and many of the factory areas — such as the supplier park that will provide the batteries, electric motors and modified VW Group four-cylinder engines for Harvester models — are still under construction.

Additionally, the validation process gives workers hands-on experience, rather than having them learn from mistakes on cars that will reach customers or being confined to a classroom.

As more parts of the factory complete construction and come online, the validation process will encompass more of the vehicle’s construction until the automaker is ready to start building full customer vehicles. Todd Johnson, Scout’s vice president of manufacturing, tells me that validation will continue into 2027 through multiple preproduction phases starting with the Traveler SUV.

The automaker expects the first customer deliveries of the Traveler Harvester to begin in early 2028, followed by the Terra Harvester and, eventually, fully electric versions of both.

Editors’ note: Antuan Goodwin’s travel costs were covered by Scout Motors. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

#3099. 74% of shoppers trust AI agents for buying advice – but checkout is another story

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Shoppers who use AI agents spend 8% more than the average buyer and purchase 23% more items per order.

Twenty percent of holiday shoppers are using AI agents as their first stop for research and advice, but they are not ready to have agents make purchases, according to the latest Salesforce research.

Also: What to know about early Black Friday sales

Salesforce surveyed more than 2,500 shoppers in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia and found that 74% of shoppers trust recommendations from AI agents. Salesforce research forecasts AI-driven shopping recommendations to drive $75.8 billion in Cyber Week spending, up 13% from 2025.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer

Brands are also being noticed by AI agents, with 30% of shoppers saying they were first introduced to a new brand via AI. And most importantly, 1 in 10 (11%) shoppers would avoid a brand if an AI agent told them to.

Here are some of the key findings from the 2026 holiday shopping research.

Retailers that use AI shopping agents are seeing bigger orders and more loyal customers. The survey found that shoppers who use AI agent referrals are twice as likely to make a purchase. In addition, 39% of shoppers have used AI agents on an e-commerce site, and 80% had a positive experience, while 75% felt more loyal to the brand as a result of the AI agent experience.

Shoppers who use AI agents spend 8% more than the average buyer and purchase 23% more items per order. Brands that use AI agents are seeing seven times faster sales growth than brands without them.

1 in 3 consumers has used an AI agent, including the widely adopted Meta Muse, now used by 12% of all consumers. Grok Bot is also in high demand.

The survey found that 28% of consumers give their agents multiple tasks per day. The most common use of AI agents is price comparisons, product reviews, and brainstorming for gift items. Brand discovery is a major benefit of AI agent use cases.

Agents as advisors are growing, but agents are not buying products yet, with only 19% of personal agent users using logic to check out. Only 9% of consumers allow their personal AI agents to have unrestricted access to their financial details, and 36% have set up a separate credit card for their AI agents.

Also: ZDNET’s favorite tech devices for 2026

The majority of consumers (73%) are not comfortable giving personal AI agents their payment information, and 49% are not interested in agents making purchases on their behalf. Consumers do not want to share their purchase history or personal data that could potentially lead to unwanted charges. Shoppers will abandon an AI agent after 2-3 mistakes. If an AI agent makes a bad recommendation, 1 in 3 consumers will blame the AI.

Retailers must adopt AI shopping agents in order to compete. Retailers must be able to service and respond to shopper agents. The ability to detect intent, buying signals, sources of dissatisfaction, and other consumer-related buying patterns at machine scale (significantly faster and higher volume than human scale) will require retailers to invest in AI agentic engagement capabilities.

Also: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Today, AI agents advise consumers on their holiday shopping journeys, but in the very near future, they will autonomously make purchasing decisions with little to no involvement from their human counterparts. The future of shopping will be more autonomous, highly personalized, and nearly frictionless. Brands that invest in agentic AI will garner the most loyalty and future business.

#3098. Ford Designed Its Fathom EV Battery Pack to Bend in a Crash, for Safety

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Ford is designing the Fathom’s LFP battery to bend in a crash, not be shielded from one — and says the resulting EV will be safer and lighter for it.

Ford’s new LFP battery pack isn’t a fragile electric car component that needs protection. During my visit this week to the automaker’s newly operational battery plant, engineers proudly showed me a video of the battery being crash-tested, the shell and the prismatic cells within bending violently under the force. My jaw practically hit the floor.

Conventional wisdom views an EV battery as a potentially explosive component that, if damaged, can cause catastrophic failure and hours-long fires that are difficult to extinguish. Years of lithium-ion batteries in phones, tablets and laptops taught us that and it’s largely held true for electric cars as well.

So the anxiety is well founded, even if, statistically, EVs are generally as safe as (if not safer than) internal combustion engine vehicles in crash testing and far less likely to catch fire.

Ford dropped that bombshell of a video on me at the end of my tour of its Blue Oval Battery Park outside Marshall, Michigan. However, I was barred from recording or photographing the footage.

The design team’s mantra was “don’t assume a cell must never deform.” For the upcoming Fathom and Ford’s Universal EV platform, or UEV, the pack is designed to carry up to 40% of side-impact forces and is treated as part of the vehicle’s crash structure. The company’s leadership and engineers are confident that the EV won’t catch fire or explode despite the bent cells.

“Traditionally the battery is thought of as payload, a fragile jewel you must protect,” said Vladimir Bogachuk, chief engineer for advanced vehicle structure architecture at Ford. That approach, he said, means heavy bracing and protective structures around the pack. “The battery is not a jewel you must protect,” he said.

Bogachuk (along with every other Ford engineer and executive I spoke with that day) takes a less-is-more stance on the new EV platform. “The best part is no part,” he told me, “and if you have to have a part, it’s pretty much got to serve multiple functions.” And so the engineers set out to remove unnecessary armor and build a battery that serves double duty as an energy reservoir and crash structure.

Without that extra protection, the resulting EV can be lighter and more efficient, with improved driving dynamics. The UEV pack is deeply integrated into the vehicle’s structure: Its top lid is the cabin floor, and the seats bolt directly onto it. The bottom of the pack is the EV’s underbody. A service door beneath the Fathom’s rear seats will provide access to the charging and power electronics for service without the need to drop the pack.

The crash videos showed deformation that would scare me on an older EV, but when I stopped to think, it wasn’t much different from what I’ve seen in conventional car side-impact crash tests. Ford says an impact strong enough to deform the battery would also deform the chassis of a conventional vehicle or traditional EV, so the vehicle would likely be totaled anyway. More importantly, the engineers say the driver would be safe from thermal runaway and fire.

When asked, Ford’s engineers said they don’t believe in a “right chemistry” for every electric vehicle. The UEV platform’s LFP — short for lithium iron phosphate — chemistry, prismatic cells and “jelly roll” construction were chosen for low manufacturing cost, resistance to temperature extremes, suitability for bidirectional energy use and the ability to deform while remaining inert under designed loads and forces.

Other automakers have floated solid-state batteries as a potential solution to battery safety and energy density, but the technology isn’t ready for use in production cars — at least not at the scale and price that Ford needs for the reasonably priced Fathom.

Ford hasn’t stated the LFP pack’s energy capacity, the cell capacity or the number of cells the Fathom’s pack will comprise. Based on a cutaway displayed during my tour, I estimate 90 to 108 individual prismatic cells. The aluminum prismatic cans that enclose the cathode-anode “jelly roll” battery provide structural support and aid thermal dissipation throughout the larger pack.

Wes Thibault, chief engineer for global energy storage systems, described the rigorous validation that the cells and packs underwent to reach the point where they can be trusted to bend like a taco. He told me that Ford has “a dedicated abuse-testing team” integrated with battery design and engineering at every level and stage of the manufacturing process, searching for edge cases and probing the limits of what the chemistry, the cells and full production-spec battery packs can take, from withstanding over 150,000 miles of simulated daily driving to remaining safe and inert in a crash. Along the way, CT scans of the cells offered an inside look at the jelly roll and how it was responding.

Ford’s testing covers structural integrity and load-bearing capability, heat soak from minus 40 to 60 degrees Celsius, IP67 water resistance and humidity cycling, and high-charge and high-discharge tests. For multiaxis vibration, the battery, seats and brackets are strapped to what I can describe only as a giant mechanical bull that shakes the hardware through roll, pitch, yaw and multiple harmonic frequencies. Ford can combine multiple factors in a single test, such as a high-humidity heat soak under vibration during high discharge.

Once the first batch of UEV vehicles are on the road, Ford says it’ll be able to capture real-world data from the fleet to further fine-tune its validation methods for future generations of EVs.

Given how well the first model year of Ford’s Mustang Mach-E‘s batteries have held up after six years and thousands of real-world miles, it’s clear the automaker knows a thing or two about building a reliable battery.

That said, the UEV platform’s LFP chemistry and construction are very different from those of the earlier generation, and the automaker is asking much, much more of the pack than just holding and discharging energy. It’s asking the pack to actively protect the souls onboard in the event of a crash. Testing to failure early and learning from those mistakes quickly is something the engineers I spoke to seem to take very seriously.

This bold, out-of-the-box approach to how the automaker thinks about battery fragility — protecting the souls onboard rather than the “jewel” that is the battery from a potential crash at the end of the vehicle’s life — comes with the promise of more range and efficiency, less weight and more driving fun over the vehicle’s lifetime.

I’m ready to believe. I want EV batteries to be safer and less scary. That promise depends heavily on whether the Fathom’s UEV battery pack is as safe as Ford says it is when it reaches driveways and dealerships in late 2027.

Editors’ note: Antuan Goodwin’s travel costs were covered by Ford. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 19, 2026 at 1:39PM EST

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 19, 2026, NetEase (NTES -9.99%) announced net revenues of RMB 27.9 billion. Lower revenue-sharing costs expanded profit margins across its gaming portfolio. Cash reserves reached RMB 175.2 billion to support ongoing capital returns. Three key takeaways from management stand out.

Value-added services, or VAS, like in-game purchases and subscriptions, became more profitable as distribution expenses fell. Lower revenue-sharing costs allowed profitability to expand even as gaming net revenue fluctuated quarter over quarter.

Player retention and continuous content updates take priority over initial launch hype. Expanding existing titles through new servers and updates creates predictable, multi-year cash flows from established communities.

Liquidity remains a key advantage, backed by a net cash balance of RMB 175.2 billion. Management continues to return cash to holders of American Depositary Shares, or ADSs, through quarterly dividends and ongoing stock repurchases.

Game franchises are extending their operational lifespans through worldwide expansions and seasonal content releases. Internal development expertise and live operations provide structural advantages that help NetEase scale original titles internationally.

Sustaining player engagement across global markets requires disciplined content investments and active community management.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

At least if Tasks disappoints, it won't cost you - unlike OpenAI and Anthropic's subscription-based agents.

Just months after its release, Google is making its Spark agent free and officially renaming its capabilities “Tasks.” You can now toggle to it from the standard Gemini Chat setting. Reports show the rebrand started gradually in mid-October.

Also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

If Tasks sounds familiar, it should: The company already has a product called Google Tasks, which lets you turn emails into a checkable to-do list on the side of your inbox, among other places like Chat and Docs. This is the agentic version, obviously.

Gewirtz, ZDNET’s AI tester-in-residence, wasn’t blown away by then-Spark when he tried it last month, but had reason to believe in its eventual improvement. It’s unclear whether Tasks is meaningfully different from Spark, aside from being out of beta.

Abilities aside, what sets Tasks apart here is cost. Dots and Duet haven’t exactly impressed thus far, so free alternatives don’t have a high bar to reach yet.

Also: I tested OpenAI Dot and Anthropic Duet for weeks

During Gewirtz’s test, when the agent was part of his $20 per month Google AI Pro plan, he used only 20% of the total five hours of usage on “four fairly substantial tests.” Without an AI plan, Gemini’s context window is 32k tokens.

At launch in September, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Muse is “free to use for up to 100M tokens per week,” though Meta’s help center is not so explicit. As with most agentic products, more frequent users may want to buy more access, but more casual users now have two options to compare.

Also: Don’t use Muse? How Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

As with other agents, Tasks, which runs on its newest Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, can handle a variety of jobs for you, from grocery shopping to booking appointments and analyzing your heating bill. Agents like these are designed for a chronically overwhelmed society trained by a reliance on tech to seek convenience and productivity in nearly every aspect of life.

The feature is free in the US, Canada, Korea, Japan, Australia, and India. US users can also start tasks by emailing or texting Gemini, and can have the agent call businesses for them (except in Indiana, Louisiana, Minnesota, Montana, and Nebraska).

The change from Spark to Tasks comes just a day after Google retired Gems (which let you tailor Gemini to specific tasks), and converted existing Gems into Skills. The new landing page for Tasks emphasizes personal finance and cost-cutting as a use case, positioning itself alongside personal finance features from Anthropic and OpenAI.

“Put Gemini on the hunt for ways to save. Identify recurring expenses you no longer need, get alerts for your most-desired deals, and more,” the page reads.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer

“You can adjust task settings, disconnect Google and third-party apps, or delete chat history anytime,’ Google’s blog on the release said. Google’s new Memory summary feature for Gemini lets users view and edit the personal info the chatbot has on them.

#3091. 5 new Apple Health features you should try in iOS 27.3 – if your phone qualifies

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Apple's redesigned Health app arrives in December with some major upgrades, but not every iPhone will get the full experience.

Apple is kicking off a new and improved Health app next month with the release of iOS 27.3. Instead of just recording and displaying your health-related stats, the app will tap into Apple Intelligence to analyze the data and dispense advice on how to improve your health and fitness. But that reliance on AI means you’ll need the right type of iPhone to enjoy all the benefits.

Also: Apple could build its AI health chatbot from this study – how to enroll

Here are five helpful new features built into the app, along with what you’ll need to access them.

First up, the app will offer suggestions based on data from different sources. For example, it might advise you to go for a walk at a nearby park if it detects that you’re not getting enough exercise. It may show you articles and videos about sleep if it finds that you’re not well-rested. It could also highlight possible conditions based on your lab and test results. You can easily view these recommendations from the Insights screen.

Also: Health is Tim Cook’s defining legacy – and your Apple Watch proves it

A new feature called Health Age compares your physical health to your actual age to show how you’re doing. The analysis draws on certain stats and lab data, such as your resting heart rate, sleep, heart rate variability (HRV), cholesterol, and A1C (average blood glucose levels), to deliver a health age, which may differ from your chronological age. The results can show you areas that may be of concern or that you need to focus on.

Also: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Finally, the health tracker I’ve been waiting for

With a new feature called Movement Evaluations and an iPhone and Apple Watch, the Health app can assess your flexibility, strength, balance, VO2 max (maximum oxygen absorption), and overall movement. You perform a physical routine while your iPhone “watches” you via the camera. Using built-in AI, the app will provide audio and visual feedback in real-time to tell you how you’re faring.

Apple promises that the analysis is performed on your device without recording, storing, or sharing the video.

The new app will be able to correlate your test results with data collected by your iPhone and Apple Watch to give you a more comprehensive picture of your health. Plus, Apple and Quest Diagnostics have teamed up to offer people in the US an optional $119 bloodwork panel that covers more than 50 biomarkers to scan for different health and medical conditions.

Also: I tested the Apple Watch Series 12 heart-rate claims against my gold-standard Polar strap

Normally, you need an Apple Fitness+ subscription to fire up workout videos to help you exercise. But the new Health app will come with its own comprehensive set of training videos. Available from the Insights section, a series of strength exercise videos are designed to help you build your body strength. The videos cover all the key areas of your body to give you a full workout.

Some of the new features, such as the strength videos, will be available to all iPhone users. But the ones that rely on AI will run only on phones that support Apple Intelligence. That means you’ll need an iPhone 15 Pro or Pro Max, any iPhone 16 or 17, an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, an iPhone Air, or an iPhone Duo.

One lets you turn off AI tools in Canva, and the other lets you filter out AI-created content from Canva’s library of templates and other elements.

The settings are available now for free and paying users globally, except for those in India, the Philippines and Indonesia. Canva administrators for business and team plans can enable the two new settings for their entire organization.

To turn off Canva’s AI, go to your Profile > Settings > Preferences and toggle Enable generative AI features on or off. To filter out AI in your Canva library, go to Profile > Your account > AI personalization and enable the feature that says show less AI-generated content.

It’s hard not to compare Canva’s new opt-out features to Adobe, which spent all of last week at Adobe Max trying to convince creative professionals to embrace its AI tools. Adobe’s chief technology officer told CNET that he thought the problem was slop, not AI.

As criticisms of AI mount, it’s smart, albeit rare, to see a tech company give its users a definitive, one-click solution to filter out AI tools. We will have to put Canva’s settings to the test to see how effectively they work, though.

If you do want to use AI, Canva has no shortage. Its magic layers tool lets you break apart an AI-generated image into editable layers, a hugely helpful capability for fixing errors and customizing content. Its foundational models, along with other third-party models, can help you generate new image, video and audio content. Outside of graphic design, Canva has added AI tools for spreadsheet, document and presentation work over the past year. And like every other tech company, Canva says it plans to continue investing in AI.

For more, check out our guides to muting Meta AI and disabling Google’s AI on your Pixel.

The new Google Wallet app brings Gemini agentic shopping to US-based iOS users - sorry, no tap-to-pay.

The Google Wallet app is available for iPhone users in the US for the first time. iOS users who download the new Google Wallet app can manage online payments for faster checkout at places that support Google Pay. However, Apple restricts Google’s ability to offer tap-to-pay service on the iOS app, so users won’t be able to use Google Wallet for contactless checkout on iPhone.

Also: You can use Google’s Spark AI agent, renamed Tasks, for free now – with limits

The new Google Wallet app lets you digitize physical cards, including payment, loyalty, and membership cards, as well as boarding passes. Google Wallet app users on iOS will also be able to view receipts and track orders pulled from Gmail in one app.

The biggest difference between the old Google Pay app for iOS and the new Google Wallet is the AI component, which supports agentic shopping, likely as Google’s longer-term play.

The Google Wallet app for iOS becomes the central hub for purchase management in agentic commerce through Gemini. In it, you can view active tasks to see which purchases Gemini is working on, as well as completed purchases and receipts.

Google has been working on two technologies to support its agentic commerce strategy: Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) and Agent Payments Protocol (AP2).

UCP is a technical language that enables AI agents to communicate with retailers and make purchases, while AP2 is the payment framework that establishes rules and authorization for agents to make payments.

Google Wallet serves as both the AI-powered wallet and the consumer-facing record of transactions made by Gemini.

#3087. iPhone Duo, One Month Later: I’m Not Ready to End the Love Affair

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

After making Apple's foldable my daily companion, I've made peace with some shortcomings while resigning myself to others. Mostly, though, there's been a lot to admire.

One month after getting the iPhone Duo, I’ve stuck to my commitment to keep using it even after publishing my review. Well, mostly.

Apple’s debut foldable has proven to be a practical everyday device, whether I’m streaming movies, texting or getting work done. I’ve grown so accustomed to using it that I sometimes forget how much attention it draws when I pull it out of my pocket, especially given its limited availability and lengthy preorder windows – not to mention its sky-high $1,999 starting price.

Still, there have been times when I’ve reached for the iPhone 18 Pro Max instead for its more advanced camera system, as well as its familiar, straightforward design. The Duo’s cameras pull their weight with casual photography, but while filming social content at F1’s US Grand Prix and chatting with filmmakers at an SFFilm screening, I couldn’t resist going for the best cameras at my disposal on the Pro Max. There are times a conventional slab phone just does the trick – without all the frills and novelty of a folding one.

That hasn’t stopped me from keeping the Duo as my primary device. It’s an enjoyable phone to use, with its compact, palm-sized build and spacious inner display. Plus, as CNET’s ongoing folding test demonstrates, it has a durable build that ensures I can fold and unfold it to my heart’s content.

And if I’m being honest, I kind of love how much of a statement piece it’s become.

The Duo’s versatility has really shown its appeal the more I live with it. I find myself using the 5.4-inch cover screen and 7.6-inch inner display pretty equally, demonstrating the practicality of each.

When I’m on the move, the cover screen suffices for sending texts, responding to emails and checking notifications. Lounging around at home, I’m more inclined to use the larger inner display to endlessly scroll through Instagram or binge YouTube videos.

The matte inner display remains one of my favorite elements. It reduces the appearance of the crease as well as glare, making it easier to see content even outdoors. Yes, the coating can dim the vibrant colors in images and videos, even with the screen’s 3,000-nit peak brightness, and smudges become prominent. But I can live with both of those drawbacks, and a microfiber cloth fixes the latter.

Apple’s phone-tablet hybrid came in clutch when I was on a recent flight and didn’t want to pull out my laptop. Instead, I used the Duo’s split-screen mode to place the Notes app on one half of the screen and an informational video on the other so I could quickly jot down the main points. The Duo has also become my gym buddy; I prop it open on the treadmill so I can watch Magpie Murders on a tablet-like display, then fold it up and toss it in my pocket when I’m done.

Apple Pencil support really helps the Duo feel like a mini iPad, and the matte coating on the inner display adds a satisfying resistance that more closely emulates the feel of writing on paper than a glossy surface. It gives jotting down notes, highlighting book passages and marking up documents a more tactile feel. I’m not much of a doodler, but I imagine that’s fun, too.

The Apple Pencil can magnetically attach to the outer surface of the hinge, though it definitely sticks out, so there’s not really a practical, secure way to carry it around with the Duo (at least not that Apple has shared, but case-makers are sure to cook up a solution). I’m glad the stylus also works on the Duo’s cover screen, though the smaller size and glossy display make that experience slightly less satisfying.

The number of apps optimized for the Duo at launch was relatively small, but it’s steadily increased. I gasped aloud on the train platform one morning while sending an email, realizing Gmail had finally been adapted for the Duo. It’s refreshing to see apps that feel intentional and fill the screen, rather than being awkwardly letterboxed.

Apple said in early November that more than 100,000 apps built for the iPhone Duo were live in the App Store. A week later, that number ballooned to over 200,000 apps. So despite a rather slow start, virtually all apps I regularly use now work seamlessly on Apple’s foldable.

One of my favorite apps on the Duo is Instagram’s Edits. When holding the phone open in landscape orientation, I can view the video timeline and make edits on the right side of the screen while seeing a preview of the video on the left. Rotated to portrait orientation, the layout resembles the interface on a traditional smartphone, but on a larger scale, which is helpful especially for making smaller tweaks.

It’s great to see more apps that don’t just expand to the larger screen, but make meaningful use of the Duo’s design.

As I found during my review, the Duo’s battery life has been pretty good. It consistently lasts through the day, even as I hop between displays. I usually charge my phone at night, but even if I don’t, I know I’ll have some remaining battery in the morning.

For instance, one day I started at 6:30 a.m. with a full battery. After my usual routine of checking emails, texting, scrolling through social media and browsing YouTube throughout the day, my battery was at 55% by 9:12 p.m. The next morning, I woke up with 48% battery, and that charge lasted through a similar routine, along with phone calls, texting and music and video streaming, before the battery finally died at 7:30 p.m.

The Duo has yet to give me a reason to stress about its battery life.

I will acknowledge I’m a tad pretentious when it comes to smartphone cameras. But if I’m documenting an event or photographing my fancy tea sets, I want the best cameras I can get. Unlike the Duo, iPhone 18 Pro models have a telephoto camera, more advanced optical zoom capabilities and larger main-camera sensors.

Most of the time, the Duo’s 48-megapixel wide and ultrawide cameras do the trick just fine. Colors are vivid, details are sharp and images are bright. Videos look good, too, though the 18 Pro Max does a noticeably better job with nighttime footage, which can look more muddy on the Duo. Digital video on the Duo also tops out at 6x, versus 24x on the Pros. Most of the time, though, I’m quite content with what I capture with the Duo’s cameras.

As I noted in my review, the under-display FaceTime camera on the inner screen isn’t great, but I never really take selfies using that camera. It feels much more natural to use the 12-megapixel selfie camera on the cover screen, which serves up sharp photos every time.

The cover screen selfie camera plays a critical role in an update that makes using the Duo even more seamless. In its latest iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple added an option to unlock the iPhone Duo using the front camera.

In the absence of Face ID, which I have felt rather painfully, this has been a solid workaround, even if it’s not as secure as Apple’s biometric facial recognition and authentication system. You’ll still need to use Touch ID or a passcode when using Apple Pay or accessing passwords, and to unlock the phone after leaving it alone for around 45 minutes. But a win is a win. (You can also unlock the Duo using an Apple Watch, but I don’t have one.)

I’ll admit I still feel a little bashful when pulling out the Duo because of how much attention it drums up, despite being far from the first foldable phone. But its limited availability and hype paired with the unique design make it eye-catching, for better or worse. Using the Duo has led to some fun conversations, whether it’s with a sales associate as I pay for a pastry or with Project Hail Mary directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller, who spotted the phone in my hand during an interview and geeked out over it. That’s been a fun side effect of using Apple’s first foldable in my everyday life.

I’ve been living dangerously without a case; I don’t want anything to detract from the phone’s sleek feel. This is one of those “do as I say, not as I do” moments, as I’d recommend slapping a case on a phone that costs nearly $2,000. I did put a tempered glass screen protector on the cover display to guard against scratches. I can feel its edge against the otherwise flush surface of the phone when I hold it open, but aesthetic sacrifices must be made.

The Duo isn’t perfect, even if I love using this phone. After holding Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, the iPhone Duo can feel slightly chunky. The Z Fold 8 measures 4.5mm thick when open and 9.7mm when closed. Meanwhile, the Duo is 5.2mm thick when open and 11.3mm when closed. It’s not a huge difference, but it makes me look forward to Apple hopefully slimming down the second-generation version, if and when it comes.

The Duo is also slightly heavier than the Z Fold 8, weighing 254 grams (compared to 201 grams for Samsung’s foldable). I’m always surprised when people remark how heavy the Duo is, but I think the reason I don’t share that sentiment is that I’m accustomed to the iPhone 18 Pro Max, which weighs 249 grams.

When the Duo is open in landscape orientation, I’m glad there’s an option to split the keyboard so it’s easier to type across the wider expanse, but I wish the swipe functionality worked in that configuration, too. It’s a little thing that would make a noticeable difference for those of us who rely heavily on swipe-to-text.

One drawback of the Duo’s compact design is that some existing MagSafe wallets and other accessories won’t stick to the back without awkwardly jutting out. So you might have to invest in some new accessories specifically designed for the Duo.

Until the recent addition of face unlock, the Duo’s biggest drawback was the lack of Face ID. It’s a feature I’d expect on such a premium device, especially given that even the budget-focused iPhone 17E supports it.

Touch ID works reliably on the Duo, but it’s slow compared to fingerprint unlock on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which also supports facial recognition). And while the new face unlock capability on the Duo isn’t an exact replacement for Face ID, which is more secure, it helps make accessing the phone’s contents more convenient and in line with the Duo’s modern aesthetics.

I’ve finished my homework: My review is done, and now, so is this one-month follow-up. What’s next?

I’m not sure I’m ready to throw in the towel on Apple’s foldable just yet. The novelty of the iPhone Duo hasn’t worn off, and I’ve become quite used to my passport-size companion. It does just about everything I need, despite some slight imperfections, and it’s fun to use. It’s also amusing to see how people react when they see it in my hand.

So for now, it looks like the Duo will remain my daily driver. Whether the honeymoon phase eventually wears off remains to be seen, but I’m not in any hurry to end this love affair.

#3085. The S&P 500 Is Flashing Warning Signs. Here's Why Long-Term Investors Should Stay the Course.

High valuations don't tell the whole story.

By Adam Levy – Nov 19, 2026 at 1:45PM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

The S&P 500 (^GSPC -1.59%) just entered its fifth year of the current bull market that kicked off in 2022 when the Federal Reserve lowered rates just as the generative AI revolution was taking off.

But now, with the Fed raising rates again and investors worried about financing and regulations slowing the growth of AI, investors have been capitulating. The benchmark index has experienced significant volatility in November following the midterm elections, an inflation report that came in higher than expected, and Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia.

Investors point to a major warning sign that the S&P 500 has been flashing since May, suggesting stock prices could collapse. While long-term investors shouldn't ignore the warning sign, understanding the current context is important.

Ultimately, it's not a good enough reason to stop holding stocks. Here’s why.

One of the most common valuation metrics used to project long-term investment potential is the cyclically-adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio. Developed by Nobel laureate Robert Shiller, the metric takes the last 10 years of earnings of all the S&P 500 companies, adjusts the total for inflation, and compares that number to the current price of the index. The goal is to smooth out economic cycles and provide a clear understanding of where prices stand today.

Historically, a higher CAPE ratio is correlated with lower future returns for stocks. Likewise, a low CAPE ratio corresponds to high returns. In May, the CAPE ratio exceeded 40 for just the second time dating back to 1870.

The CAPE ratio peaked at around 44 in late 1999 and remained elevated throughout 1999 and 2000. The S&P 500 level peaked in March 2000 before collapsing 49% over the next two and a half years.

Indeed, history doesn't paint an optimistic picture about the stock market. But context is key. The CAPE ratio is, by definition, looking in the rearview mirror to try to see where we're going. While it's important to check your mirrors, a driver who doesn't look out the front windshield is much more likely to make a mistake.

The CAPE ratio isn't much use in predicting short-term returns; it's used to forecast long-term returns. But we only have one usable data point on what happens to the market in the long term when the CAPE ratio goes above 40. The 10-year returns from 1999 to 2009 included not just the dot-com bubble, but the great financial crisis of 2007-2008. Those events are unrelated, but they occurred in the same 10-year period, resulting in the so-called lost decade. The 2007 crash didn't happen just because stock prices were high in 1999.

The CAPE ratio is unreliable at calling peaks in the stock market, too. While 1999 is an example of when it successfully did so, the CAPE was also elevated throughout the late 1990s, when it climbed above 30. The only other time it had reached 30 was right before the Great Depression. If investors sold when the ratio reached 30 in the 90s, they'd miss out on years of further growth. The ratio also exceeded 30 in 2017, and it's mostly stayed at or above that level except for a few pullbacks since.

One reason for elevated valuations is that corporate profits are so much stronger than they've been in the past. During the dot-com bubble, a lot of stocks had egregious P/E ratios or ratios that were incalculable because they didn't have any profits. Today, the largest companies in the S&P 500 are immensely profitable and sport below-average P/E ratios on a forward-looking basis.

Analysts expect profits to keep climbing faster than average. The analyst consensus calls for earnings growth of 16.2% in 2027, well above the historic average. Overall, the S&P 500 sports a forward P/E ratio around 18, which is below its average valuation for the past 10 years. That suggests the index can keep climbing from here if analysts are even close to correct.

Importantly, the CAPE ratio can decline even as stock prices rise. We've already seen that pattern play out with the standard P/E ratio for the S&P 500 this year, as earnings grow faster than stock prices. The CAPE ratio just takes longer to catch up since it looks back 10 years.

#3083. 90% of employers reject resumes that look like AI – yet half use AI to interview

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

In today's job market, do applicants really have a choice of whether to comply with AI hiring tools?

Hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider. At the same time, they’re turning to AI to help screen more candidates — meaning those videos you’ve seen on the internet of people pranking AI interviewers aren’t going away anytime soon.

New data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost

“The survey data is self-reported, so it reflects what employers believe has happened, not a measured outcome,” Greenhouse’s Head of Voice AI Ophir Samson told ZDNET via email.

Employers are also reacting to AI by adjusting their hiring processes: 86% of those surveyed reported changes to account for AI’s impact. 57% of them did so by adding another human interview.

“As jobseekers rely more on AI to polish and send out their job applications, employers are finding it harder to tell who’s actually right for the role,” the report stated, echoing an ongoing push-and-pull between applicants and hiring teams. AI resume screeners automatically toss a majority of applications they deem unfit, so applicants try not to get tossed by formatting their material for the screener, which then backfires anyway.

The report shows how a tough economy and an influx of AI hiring tools are colliding, arguably to benefit employers over applicants. Greenhouse noted that, ironically, AI tools are helping hiring managers while also making resumes untrustworthy, and applicants would rather be interviewed by AI than not at all.

Also: How to beat the AI algorithm and get the job of your dreams

“A growing number of employers are using AI not just to filter candidates out, but to have conversations with more candidates, earlier, through AI-powered voice technology,” Greenhouse said, adding that “half now use AI interviews to hear from more candidates, and 40% of those have found strong candidates they would have missed.”

Greenhouse itself offers a voice AI screening interview tool. Samson told ZDNET that an HR professional ran 200 candidates she’d rejected through Greenhouse’s tool, and it suggested 19.

“All five of the finalists came from that group, and she ultimately hired one from the group,” Samson said.

What we don’t, and maybe can’t, know is the inverse: whether AI screeners influence hiring managers to turn away candidates they actually should have considered. At least in Greenhouse’s case, Samson said Voice AI doesn’t make hiring decisions or “automatically advance, reject, or rank candidates.”

“Recruiters review every output, and one recruiter owns the outcome and can explain how they reached it,” he said.

Greenhouse’s report surveyed 1,347 hiring managers and recruiters across the US, UK, Germany, Australia, and Ireland from late September to mid-October, and found that half of employers using voice AI “say the early-stage candidate experience has improved.”

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

It’s unclear what “improved” means there, though, and whether applicants themselves would agree with that. Still, when given the choice, only 7% of applicants in the US would turn down an AI interview, per an earlier Greenhouse report. Additionally, “70% of those who’ve had a live AI interview say it helped them show their skills,” that report said.

But how swayed is that by the state of the US job market? October’s job report was better than expected, but it’s still been a tough year overall for job-seekers. Greenhouse’s findings could be as much a reflection of how desperate applicants are as an endorsement of or comfort with AI screenings.

“The job market could be a factor. Our Future of Hiring Candidate Report shows 81% of job seekers were rejected from a job in the past year without speaking to anyone at the company, human or AI,” Samson said. “But I’d be careful about reading the data as desperation. Candidates are setting clear conditions: nearly half (49%) want to know if a human will review their responses and 40% want to know how they’ll be evaluated.”

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires – and 5 ways smart leaders generate real value instead

Samson said that a software engineer named Ryan Quinlan, who was hired at Blissway, initially thought “talking to an AI” sounded stranger, but that it ultimately “felt like a conversation” that let him mention skills he’d forgotten to include on his resume. Samson said that Ryan has been “a ‘maybe’ on paper,” but that the AI interview helped him get over the line to be considered.

“For most applicants, a human conversation was never on the table,” Samson said. “The real choice is a resume lost in a pile, or 15 minutes to tell their story.”

Greenhouse found that while employers are using AI to screen more candidates, most are maintaining human oversight over the most important decisions in the hiring process.

“Of all the tasks employers would hand to an AI agent, deciding which candidates to advance came last, at just 7%,” Greenhouse said.

A recent California law aims to protect employees from being fired by AI systems that make determinations about their performance without a human co-signing the assessment. As with many AI productivity tools in the workplace, proper adoption ideally equates to more time for human workers to handle more important tasks.

Also: 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside

“Of employers who’ve saved time with AI, 85% put it back into candidates, most often by spending more time with shortlisted candidates (45%) and interviewing more candidates earlier (40%),” Greenhouse said.

The main question around AI interviewers remains whether they’re correctly capturing your interview the way you’d hope a human interviewer would (though that’s still deeply subjective and out of applicants’ control anyway).

“When AI interviews are implemented thoughtfully and transparently, they pay off for both candidates and recruiters,” Samson said. “Every candidate who uses our Voice AI can opt out, and about 90% rate the experience as excellent.”
