#3068. Evaxion (EVAX) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Runway stretches to 2027 as oncology vaccine focus sharpens.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 19, 2026 at 1:54PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Evaxion (EVAX -8.46%) management announced a strategic refocus to prioritize the AI-Immunology platform toward oncology programs, specifically advancing its off-the-shelf and personalized cancer vaccines. The company reported the extension of its cash runway into the end of 2027, supported by disciplined resource allocation and at-the-market equity sales. Clinical validation for the platform was highlighted through three-year phase II data for the EVX-01 vaccine, showing high target precision and durable immune responses in metastatic melanoma. Management indicated that future development of infectious disease and autoimmune assets will be conducted exclusively through external partnerships to maximize the value of internal resources.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Evaxion Strategy and Business Update and Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Webcast and Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during the session, you will need to press star, one, and one on your telephone. You will then hear an automated message advising your hand is raised. To withdraw your question, please press star, one, and one again. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your speaker today, Helen Tayton-Martin, Chief Executive Officer. Please go ahead.

Helen Tayton-Martin: Thank you, and good morning and welcome, to everyone to Evaxion's Strategy and Business Update for Q3. I'm Helen Tayton-Martin. I'm the Chief Executive Officer of Evaxion, and I'm joined today on the call by Birgitte Rønø, our Chief Scientific Officer and Chief Operating Officer, and Thomas Schmidt, Chief Financial Officer, Mads Kronborg, our Head of Investor Relations and Communications. In our agenda today, I will walk you through how we are refocusing our strategy to create the maximal value, and will then hand over to Birgitte, who will take us through the highlights of our R&D activities during the quarter, and some of the key data and developments with our AI-Immunology platform, which is driving this strategy shift.

Thomas will take you through the financial results for the quarter before we wrap up with some concluding remarks and take questions. As a reminder, we may make forward-looking statements during today's call, and in that context, I would refer you to our most recent filed statements. Turning to the first agenda point, our strategy update. Put very simply, Evaxion is now refocusing all of its own resources in the application of our AI-Immunology platform towards our oncology portfolio.

With Moderna's recent phase III groundbreaking data validating personalized cancer vaccines as truly capable of delivering meaningful clinical benefit in adjuvant melanoma, we have been proud and excited to share our own phase II three-year clinical data in recent weeks, in which patients with metastatic melanoma, where we used our AI-Immunology platform to predict high-quality and relevant antigens for patients, which was correlated with high precision in terms of the immune response generated, and more importantly, in deep and durable outcomes, as Birgitte will highlight later.

In addition, we have been able to use AI-Immunology to drill deeper into the dark genome and identify other types of antigens, especially endogenous retroviral elements, or ERVs, where we can identify unique and highly conserved sets of antigens to enable an off-the-shelf vaccine approach, in addition to the personalized neoantigen vaccines. We believe there is enormous opportunity in Evaxion's AI-Immunology platform to identify and develop both personalized and off-the-shelf cancer vaccines across multiple indications, customized according to antigen source and scope, and this is where maximum value lies in Evaxion. As a result, going forward, we will be focusing our own resources in the three key areas shown at the bottom of this slide.

Firstly, taking our two off-the-shelf cancer vaccines, EVX-04 in AML and EVX-05 in GBM, into the clinic, the latter in collaboration with Duke University. Secondly, we will be looking at broadening the potential of EVX-01 beyond advanced melanoma, and most likely, we expect to do this through partnership. Thirdly, we plan to continue to identify other new antigens and indications from deeper analysis of the dark genome with AI-Immunology. In terms of our pipeline going forward, we will be progressing only our oncology assets, as just mentioned.

Elsewhere, we believe we have built significant value in the preclinical assets and capabilities we have developed in the infectious disease area over many years, with EVX-B1 in Staph aureus, EVX-B2 in gonorrhea, EVX-B4 in Group A Streptococcus, and EVX-V1 in CMV. We will continue to look for partnerships for these assets and work with partners only in other infectious disease programs where the partner comes forward. In autoimmune disease, we are testing the concepts we identified for tolerogenic vaccines and autoantibody binders using AI-Immunology, and we will complete that work to validate the approach for potential partnering.

Looking to the achievements we have made in the last quarter, on business development, we have had a very busy time and continue to progress multiple parallel conversations, all leveraging the recent data and validation of AI-Immunology with the EVX-01 and the future off-the-shelf potential with EVX-04 and EVX-05, and more broadly with other indications, other cancer indications. On R&D, much of the latest three-year data for EVX-01 was presented at ESMO and SITC, as Birgitte will cover, and we will be providing a further update for the EVX-04 program at ASH next month. We completed the initial work with our EVX-B4 Group A Strep program and started the initial concept testing for the targets identified for autoimmune disease.

On the platform itself, we were truly honored to see AI-Immunology recognized on the international stage at the International Prix Galien Awards, winning the Best Digital Health Solution prize, we believe adding further validation to how the Evaxion AI platform delivers meaningful clinical benefit. Finally, we have continued to maintain rigorous discipline in managing our financial resources aligned to the greatest areas of value, as well as being able to make prudent use of our ATM to enable us to extend the runway towards the end of 2027. When we look at our milestones for 2026, we have now achieved all of them except for the filing of our EVX-04 clinical trial application.

This is on track to be filed by the end of the year, in keeping with our refocused strategy on our IO programs and capabilities. With that, I will hand over to Birgitte to take us through the key R&D and AI-Immunology updates.

Birgitte Rønø: Thank you for that, Helen. As Helen outlined, we are focusing our strategy on oncology, building on the clinical and translational evidence from our personalized EVX-01 cancer vaccine, and the broader capability of our proprietary AI platform, AI-Immunology, to discover clinically relevant cancer antigens and to design vaccines. Our priorities are, as mentioned, to advance our off-the-shelf cancer vaccines, EVX-04 and EVX-05, toward clinical development, and further to expand EVX-01's potential across indications through partnerships, and to continue mining the dark genome for cancer vaccine antigens. The scientific update that follows show the evidence behind this focus and how we are translating our AI platform's capability into oncology product opportunities. Let me start with the rationale behind personalized cancer vaccines.

Personalized cancer vaccines targets neoantigens. These are sequences that are arising from cancer-specific mutations, and they're found exclusively in the tumor, but absent in normal tissue, making them highly attractive therapeutic targets. The challenge lies in identifying which of the patient's neoantigens that will generate a tumor-targeting immune response. AI-Immunology selects the most promising neoantigens by modeling the steps from cancer-specific mutations through expression, translation, presentation on the MHC molecules, and T-cell recognition. The AI-Immunology platform sits within a broader patient-to-vaccine process. For each patient, tumor and blood samples are collected, and they undergo DNA and RNA sequencing. AI-Immunology then, based on this information, predicts the patient-specific neoantigens in 24 hours, informing the design of the personalized EVX-01 vaccine.

Following manufacture, the vaccine is then administered in combination with checkpoint inhibitors. The total turnaround time from biopsy to vaccine administration is approximately seven weeks. In our EVX-01 phase II study, we reported an 89% precision in predicting immunogenic neoantigens. I'll now turn to the clinical results and the immune response data behind this record-high precision. In our EVX-01 phase II study in advanced melanoma, the two-year results showed an objective response rate of 75% and a complete response of 25%. We also saw improvement in the response from a week 12 assessment following initiation of EVX-01 immunization.

Seven out of 13 patients who had stable disease or a partial response after 12 weeks of anti-PD-1 therapy improved their response, corresponding to 54% following EVX-01 administration. Also of importance is that EVX-01-related adverse events were limited to grade 1 and grade 2. The one-year extension provided longer follow-up in a smaller group of patients, and the clinical responses in all six patients who participated in this extension with EVX-01 monotherapy lasted until the end of the trial. Overall, these are very encouraging clinical results that demonstrated clinical benefit of EVX-01 in combination with anti-PD-1 therapy in advanced melanoma. Turning to immunogenicity, EVX-01 induces potent vaccine-specific T-cell responses against the vaccine neoantigens.

The key point is that the platform can identify antigens recognized by the immune system. EVX-01-induced vaccine-specific T-cell responses that are sustained throughout the three-year period, including in the absence of anti-PD-1 therapy, which is provided only or was provided only during the first two years. As mentioned, we were able to demonstrate a record-high vaccine target precision of 89%. That is a clear testament to the predictive power of our AI-Immunology platform. Additionally, 86% of the assessed neoantigen responses were de novo, in other words, newly induced responses rather than preexisting responses. This is important as therapy-induced new T-cells have been correlated to clinical benefit.

Let's look more closely at the phenotype of the T-cell responses and how the strength of the EVX-01-induced T-cell responses relates to AI predictions. First, EVX-01 induces both CD4+ and CD8+ antigen-specific T-cell responses. In all evaluated patients, we were able to demonstrate a CD4+ response, and in nine out of the 15 patients, we were also able to detect CD8+ responses. We are still evaluating samples from the study, so stay tuned. More immune data and biomarker data will be shared in the next year. Secondly, we were able to demonstrate a positive correlation between the AI prediction score assigned to these single neoantigens, and the magnitude of the observed immune response.

Higher prediction score also were associated with a stronger immune response. This is an important link between the platform's predictions and the biological responses measured in the patients. With that clinical and translational foundation, let's look at how AI-Immunology can be applied more broadly. The broader opportunity is to use AI-Immunology across antigen sources, cancer indications, and vaccine approaches. The platform processes complex patient data, including genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic data, to identify and prioritize cancer antigens. As shown here, our work spans neoantigens and endogenous retrovirus, or ERVs, from the dark genome, and we are now looking at additional dark genome antigens.

That creates two complementary vaccine approaches: personalized vaccines that are tailored to an individual patient and targets private antigen, as exemplified by EVX-01 in melanoma, and off-the-shelf vaccines that are tailored to a patient population and target conserved ERV antigens, as in EVX-04 for acute myeloid leukemia and EVX-05 for GBM. The other indications shown on this slide, including head and neck, lung, ovarian, bladder, colon, esophageal, testicular, and stomach cancers, illustrate the potential breadth of the application based on deep data mining and antigen profiling of patients. The strategic point is that the platform is not confined to one cancer type or to one vaccine approach. It gives us basis for pursuing opportunities across personalized and off-the-shelf cancer vaccines.

Let's now look at AI-Immunology's key differentiators. Broad discovery across multiple antigens, sources, and high target precision. That translate into strategic product opportunities for both personalized and off-the-shelf cancer vaccines across more patients and cancer types. AI-Immunology, as mentioned, explores neoantigens from cancer-specific somatic mutations, ERV antigens from genome-integrated viral sequences, and additional dark genome antigens which are currently in development. This provides a broader antigen repertoire. With our record-high target precision demonstrated in clinical trials, exemplified by the 89% vaccine target precision rate in EVX-01 phase II trial, we are well-positioned in finding the right targets.

The core component of AI-Immunology is instrumental in identifying the most relevant T-cell epitopes, and this one is a key driver of the high target precision rate. The core code is antigen type agnostic and provides a common foundation for designing high-precision cancer vaccines irrespective of the antigen of choice. These two AI-Immunology differentiators, broad antigen repertoire and high target precision, translate into strategic product opportunities. Greater antigen breadth significantly increases the chance of finding effective targets for more patients and cancer types. The precision at the target level increases the likelihood of clinical success, as it is the foundation for stronger clinical outcome.

Taking together, this positions AI-Immunology not just as a platform for a single vaccine, but as a foundation for developing a broader portfolio of cancer vaccines, combining the opportunity to reach more patients with the potential for stronger clinical outcome. EVX-04 is a concrete example of how we are translating this broader discovery capability into an off-the-shelf cancer vaccine program. Starting with sequencing data from AML patients, we identified ERV tumor antigens. From 5 million ERV antigen fragments and corresponding MHC ligands, AI-Immunology selected the 16 optimal antigen fragment sets. Currently, multiple vaccine candidates were designed and tested, and the lead candidate is now moving forward in GMP manufacturing.

We are now progressing through final preclinical testing and validation of the selected ERV antigens alongside activities to enable clinical trial application, or CTA, with the submission expected in the second half of this year. In summary, AI-Immunology combines broad antigen discovery with high target precision. We can identify cancer antigens from multiple sources, neoantigens, ERVs, and additional dark genome antigen approaches in development using the same core predictive technology across antigen sources. Together, these capabilities create the opportunity to identify relevant targets for more patients and more cancer types, supporting both personalized and off-the-shelf approaches, and providing a foundation for a stronger clinical outcome. With that, I'll hand over to Thomas to present our Q3 financial results.

Thomas Schmidt: Yes, thank you, Birgitte, and also a warm welcome from my side to everyone on the call. Let me take you through the financial results for Q3, and we shift to the financial highlights. As key financial highlights for the quarter, we have now successfully further extended our cash runway now towards the end of 2027. Both the ATM and certainly also our continued disciplined resource allocation is also in support of our now refocused strategy and the updated pipeline, as we have just heard and seen. Looking into our profit and loss details, the statement clearly shows a net loss for the quarter of $3.5 million, which compares to $4.6 million profit in the same quarter last year.

Main reason for that lies within the recognized revenue. We've not recorded any recognized revenue in Q3 this year, whereas last year, we out-licensed our EVX-B3 program to Merck, or as called in Europe, MSD. At the same time, however, this year, we have reduced our operating cost compared to last year, both within R&D due to fewer headcounts, but certainly also in G&A with lower capital market costs, while we at the same time have put more resources into BD, business development activities, and therefore costs.

Our financial income and expenses for the quarter also now reflect a more normalized financial operation of ours, where the financial expense and income relate to interest from our debt and interest from income from our bank and cash position. This compares to last year, where we had high financial income from our debt-to-equity agreement that we did with the European Investment Bank, and on the other side, we had financial expenses which related to remeasurement of our derivative liability. This derivative liability has been reduced significantly and has no longer any significant impact on our financial expenses and income.

Moving to our balance sheet, our main balance sheet items include obviously our cash position, now end of September, of $13.3 million. This includes proceeds from our ATM program of $2.2 million, which we utilized and received in August 2026. We have received further proceeds from our ATM program in October of another $800,000, but that is not reflected in the cash position end of September, however, is included in our cash runway that, as mentioned earlier, has now been extended towards the end of 2027. Equity stands at $8.1 million, which obviously also has been increased by the ATM sales in August, and obviously impacted by the net loss from the period also.

These warrants, once exercised, will mean that we may receive up to another $1.5 million when and if exercised by the European Investment Bank. With that, I conclude the financial for the quarter and hand it back to Helen for some concluding remarks.

Thomas Flaten: Okay. Just one for Birgitte. Have you guys looked at, and you may have presented this in the past, and I apologize if you have, the correlation between CD8+ response and clinical response? Given that you had broad-based CD4+, we can kind of write that off as a universal response, but what about the CD8+ correlating to clinical response?

Helen Tayton-Martin: I'll let Birgitte take that one.

Birgitte Rønø: Yeah. No, it is a really good question. For the few patients that are not responding to study therapy, we actually do not have a strong immune dataset because they are early progressors. I would say the dataset we have available currently cannot fully answer that question.

Thomas Flaten: Got it. Appreciate it. No worries. Thanks for taking the questions.

Operator: Thank you. We are now going to take the next question. This one comes from Jason McCarthy from Maxim Group. Please go ahead.

Michael Okunewitch: Hey, guys. Good morning. This is Michael Okunewitch. I wanted to see if you could talk just a little bit about the expansion strategy for EVX-01, and is this something where you would need to do some smaller proof of concept or preclinical work and then seek partners, or is the melanoma validation itself sufficient to support expansion in those partner discussions?

Helen Tayton-Martin: Great question. We believe, and certainly the engagement that we have is very much around the validation we've already seen in advanced melanoma, which I think is a distinction for the Evaxion platform and clinical data. I think what we've been able to highlight is where, as Birgitte showed on the slides, that we have already done quite a bit of work to look at other indications that are potentially possible with the EVX-01 approach alone. I think what's also interesting to us and to partners is we can go beyond neoantigens in a personalized setting.

So, there could be the indications where a combination of personalized and ERVs is feasible, and that doesn't really change the process of making and delivering the vaccine. So, it opens up opportunity for where we currently are. We can take the current clinical package, we can take the ability of AI-Immunology to derive neoantigens and other antigens, and potentially move forward quickly into other initial, potentially phase II settings in other indications. I think that's a real advantage from where we are right now. Those are the sort of issues and questions that we're looking at in terms of where's the best opportunity and how to broaden out scope. It's again, lots of opportunity.

It's working through best fit, best setting, best antigens.

Michael Okunewitch: Thank you. Then, just with the strategic refocusing, how does that impact your plans for the autoimmune platform? Are you still planning to build this out, given that it is earlier along in that value creation pipeline and likely requires less resources versus clinical stage assets?

Helen Tayton-Martin: Yeah. No, great question. We are planning to complete. We have set out to identify the right targets for concept testing in autoimmune disease. Obviously, we're looking at ways of reducing immune inflammation in different settings, and that concept testing has progressed. We anticipate completing the validation of that, the work in the lab to do some testing around those concepts. I think we plan to at least complete that work to see whether we can show a compelling case for how we would take those programs forward, again, potentially with partnerships.

It's not requiring additional resource at the moment, and we plan to complete that work so that we can actually talk more about the scope for AI-Immunology to deliver in the autoimmune space. That's ongoing. That won't stop right now.

Michael Okunewitch: Thank you. Just one follow-up on that one, and I'll hop back into the queue. Just when thinking about that validation work that you need to get a partnerable package, what does that actually entail? Would this be producing an IND-ready product candidate for a specific disease, more along the lines of target discovery? I'm trying to understand what level of validation you need before you can bring it to partners.

Helen Tayton-Martin: I think that depends. I'll ask Birgitte to just comment on thoughts about where we are and the value of what we think we can generate, but I think we'll be early, basically.

Birgitte Rønø: Yeah. We have so far developed two therapeutic concepts. One is a tolerogenic vaccine that aims at re-educating the immune system towards self-tolerance. The AI-Immunology team and the bioinformaticians have worked on this concept. We are slowly getting ready in the lab to test some of these concepts. Then we have the other therapeutic approach, which is based on an autoantibody binders, and that is with the aim of reducing levels of pathogenic autoantibodies. We have started talking about these concepts and presenting at different conferences, so we hope that we'll be able to at least get some interest from potential partners early on, so before even having a defined product candidate.

Helen Tayton-Martin: So, it's really early proof of concept.

Michael Okunewitch: All right. Thank you very much. I appreciate the additional clarity.

Operator: Thank you. We're now going to take the next question. This one comes from Charles Wallace from H.C. Wainwright. Please go ahead.

Charles Wallace: Hi. Thanks for taking my question. Maybe the first from me. Now with the two positive phase III cancer vaccine readouts in the field, INTerpath-001 in adjuvant melanoma, and then just two days ago, the REGAL study at transplant-ineligible AML. I am just curious, regarding your pipeline, where is the interest specifically? Is it more in the personalized vaccine approach or in the off-the-shelf vaccine approach? That is my first question. Thank you.

Helen Tayton-Martin: Okay. I would definitely say it is in both, to the extent that we can share anything at all at this stage. I think that the broader potential across indications is definitely of interest, but clearly there are advantages in an off-the-shelf vaccine in terms of simpler supply chain, simpler delivery, simpler ability to deliver a product, and that is obviously of significant interest. However, at this point, that is not clinically validated. There is a belief in the personalized vaccine approach that can deliver clinically. We have shown that, others have shown that. And off-the-shelf is very much of interest, and it is really about moving along to clinical validation.

So, I would say there is equal interest in both areas at the moment.

Charles Wallace: Okay. That is helpful. And then I guess, on the infectious disease programs, the out-license program, EVX-B3, and then also the co-development program of EVX-B2. Can we assume that nothing is really changed in these two programs? Yeah, that is my next question. Thank you.

Helen Tayton-Martin: B3 is obviously out-licensed in a collaboration with MSD and is moving forward. The further updates from that will really come as a result of the MSD activities. And the B2 program is in collaboration with Afrigen and our RNA platform, and again, things have continued there. There will be data packages for B2, as with B1 and B4, as well as B1, as I mentioned in my comments, that are available for that we have continued to build on during the course of this year and are available, will be available in those partnering conversations.

So, from a partner perspective, B3 is moving along with MSD, and in the fullness of time, we will be able to talk more about that, but that is really driven off the next stages with them. And so things have not moved significantly from our perspective at this point until we hit the next point with that one.

Charles Wallace: Great. Thanks for taking my questions.

Operator: Thank you. We are now going to take the next question. This one is from Danya Ben-Hail from JonesTrading. Please go ahead.

Danya Ben-Hail: Hi. Thank you for taking our questions. To follow up on the previous ones, can you share if there are any questions, diligence that potential partners have around EVX-01?

Helen Tayton-Martin: Not really, but I can talk to the fact that they ask all the questions, many questions that would be asked in this setting too, is really understanding turnaround time, the depth of the immune responses that we see, the correlations there, the quality of the antigens and the scoring that we generate. Really looking very closely, given that the whole world, the whole landscape around cancer vaccines has now shifted gears, it is really important to understand key scientific differentiators and also platform delivery opportunities where maybe there is scope to reduce the timeframe, they look at the modality of delivery, et cetera.

So all the sorts of things that come with drilling into how a product platform like this works. Then thinking about that more broadly in terms of different indication contexts, which is very much what we are doing too.

Danya Ben-Hail: Mm-hmm. Thank you. For the manufacturing, are you working on speeding up the vein-to-vein from the seven weeks you mentioned?

Helen Tayton-Martin: We know that it can be done. Birgitte, do you want to comment on the things that we are aware of?

Birgitte Rønø: Yes. The way that we have set up the supply chain is in a decentralized manner, meaning that we have been working with multiple different CDMOs. There is definitely an opportunity to get all of these many activities under one roof to reduce the manufacturing time. There has also been global shipping, going from the clinical site to the sequencing facility and for the drug product to be shipped back to the clinical site. This adds up in those overall timelines. There will be multiple ways that the turnaround time could be significantly reduced.

Danya Ben-Hail: Great. Thank you for that. Last question about EVX-04. When should we get more details on the clinical trial design?

Birgitte Rønø: We will be, as Helen Tayton-Martin mentioned, presenting target validation data at ASH in December. We are also running fast towards clinical trial application later this year. At that time point, we will most likely be able to share more details around patient population and trial design.

Danya Ben-Hail: Perfect. Thank you very much.

Operator: Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, you will need to press star, one, and one on your telephone. That is star, one, and one to ask a question. There seems to be no further questions for today. I will now hand the call back to Helen Tayton-Martin for closing remarks.

Helen Tayton-Martin: Thank you. Thank you very much for listening to our strategy and business update for Q3 today. We are very excited about the path forward for Evaxion, and thanks for the questions. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

#3067. You Can Now Fix Your Typos on Instagram Stories With an Edit Option

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Instagram Stories can be edited for up to 15 minutes without losing engagement metrics.

There are few things more anxiety-inducing than creating a well-crafted social media post and instantly finding it has a typo in it. Instagram Stories now lets you fix that.

Thanks to a recent update that includes several platform improvements, Instagram creators can edit their Stories up to 15 minutes after posting. You no longer have to start from scratch, and the edits won’t tank your engagement or sacrifice performance. To make changes to text, music, stickers, drawings or their placement or style, simply tap the menu at the bottom or the More button on your story to find the edit option. Instagram says that you won’t lose views, likes or replies as a result. After the 15-minute window closes, your Story can’t be changed without deleting it.

The edit option is a minor update but a welcome enhancement for those who regularly post on Instagram, said CNET’s Abrar Al-Heeti. It’s especially a plus if you always find something to nitpick after you set it live, she said.

Al-Heeti also pointed to a recent update that lets you change a song on a published post. “It’s great to see Instagram adding more features that let you tweak something after it’s reached your audience, without losing out on any existing views or engagement.”

The Stories edit feature is slowly rolling out to all accounts, so first check whether your app is running the latest version.

In addition, Instagram is adding new stickers with a new sticker sheet, photo dumps that let you choose multiple pics more easily and new backgrounds including blur, colors and gradients.

Earlier this week, Meta unveiled the Instagram-based chat app called Direct, which is currently in testing in Thailand and Turkey.

#3066. Missed the Anthropic IPO? These 3 Stocks Give You Immediate Exposure.

Nvidia, Amazon, and Alphabet are all benefiting from Anthropic's success.

By Keithen Drury – Nov 19, 2026 at 1:57PM EST

Anthropic (ANT +17.65%) is Wall Street’s newest public AI stock, and there is a ton of excitement surrounding it. However, not everyone wants to be a Day 1 investor. Stocks frequently behave oddly and erratically over their first few months of trading, and many investors don't want to invest in a company until it has released a few quarterly earnings reports’ worth of data about the business.

I fall into that more-cautious category, but there are a few stocks that don't have new-stock risk that are well positioned to benefit from Anthropic going public. Three of those that I'm eyeing are Nvidia (NVDA -2.18%), Amazon (AMZN -3.56%), and Alphabet (GOOG -1.65%) (GOOGL -1.73%).

These three benefit in different ways, but I think each of them serves as an excellent alternative to investing in Anthropic right away.

Nvidia is well-known in the tech world for having developed the best accelerated computing ecosystem available. It has no rival when it comes to its combination of hardware prowess, controlling software, and other attributes.

Anthropic recognizes this, which is why it has chosen Nvidia to be one of its primary computing unit suppliers. Now that Anthropic has secured more funding for computing resources via its IPO, Nvidia will be a big beneficiary.

Additionally, Nvidia owns Anthropic shares and planned to buy more during the IPO process. If Anthropic thrives, then so will its investment.

Nvidia is currently undergoing some leadership turmoil, and the stock has sold off heavily as a result. This could be an excellent buying opportunity, as the business model is still intact and revenues are growing quickly, as evidenced by its most recent quarterly results.

Nvidia is still a great company and a force to be reckoned with in the AI computing world. As more and more computing power is needed to run a growing number of AI workloads, Nvidia will be one of the primary beneficiaries.

Amazon and Alphabet are two of Anthropic's biggest partners. Anthropic doesn't own any of its computing power; it chooses to rent it from cloud computing providers like Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Alphabet's Google Cloud.

From these two, Anthropic selects the best computing unit for the workload, whether it's an Nvidia graphics processing unit (GPU) or one of the custom AI chips available on either of these cloud platforms. Moreover, Amazon and Alphabet have invested heavily in the AI lab; between them, they own nearly 30% of Anthropic.

Between their relationships as compute providers and their massive ownership stakes, both companies have plenty of potential for upside if Anthropic ends up being the AI lab of choice and proves a profitable operation long term.

So, even if you choose not to invest in Anthropic directly, by owning shares of these two, you're indirectly investing in Anthropic. It is a wise move for investors to hold stakes in Amazon, Alphabet, and Nvidia, and to be patient as we wait to see what happens with Anthropic stock.

Indeed, even without the Anthropic connection, these three look pretty attractively valued right now relative to next year's expected earnings.

GOOG PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

With Nvidia trading at a dirt-cheap 9.5 times next year's expected earnings, it's easily the lowest-priced stock of this trio. Alphabet trades at a very reasonable 18.5 times forward earnings, especially considering that the S&P 500 (^GSPC -1.59%) trades at 18.8. Amazon is the most expensive at 24.5 times next year's earnings, but I still think that's a fair price tag for a company of its dominance.

These stocks will benefit immensely from Anthropic's IPO. They serve as great alternatives to investing directly in it right now, and investors may be better off buying these three instead of Anthropic, at least until more is known about the business.

#3065. What You Can Pay for with Scholarship Money

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

Scholarships are usually restricted to the necessary costs of attending college, but some scholarships let you apply the money to more than tuition.

Scholarships are meant to pay for the cost of attendance to study at a college or university. This often includes required bills and purchases, such as tuition, textbooks and on-campus living expenses.

Some scholarships restrict the funds to specific costs, such as tuition. How you can apply the money may depend on the scholarship’s requirements.

Here are the most common college costs you can pay with scholarship money.

Scholarships commonly pay toward the tuition and fees your college charges.

Tuition usually covers only the cost to enroll in classes. Your college will also charge fees for a variety of reasons, such as attending a lab portion of a class, access to on-campus technology, facility maintenance and student activities. You’ll have to pay many of these fees regardless of if you use those facilities or participate in campus activities. Fees are often charged with tuition on the same bill so that you pay them together.

Tuition and fees cost students at public four-year institutions an average of $32,730 for the 2026-2027 school year, according to College Board’s 2026 report. If you use scholarship money to pay for these costs upfront, it can help you save a good chunk of money.

Scholarship money also pays for textbooks and supplies you need to complete your courses. These can include physical books, e-books and software licenses to access online content.

Depending on the scholarship, the cost of additional supplies that are required for certain courses might be covered as well. For example, nursing students might have to purchase scrubs with their college’s logo or medical supplies such as stethoscopes for clinical shifts.

Some scholarships will pay for the purchase of a laptop because you’ll likely need one to complete your coursework; however, you’ll want to confirm that the money can be used for that purchase before buying one.

Your scholarship might help cover some of the costs of living on campus, including paying for a dorm room and meal plans (often called room and board). To apply the funds, you usually have to live in university housing, which might be in a dormitory or even university apartments.

Many students can purchase meal plans to eat meals in their college and university cafeterias. These plans are usually for a set number of meals each week and might be required for first-year students. Because meal plans are part of college expenses, some scholarships will let you apply the funds to purchase a meal plan.

Some scholarships might also allow money to pay for campus parking fees because those are paid directly to the college or university.

» MORE: What is need-based financial aid for college?

Scholarships are generally intended only for educational expenses such as those explained above, but there are some scholarships that want you to use the money for specific expenses. If your scholarship has this type of restriction, your award letter should outline how the funds must be used, such as paying for tuition and fees only.

If you aren’t certain whether there are restrictions on how you can spend your scholarship money and the scholarship was paid directly to your college, you can call your financial aid office to ask. But you’ll want to contact the organization that awarded you the scholarship to ask about restrictions if the scholarship money was sent to you instead.

Even if a scholarship is open to most educational costs, expenses that are rarely allowed to be covered by a scholarship include:

Some transportation costs such as car payments.

Non-essential supplies such as clothing or entertainment.

Scholarships can be paid directly to your college or to you, depending on the individual scholarship. If the money goes to your college, it’s applied to your account based on the scholarship’s requirements. For example, if the funds are only allowed to pay for tuition, the financial aid office will apply the money to your tuition bill to reduce how much you owe.

Scholarships work the same way for room and board. If your scholarship will pay toward the costs of living on campus, the money will reduce how much you owe or cover the costs entirely so that you don’t owe anything.

In some cases, you might be able to use your scholarship money to pay for books or supplies. If that’s allowed, the funds might be available on your account through the college bookstore. Instead of paying the entire cost of your textbooks with cash or your student loans, you can pay with the scholarship money.

If your scholarship sends you the money instead of giving it to your college, you’ll be responsible for using the funds to pay for eligible costs instead of your university automatically applying it toward your bill.

#3063. Showing Up In AI Search Isn't The Same As Getting Recommended

Andrew Higgins is CEO of Parsnipp, an AI search marketing company.

​For the last 12 months, a lot of marketers have been diving into AI search marketing, and most have been defining success with a new KPI: “AI visibility.”

AI visibility has been our primary measure of whether a brand is succeeding in AI search and appearing in LLM-generated answers related to its brand and market. But what we’ve learned at Parsnipp is that visibility tells only part of the story. There’s a much larger conversation (pun intended) happening around how people interact with AI, and it’s one we need to start paying closer attention to.

When we started building in AI search, we measured what everyone measures: how often a brand shows up in an AI answer. We tracked mentions, citations, share of voice, visibility scores, etc. A lot of this is derived from traditional search, and it’s the habit that’s trained into all of us. Win the keyword—or in this case prompt—and move on to the next.

The more we tested and replicated the ways people actually use AI, the more it changed how I thought about the channel and what it means for brands.

We wanted to see what happens after the first answer, because while most tools measure a set of prompts and AI responses for visibility, that’s not an accurate reflection of how real people use answer engines. So instead of firing single prompts at a model, my team simulated full shopper conversations: a person with a need, follow-up questions and constraints that come up along the way (i.e., the way people actually talk to LLMs).

The scenario was simple: headphones under $150. We ran 320 conversations across ChatGPT and Gemini 3.8 Flash in two independent batches of 160 to check if the pattern held. What we found was that across 960 brand mentions, only 700 became an actual recommendation. Nearly three in 10 mentions went nowhere. This means what marketers considered a “win” was actually far from it.

We had brands that scored incredibly well on visibility but almost never were the product or brand actually recommended by the end of the interaction with the shopper. On a visibility dashboard, that looks like a strong brand, but it was missing the last two-thirds of the shopper’s journey through AI.

In traditional search, appearing in results was the first step in the customer journey. From there, our website and retail partners took over the consideration phase, helping customers compare products, read reviews, shop for the best price and, ultimately, make a purchase.​

But in today’s world, with so much of that interaction taking place on one surface, between a shopper and their agent, AI now folds much more of this funnel into one channel. So, we’ve started thinking full funnel again, just inside the AI Search experience:

• Mentioned: The assistant brings you up.

• Considered: You stay on the shortlist as the shopper adds needs.

• Recommended: You’re the pick, not the runner-up.

• Chosen: The shopper, or their agent, buys.

Each stage leaks for a different reason, and most brands are only measuring the first one.

You don’t need special software for a first pass. Here’s the process I’d hand any marketing team:

1. Start With One Category Of Prompts: Pick the one that drives the most revenue, and don’t try to map everything at once. Maybe it’s your competitive prompts, broad industry prompts, etc. ​

2. Write Briefs, Not Keywords: List 20 to 30 real buying situations with the constraints included. “Running shoes” are keywords whereas “moderately frequent runner with wide feet that is over 35” is a brief.​

3. Script The Conversation: Simulate the conversation broadly, then add constraints one at a time (budget, use case, fit, deal breakers). I’d also switch around the order of questions, too. As an example, in our test, results shifted depending on whether the budget came first or last.​

4. Run It More Than Once, On More Than One Model: Answers vary run to run as LLMs still have a fair bit of drift response to response. Running multiple batches is what told us our pattern was real.​

5. Log Two Numbers Per Brand: Start off simple. You don’ t need to track too many points along the journey at first. Even jumping from 1 (visibility) to 2 (visibility + mention) will make a huge impact. This means you’ll be measuring how often your brand is mentioned and how often it’s recommended. You can do it for your competitors too in the same research. Recommendations divided by mentions is your recommendation rate.​

6. Find Your Sweet Spot: Being both mentioned and recommended is the ideal position. If a brand is rarely mentioned but consistently recommended when it does come up, that’s primarily a discovery problem—and generally the easier one to fix. Neither position is ideal, but the more concerning scenario is a brand that’s frequently mentioned but rarely recommended. It creates the appearance of visibility without actually translating into preference or consideration.​

7. Identify What’s Holding You Back: Whether it’s price, product fit, a missing specification or a use case your brand doesn’t adequately address, identify the factors causing AI to steer customers elsewhere. These gaps are likely where you’re losing sales—and where your AI search marketing efforts should focus.

8. Fix The Evidence, Then Re-Run: Make your product pages, reviews and third-party coverage answer that gap directly since LLMs have a tendency to repeat what they can find. Then test again next month because models change super fast.​

If your AI search report only counts mentions, it’s telling you half the story—and maybe the wrong half. Count the mentions, track the picks, fix the gap, and start thinking of AI search as a full funnel marketing channel instead of just a visibility goal.

#3060. AI Is Accelerating: It’s Time To Address Governance, Visibility And Security

​Many organizations now have an agentic workforce. AI agents are everywhere, reading emails, writing code and connecting to systems on our behalf, analyzing financial reports, creating dashboards and doing the work for your human workforce.

Unfortunately, in most businesses, security teams can’t tell you which ones are running, what they can reach, where they send data or what they’re costing us.

Attackers have also built their own agentic workforce. In Ocean’s Eleven, pulling off one heist took a crew of 11 specialists: someone to recon the target, someone to crack the vault and someone to drive. Today, a single operator can hand most of those roles to AI agents that work around the clock and never ask for a coffee break.

The numbers bear this out. Microsoft’s 2026 Digital Defense Report found that the median time from a vulnerability’s discovery in the wild to its weaponization has fallen to well below 24 hours. In late 2025, Anthropic documented an espionage campaign in which AI executed an estimated 80% to 90% of tactical operations independently. The company characterized it as “the first documented case of a cyberattack largely executed without human intervention at scale.”

The cases are piling up, too. In July 2026, a report was published on JadePuffer, which it assessed as the first documented case of agentic ransomware. The agent broke into an exposed server, harvested credentials, pivoted to a separate production database and encrypted more than 1,300 configuration items. When one step failed, it deployed a working fix in 31 seconds. In September 2026, the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD), an organization that hunts bugs for a living, was breached by an agentic AI attacker who chained two zero-days in the institute’s help desk software and achieved root access in seconds.

A crew like that changes the economics of cybercrime. Persistence is automated, reconnaissance runs in parallel and failed tactics are retried instantly. In my view, the limiting resource is increasingly compute, and lower-cost models are making that resource cheaper for attackers every quarter.

Defenders need the same speed, with one key difference: accountability. Purpose-built agents should carry the high-volume, repetitive work while people keep authority over consequential decisions.

That balance only holds when organizations can set the rules for their agents, understand what those agents are doing and protect them from being turned against the business. AI usage and adoption at machine speed rests on three tenets: governance, visibility and security.

Governance starts with decision rights. Before an agent touches production, define what it may do by itself: Execute a specific fix, isolate an endpoint or revoke a user session. Then define how it acts within these rights.

Tie that authority to the criticality of what the agent touches. An agent quarantining an entry-level employee’s laptop is probably a non-event; an agent taking a payment server offline is a disruption you created yourself. Adaptive guardrails scale an agent’s freedom to the stakes, with a human in the loop exactly where the stakes demand one.

Every good crew still has someone who calls the big moves. In the campaign Anthropic disrupted, humans stepped in at only a handful of decision points, such as approving active exploitation and deciding how much data to take. If attackers reserve their biggest calls for people, defenders should be at least as deliberate.

But this must be ongoing. Due to the speed of agentic advancement, guardrails reviewed once a quarter are out of date before the meeting ends.​

No heist crew moves before it cases the target. Treat agents like the workforce they are, each with an identity, an owner and a budget. Few leaders can list every agent running in their environment, the privileges each one holds, the data it can reach, the actions it is authorized to take and what it costs to run.

JadePuffer showed the stakes. Its way in was an AI development tool: an internet-facing Langflow server with a flaw patched more than a year earlier. The agent mined it for stored credentials and hunted for keys to commercial AI services, which let attackers run their agents on someone else’s bill. Every AI tool an organization stands up is both an asset and an attack surface.

Visibility also means seeing how findings connect. A vulnerability scanner may flag one weakness, an identity tool another and the security operations center a third, without anyone noticing that together they form a viable attack path.

The key metric here is time-to-engage: the time from the first meaningful signal to active investigation or containment.

Heist movies always need an insider, and every agent you deploy could become one, too.

Instructions hidden in an email, document or web page can turn an agent into a super-agent with broad access. You need to secure and manage agents like the privileged users they are, with least-privilege credentials, monitored access to tools and data and defenses against hidden instructions.

Then you need to secure the stack that builds and runs them. AI frameworks, model connectors and agent platforms are reaching production faster than most patching and review processes can follow. Hold them to production standards: Patch them promptly, keep them off the open internet unless they need to be there and review every new agent connection before it goes live.

Layered defense still works. DIVD said network segmentation and its incident responders kept the attacker from going deeper, and the attack was loud and messy enough to spot. Agentic attackers are fast. They lose to defenders able to watch and contain at machine speed.

AI will keep accelerating, and attackers will keep assembling their own crews. The organizations that come out ahead will treat governance, visibility and security as the foundation for moving fast: deciding what agents may do on their own, knowing every one that is running and protecting them like the privileged workforce they are.

Some of the best Southwest redemptions are only available if you hold one of the airline’s credit cards.

In a world of transferable points currencies, you might not think holding an airline or hotel credit card is necessary. But travel brands are pushing back against that narrative, offering exclusive perks and redemption packages to those who carry their cards.

Take Southwest Airlines, for example. Its Rapid Rewards loyalty program allows you to redeem points for flights, but it also offers a special program called Rapid Rewards Access Events exclusively for Southwest credit cardholders. In exchange for a decent chunk of points, you can get a vacation package that’s worth significantly more than the price you pay. Instead of a traditional flight award redemption, you get a cohesive travel experience.

"Experiences create lifetime memories,” says Nandika Suri, Southwest’s vice president of Rapid Rewards. “For us, we really want them to have great memories and remember our brand as part of that.”

Southwest invited me to participate in one of its Rapid Rewards Access Events. While Southwest covered the cost of my trip, these opinions are my own. Here’s what I learned.

Every event is different (ranging from concerts to multiday trips), but big-ticket Rapid Rewards Access Events tend to include flights, hotel accommodations, meals and excursions.

The event I participated in was in Maui to celebrate the 30th anniversary of Southwest and Chase’s partnership. This was a bigger production than the typical event, with about 60 cardholders (and a plus one) participating. A typical multiday event might have 20 or 25 packages for sale.

In exchange for 275,000 Rapid Rewards points, cardholders received for themselves and one guest:

A four-night stay in an ocean-view room at the Grand Wailea, a Waldorf Astoria Resort, in Maui, including daily breakfast.

Ground transportation between the airport and the resort, as well as for any scheduled group activities.

A special welcome reception and farewell dinner.

A snorkeling cruise with lunch and beverages included.

A choice between several excursions, including a spa treatment, golf, ziplining and more.

Even at extremely conservative estimates, I would value all of those things at roughly $4,600. That’s $750 more than what NerdWallet values 275,000 Rapid Rewards points at, according to our 2026 data. If we took a more liberal approach, I think it would be fair to say the package was worth more than $7,000. That puts this redemption between 1.7 and 2.5 cents per point. (Expand the section below to see how I arrived at those numbers.)

As of 2026, NerdWallet values Southwest Rapid Rewards points at 1.4 cents apiece. That puts the 275,000-point Southwest event package at $3,850.

Let’s put some numbers to the package inclusions and see how the points price stacks up to the cash valuation.

$1,000 Southwest gift card: It’s pretty easy to value a $1,000 Southwest gift card at $1,000. You need to fly to the event, so that can be taken at face value. (You could also use it toward a different trip, if you wanted to use points or fly with a different carrier.)

Four-night hotel stay: For the Grand Wailea stay, a nonrefundable Hilton Honors discount rate for an ocean-view room on the exact same dates in 2027 costs $4,490.19, after factoring in taxes and fees. (The base-level terrace-view room would cost $3,992.17.)

If you were to use points, a standard room without an ocean view would cost 130,000 Hilton points per night. An ocean-view room’s rate shoots up to 281,000 Hilton points per night.

Using NerdWallet’s 2026 valuation of Hilton points at 0.4 cent per point, that puts the value of the two rooms at $2,080 and $4,496, respectively. To make things interesting, let’s say the hotel stay is worth $2,080.

Daily breakfast at the hotel buffet is about $60 per person, before tax and tip. For four days, let’s put that at around another $500, bringing the total stay value to $2,580.

Ground transportation: Let’s make things simple and just say it’s $30 each way between the airport and the resort. For two people, that would be worth $120.

Welcome reception and farewell dinner: Southwest and Chase put a lot of effort into making these events nice, from the food and free-flowing alcohol to the entertainment (there was even a fire performance at the farewell dinner).

I would value this at $50 per person, conservatively, or $200 total.

Snorkeling cruise: I went on Viator to find a similar experience, and the cheapest option I found was priced at $100 per person.

Again, let’s price it conservatively and say it’s worth $200. That price doesn't include hotel transportation, gratuities, towels or alcoholic beverages, while the Southwest package did.

Excursion choice: Southwest let everyone choose an excursion, ranging from a chill pool or spa day to ziplining through the jungle or learning to surf.

It’s hard to put a number on this, because the activities varied in cost.

I went ziplining, and it was $240 for six lines. That price doesn’t include transportation to the excursion, which was covered by Southwest. Meanwhile, a standard massage at the hotel spa is $275 (and that doesn’t even factor in the 20% service charge).

Let’s put this at $250 per person, giving us a round $500 for two people’s excursions.

Grand total: Summing up these numbers gets us $4,600. That’s $750 more than the $3,850 NerdWallet values 275,000 points at, but keep in mind that we probably undervalued several of the inclusions. The actual value of a trip like this could be much higher.

It also doesn’t factor in other things, like snacks provided at the hospitality booth, as well as surprise gifts and goodie bags prepared by Southwest and Chase for attendees.

Before you book a Rapid Rewards Access Event, there are some drawbacks to booking a vacation this way.

The biggest one is if you don’t like group trips or following a schedule on your vacations. Given the nature of these events, you’ll be surrounded by a group of travelers, many of whom will likely be longtime Southwest flyers. If you prefer to keep to yourself, then this type of trip is likely not a good fit.

You’ll also have multiple scheduled activities on your itinerary. While you can choose to not show up, those activities add a lot of value to the trip.

With that said, I found the itinerary quite laid back. The amount of scheduled activities wasn’t overwhelming, and there was plenty of free time to do whatever you wanted. One couple I met even rented a car and explored Maui in their downtime, so they kept themselves busy.

These events are extremely popular, and many attendees I met at the Maui event had been on multiple Southwest cardmember trips.

Scoring a ticket to a Rapid Rewards Access Event might even require setting your alarm for when tickets drop. Several cardmembers told me they’ve experienced times when the event they wanted was sold out in hours, if not minutes. (The Maui one took a few hours to sell out, because it was larger than most.)

Finally, 275,000 points is a lot — even if you're getting great value. If your Rapid Rewards points are collecting dust in your account, then it could make sense. But if you have a transferable currency, then you'd have to weigh whether you might get better value elsewhere, such as booking round-trip business class flights.

Southwest isn’t the only airline or travel brand to offer special events for cardholders. United Airlines has MileagePlus Exclusives and United Card Events from Chase; Delta Air Lines offers cardmember-exclusive redemptions in its SkyMiles Experiences program; and Marriott has its Marriott Bonvoy Moments program.

But every redemption option is different — even if it’s within the same loyalty program. For example, some Rapid Rewards Access Events are packages you can purchase immediately for a set price, while others are auction-style listings. Some programs offer paid experiences, so you can only pay in cash, not points.

Personally, I’m a fan of the fixed-price points option. You know the upfront price, and you don’t have to worry about getting into a last-minute bidding war that could lead you to paying more than you intended. Plus, Southwest has historically had limited award redemption options, although that will change in 2027 when it allows international partner award bookings.

Ultimately, whether you think a Rapid Rewards Access Event is a worthwhile redemption will depend on your interests, and Southwest is working to expand its offerings to meet people’s passions.

"We do offer a lot of breadth because we want to get different types of customers engaged with different types of things based on their individual passion points and what they're really interested in,” says Suri, the Rapid Rewards chief.

If you’d rather spend time in the mountains than on the beach, you might not want to spend 275,000 Rapid Rewards points on the Maui package.

Instead, you probably would've been interested in the 250,000-point package for "Boots, Bourbon and Bonfires" — a three-day trip to Devil's Thumb Ranch, an upscale dude ranch resort about 1.5 hours outside of Denver.

Before you book, just remember: You’ll need a Southwest credit card to purchase.

#3058. If I Could Buy Only 1 Dividend Stock With $1,000 Before 2027, It Would Be This One

There are several good ones to choose from right now, but the factors holding this one back should begin abating soon.

By James Brumley – Nov 19, 2026 at 2:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Realty Income ›

Attempting to perfectly time your entry into a new trade usually isn't worth the effort. If you've got the capital available and are happy enough with the price, in most instances you're better off just diving in once you've made your pick.

Every now and then, though, an overlooked opportunity surfaces. This is one of those times. If you're looking for a new income-generating investment for your portfolio, consider Realty Income (O -1.19%) before the end of the year while its forward-looking dividend yield is 5.6%. Here's why.

Realty Income isn't a conventional company. It's a real estate investment trust, or REIT. That just means it owns a portfolio of revenue-bearing real estate, such as apartment complexes, office buildings, and the like, and passes along the majority of its profits to shareholders as dividends (though sometimes these payments are called distributions). REITs typically yield in the same ballpark as longer-term bonds, although like bonds, these yields can vary widely with quality.

Even by REIT standards, however, Realty Income is unique. Its specialty is brick-and-mortar retailing, with its top tenants including Dollar General, 7-Eleven, Walgreens, and Walmart. It owns 357 million square feet of consumer-facing space, divided across more than 15,000 storefronts, collectively worth $83 billion and generating about $5.4 billion in annual rent payments.

At first blush, it feels risky. The ongoing growth of e-commerce is still chipping away at in-person shopping. Coresight Research expects about 8,000 U.S. store closures this year alone, versus around 5,500 new store openings, extending a multi-year streak of net losses.

Realty Income is largely sidestepping this headwind, though. Give credit to the quality of its tenants. Once outfits like Walgreens, Home Depot, and Walmart incur the time, trouble, and expense of establishing a new location, they tend to stay put, holding out for a return on their investment. And unlike many smaller retailers, these bigger and better-known names have the financial wherewithal to continue making their rent payments.

To this end, this REIT's occupancy rate is consistently right around 99%, supporting a monthly -- yes, monthly -- dividend payment that's not only been paid like clockwork for over 50 years but has also been raised every year for the past 31 years.

It's an impressive pedigree. But shares of this REIT certainly haven't performed as well as you might have expected them to of late. This ticker's barely up year to date and is still barely above its pre-COVID-pandemic peak.

What gives? There's never a single perfect cut-and-dried reason a stock performs as it does. In this instance, though, there are a couple of key contributing factors.

One of these factors is interest rates. They've been up since the current bull market began in late 2022, in an effort to curb inflation resulting from the stimulus injected into the economy during and because of the coronavirus pandemic. Although real estate investment trusts can typically pass their own higher borrowing costs along to tenants, it's not clear how well Realty Income would manage the $26.5 billion in longer-term debt already on its balance sheet while adding more debt to continue expanding. Investors have erred on the side of caution by avoiding the stock.

The other factor at play here is the economic environment. The cost of everything continues to rise, eating away at consumers' confidence and buying power. Assuming this translates into a headwind for Realty Income, the market's been cautious.

The two underpinnings of this caution may have already run their full cyclical course, however, setting the stage for a turnaround sooner rather than later.

As for interest rates, although a quarter-point increase in the fed funds rate is practically a certainty for December, this is largely already priced in. This may also be the last of any rate hikes for a while. As of September, the Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee, along with several analysts, still expect interest rates to begin inching lower again next year, easing some of Realty Income's borrowing pain.

And as for the economic backdrop, sure, everything remains expensive, and unmanageable debt is increasingly becoming a very real problem. The New York Federal Reserve recently reported that overall loan delinquency rates moved up 30 basis points to 5% during the third quarter of this year, led by mortgages and auto loans.

Now take a closer look at all of the data. While there's no denying some consumers are miserable, there's also no denying that the nation's unemployment rate of 4.1% is healthy, and retail spending continues to reach record-breaking levels. Coming up with discretionary spending money isn't a problem for most households right now.

But what about any of this makes Realty Income a buy before 2027? I suspect the market's going to start seeing -- and accepting -- these two realities before 2026 comes to a close. More specifically, I believe investors will start to recognize that, rather than slipping into the recession many people fear is brewing, the economy will be able to navigate past this weird headwind with minimal fuss.

That doesn't mean Realty Income’s shares will only climb from here. Indeed, if the broad market's recent weakness is the beginning of a full-scale (and overdue) correction, this ticker will almost certainly be dragged lower with it. That dip would be your pre-2027 buying opportunity.

Even if that dip doesn't materialize and this stock instead drifts back into bullish mode again with other stocks, the longer-term bullish argument still stands. The market can't ignore that this REIT's top and bottom lines both continue to improve despite the troubling economic rhetoric. I can see this acceptance taking shape before the end of the year.

#3057. ​The Escalation Trap: AI Can Free You Or Finish You

A Futurist and AI expert, he leads KŌSE Advisory, advises ODI Global and GLOBSEC, and is a key analyst on tech, geopolitics and value chains.

In 1519, conquistador Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with 500 men, hell-bent on conquering the Aztec empire. Wary of his crew’s commitment, Cortés ordered his ships scuttled, foreclosing any retreat to Cuba. His men had two choices: surge forward or die where they stood. They chose the former. Within two years, they had conquered the Aztec capital of Tenochtitlán.

But human psychology can just as easily flip toward panic and paralysis. Take the fall of Singapore in 1942. Knowing the island was indefensible, London still rushed in reinforcements to force a prolonged siege. But it proved a futile effort. When Japanese forces crossed over quickly, 80,000 British and Commonwealth troops surrendered.

Escalating geopolitical tensions often appear binary: Leaders must choose between doubling down or giving up. But this is a false paradigm. (Even Cortés eventually ended up mired in legal battles, stripped of both political influence and fortune.) Ultimately, both are losing options.

There is now a third choice: AI. But it’s a double-edged sword. Applied with discipline, AI gives you control over the ambiguity driving every crisis. Applied carelessly, it accelerates the escalation.

In my previous article, I discussed the Casino Doctrine: the idea that the world is already at war without declaring it, and power belongs to whoever controls the uncertainty. A prime example of controlled ambiguity is the “Is it open or is it closed?” tension in the Strait of Hormuz, where one side holds the cards, forcing everyone else to guess what’s happening.

In failed ambiguity, like the Russia-Ukraine war, the bluff has been called, the cards are face up and uncertainty is no longer a weapon.

The escalation trap is the slide from that calculated tension into open conflict. Every player bets to keep leverage, and each move that fails to deter invites a bigger raise until the table flips. Navigating that spiral requires mastering two forces: disruptive power (fast, asymmetric strikes like drones hitting Russian oil infrastructure) and structural power (the slow-built control over global thoroughfares like the Panama Canal or Peru’s Chancay port, and Beijing’s near-monopoly over the world’s rare-earth supply).

When disruptive power attacks structural chokepoints, ambiguity collapses fast. Because geopolitics, supply chains and economics now sit at the exact same table, an escalation in one shakes them all—and there is no house enforcing the rules.

Why do capable leaders walk into the escalation trap? Because most never align the two kinds of power they need to survive. Ideology builds structural power: alliances, values, long-term commitments. Pragmatism yields disruptive power: fast, cheap, tactical moves that win the round. Oscillating between the two gets you the worst of both. Every pragmatic bet wins a hand but erodes the structural position; every ideological stance without pragmatism hardens into rigidity. True control means using tactical disruption to build, rather than hollow out, lasting structure, but few leaders manage this tightrope walk.

In a previous article, I wrote about Machiavelli’s advice that neutrality is a liability and choosing a side beats hesitating. For business leaders, hesitation breeds internal friction and confusion over priorities. That hesitation is the exact gap through which operational control slips, one undeclared escalation at a time.

For company leaders, what makes the geopolitical escalation ladder a trap isn’t the measurable risk you can price. Rather, it is uncontrolled ambiguity about what is actually happening on the ground. Is a strait officially closed or just too dangerous to cross? Is a new toll a routine fee or a covert blockade? Is a military drill a bluff or a rehearsal? Meanwhile, insurance premiums creep up, tankers go dark, ports are struck ... and yet no one declares war.

At each rung of that ladder, corporate leaders traditionally face two losing moves: surrendering by pulling up stakes and moving supply chains into the next region’s crisis, or scrambling to react after the market has already priced in the shock.

True control requires a different approach—not eliminating global uncertainty, but outthinking it before the rest of the market sees the cards. That is where trusted, sovereign, domain-specific AI changes the paradigm, using foresight analytics to drive the optimal decision before your competitors do.

AI began as a disruptive power, making work faster and cheaper. Today, it is evolving into a structural power, reshaping economies, national GDPs and societal norms simultaneously. I call this omnichange: the moment one technology transforms every layer of the system, accelerated by superintelligence and operational Darwinism.

To leverage it, leaders must answer two questions: What values guide your AI, and how fast can you deploy it? Answer both, and you turn disruption into lasting structure; answer only one, and you cede control.

Making that shift requires building domain-specific intelligence in disciplined stages, anchored by clear human accountability. To paraphrase Machiavelli, fortune is a river in flood that prudent leaders channel with dykes built in calm weather. Superintelligence will be either the dyke or the flood, and governance is what determines which.

Stockpiles decay; intelligence compounds. Winning in an era of gray-zone conflict requires every leader at the table to act right now:

• CEOs: Settle the ideology question today, for good. Define what you stand for, which allies you build with and what your AI is for.

• Chief Procurement Officers: No supplier, chip or cloud is neutral. Choose your intelligence stack as you would a geopolitical ally.

• Chief Supply Chain Officers: Pre-price alternative routes, and give AI agents audited, bounded authority to reroute before shocks hit.

• Boards: Govern AI as structural power, not an IT project. Keep humans accountable, and set clear stop-losses on every market and pilot.

Systems built for already-declared wars lose control first—and when they fail, developing economies pay the steepest price. The real question isn’t who stockpiles the most resources but who governs omnichange.

We are in a dangerous window. But a window is also an opening. Leaders who act decisively—and keep human accountability at the center of AI—will turn omnichange into lasting structural power. Those who wait for calm will find that the seats at the table are already taken.

As we say in Turkish, “Kurt dumanlı havayı sever“—the wolf loves foggy weather. How you govern AI will decide whether you are the wolf or the prey.​
